paragraphs.text: Striking the Amalekites: fighting the Amalekites.

Ziklag: a city lying in the south of the land of the tribe of Judah, then given to the tribe of Simeon. Afterwards the Philistines took it, then Achish, king of the Philistines, returned it to the children of Israel. When David was away from it, the Amalekites attacked it and burned it, so David fought them, recovered it and took much spoil, and he stayed in it to restore it. The camp: the encampments of the soldiers of the children of Israel during the war.

The First Book of Samuel ended by mentioning two events: David's victory over the Amalekites and his recovery of the spoil and the captives, and the other event, the death of Saul and his sons in his war against the Philistines. The beginning of the Second Book completes for us the sequence of these events. It mentions that after David returned to Ziklag and stayed in it two days, on the third day a stranger came from the battlefield of the Philistines with Saul, his clothes torn and earth upon his head, a sign of great grief, whether it was real grief or feigned, to give those he met the impression that he was pained by the news he carried. This man came to David and bowed down before him to honor him, and perhaps he hoped to gain a position with David by announcing to him the death of his enemy Saul.
It is noticed that David did not send to learn the news of the war, lest anyone think that he wished for Saul's death and was eager to obtain the kingdom. Indeed, he was not eager for that.
David asked him where he had come from, and he told him that he had escaped from the camp of Israel to save his life.

David knew of the battle that had taken place between the children of Israel and the Philistines, the battle in which Achish's men had prevented him from taking part (see 1 Sam 29:4). So he asked him eagerly what had happened in the war, and the man answered him that the fighters of Israel had fled from the field because they could not stand firm before the armies of the Philistines, and many of them had fallen dead, and Saul and Jonathan his son had also died. The man meant to bring David the good news that King Saul and Jonathan the crown prince had died and that he himself had become king. We note that David knew that the Spirit of God had departed from Saul and that he was exposed to death in this war, yet he did not send messengers to learn the result of the war, lest anyone think that he was seeking Saul's death in order to reign in his place.

To make sure of the death of Saul and Jonathan, David asked the man how he knew that they had died, because he loved them and wished that the news were untrue and that what the man had heard were mere rumor.
"As I happened": by chance, that is, this man was not one of the soldiers fighting with the children of Israel, but was passing by chance on this mountain where the battle took place.
Mount Gilboa: the north-eastern part of Mount Ephraim, lying between the River Kishon and the valley of the Jordan. It rises about 500 meters above the sea and has narrow valleys within it.

The man made him understand that he learned of it by chance, as he was on Mount Gilboa where the battle between the two armies took place, and he saw Saul leaning on his spear and the Philistine warriors coming toward him to kill him. (Up to here the man's account agrees with what is in 1 Sam 31.)

From here on the man's testimony differs from what the inspired text relates in (1 Sam 31:4), for the man claims that Saul, as he was looking behind him, saw him and called him, and the man answered and came to him. The truth is that Saul spoke with his armor-bearer and not with this man; he is lying to show David that he killed his enemy Saul, so that he might receive a reward from him.

The man went on with his claims about what had happened, and mentioned that Saul asked him who he was, and he answered him that he was an Amalekite, and perhaps he had lived among the children of Israel and joined them.
The man claimed that Saul asked him to come near and thrust him through with the sword, because he felt dizzy, though he was still alive.
(This conversation had taken place between Saul and his armor-bearer, as is recorded in (1 Sam 31:4), but the Amalekite falsely claimed that Saul's words were addressed to him.)
"I stood upon him": I came near him after he had fallen to the ground.

The man continued in his lie, saying that he did come near to Saul and killed him, justifying it by saying that he saw Saul's severe wounds and that he would surely die. He took the crown that was on Saul's head and the gold bracelet that was on his arm and brought them to David, thinking that David would be pleased with the news of Saul's death and would reward the man for this good news. He did not invent a story showing that he had killed Jonathan, because he knew that David loved Jonathan and did not want to provoke David's anger over the killing of Jonathan.

Some think that Saul's armor-bearer was Doeg the Edomite, and that this Amalekite man was his son, because Amalek was descended from Edom, and that Doeg was the one who killed Saul, as is mentioned in (1 Sam 31:4), and he sent Saul's crown and bracelet with his son to David to bring him the news, and then killed himself out of grief for his master Saul.
The impact of the news upon David was very painful, contrary to what the Amalekite had expected. David and his men grieved, and all of them tore their clothes as a sign of great sorrow.
David did not gloat over Saul's death, although Saul had pursued him all his life. This is evidence of David's forgiveness, the purity of his heart and his love for his enemies.

The men mourned the dead with sorrowful words, and wept aloud and fasted until evening, seeking the mercies of the Lord for the souls of the dead. Their grief was great for Saul their king, for Jonathan the brave and faithful friend of David, and for the people of the Lord who had been killed in the war.
David asked the man who had come to him with this heartbreaking news where he was from, and the man answered him that he was the son of a stranger, an Amalekite.

David rebuked the man for his boldness in killing Saul, and asked how he was not afraid to stretch out his hand against the Lord's anointed, who had been anointed with the holy oil, when the Lord has warned against this, as in (Ps 105:15), "Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm."
"Fell upon him": killed him.
"Thy blood be upon thy head": bear your guilt.

David commanded one of his young men to kill the Amalekite, and the young man did so. His killing was the recompense for his killing of Saul, as he confessed himself, when David told him that he bore the punishment for what he had done. This was the first case in which David judged as king after the death of Saul, and it shows his justice and his love for his enemies.

Do not rejoice at the misfortunes of those who wrong you, but have compassion on them, pray for them, make excuses for them in their wrongs against you, and look at their virtues so that you may love them. Then you will be able to stretch out a helping hand to them in their afflictions.

entries.section: (2) His lament for them

paragraphs.text: This lament was an eloquent literary work to mourn Saul and Jonathan his son. David did not gloat over Saul's death, but grieved greatly over his death.

entries.section: (2) His lament for them

paragraphs.text: Bow: a flexible metal rod with a string of leather tied between its two ends, so that it bends into the shape of an arc. The arrow is placed between the string and the bow, the bow is pushed forward and the string drawn back, and the arrow is aimed at the target; then the string is released and the arrow flies to its mark.
Book: a writing.

Jasher: its meaning is upright or righteous, and it means that it is a book for recording the deeds of the heroes of the children of Israel. It is a historical book and not one of the books of the Holy Bible, and in it were written the accounts of Joshua's victory over the five kings (Josh 10:13), and they are an abbreviation of the name Jeshurun, that is, beloved Israel.

David commanded that the children of Judah learn this song, which was called "the song of the bow," because the bow was one of the weapons of war in that time and signifies valor and skill in those wars, which are the qualities the song highlighted. And because Jonathan excelled in the use of the bow and arrows, and David loved Jonathan very much, he called the lament the song of the bow. The purpose of preserving the song was to perpetuate the memory of Saul, Jonathan and the brave warriors. The song was taught first to the children of Judah as the tribe of David, and afterwards all the tribes learned it.

entries.section: (2) His lament for them

paragraphs.text: The roe: the male gazelle, which leads the herd and is distinguished by courage and leadership.
Your high places: your heights.

David likens both Jonathan and Saul to the gazelle for their swiftness of movement and courage in fighting, and he mourns them because they were killed on Mount Gilboa, the lofty mountain, just as they themselves were great and lofty in their lives. David marvels at the fall of the heroes of Israel in this war, they who had always been victorious in all the previous wars.

entries.section: (2) His lament for them

paragraphs.text: In his poem David calls on them not to spread the news of Israel's defeat in the cities of the Philistines such as Gath and Ashkelon, nor in their streets, where people gather in crowds and news travels quickly, lest the women and daughters of the Philistines rejoice and gloat over the death of Saul and his soldiers. He called them "daughters of the uncircumcised" because they are a people foreign to the Lord who did not enter into a covenant with Him by circumcision. He chose Gath because it is the largest of the Philistine cities, and he chose Ashkelon because it has the largest temples of the goddess Ashtaroth. Perhaps the Philistines had sent the weapons of Saul and Jonathan to the temples of Ashkelon to show the power of their gods, who had won the victory in the war (1 Sam 31:10).

entries.section: (2) His lament for them

paragraphs.text: The shield: the large shield, a piece of wood covered with leather to ward off arrows from the warrior's body.

The mountains of Gilboa were the places where the soldiers and heroes of Israel fell, so David called down drought upon them, that neither rain nor dew would water them, and that no crops would grow in them from which tithes and offerings might be presented, so that the blessing would be removed from them. David explains the reason for his curse upon the place, because Saul, Jonathan and the rest of the heroes died there, and their weapons were cast down upon it, among them the large shield belonging to King Saul, which was anointed with the holy oil (as commanders were accustomed to do with their weapons in order to receive a blessing), and this holy anointing was lost through its being cast upon the ground, and every trace of the holy oil was gone.

entries.section: (2) His lament for them

paragraphs.text: In all their previous victories David remembers the valor and boldness of Saul and Jonathan, and their weapons that shed the blood of the enemies and brought down the bodies of their mighty soldiers. In all those wars Jonathan never turned back as cowards do, and his sword reaped the heads of the enemies in all the rounds of battle and never failed in any of them.

All the words that David said about Saul were words of praise in which he mentioned his good qualities and did not mention his wrongdoings. If someone sins against us, may we remember his virtues and not the mistakes he fell into.

entries.section: (2) His lament for them

paragraphs.text: The people loved and were attached to the leadership and kingship of Saul and of his son, the crown prince Jonathan, and the two of them also loved their people and worked to fulfill its hopes.

Saul and Jonathan lived clinging to one another and were not separated, neither in peace nor in war. As they were side by side in their lives, so they were also in their deaths. Both were lighter and swifter in movement than eagles, and stronger than lions in strength and courage in wars.

entries.section: (2) His lament for them

paragraphs.text: Scarlet: a dark red color, and scarlet clothes were the clothes of kings and the rich. David calls on the women of Israel to weep for Saul, whose reign was a reign of prosperity and ease, in which the women enjoyed the finest clothes, the beautiful royal red clothes, and wore ornaments of gold.

entries.section: (2) His lament for them

paragraphs.text: He returns and marvels at the death of the mighty men Saul and Jonathan, and especially his friend Jonathan, who died on the mountains of Gilboa.

entries.section: (2) His lament for them

paragraphs.text: David shows his deep grief over the death of his friend, whom he considered closer to him than a brother, so that his death was like a great shock that shook him to the depths. Jonathan's dealings with David had been exceedingly gentle and sweet, and David returned to him feelings of affection and love, so that their friendship became a proverb. Indeed, their love for one another was stronger and more wonderful than the love of a woman for a man, for it was free of every ulterior motive, an innocent and self-sacrificing love, each preferring the other to himself. Jonathan had served David by rescuing him from his father Saul, and David wanted to repay Jonathan's kindness when he became king, but sadly Jonathan died in the war with Saul, and David had no opportunity to express his love for Jonathan except by this lament, though David also tried to honor Jonathan's sons, such as Mephibosheth (ch. 9).

entries.section: (2) His lament for them

paragraphs.text: David returns once more and repeats his marvel at the death of the mighty men Saul and Jonathan, and asks in astonishment how the weapons lost their effectiveness in the war, so that their effect vanished as if they had melted away. Thus we find David mentioning Saul's virtues and forgetting his sins, because David is characterized by a simple outlook and by love even toward those who are hostile to him.
The clash between Abner and Joab

entries.section: (1) David's reign over Judah and his blessing of Jabesh Gilead

paragraphs.text: Hebron: a city in the land of Judah built on the mountains and easy to defend. It was originally called "Kirjath-arba," and Hebron had villages dependent on it, and it was one of the cities of refuge. It is one of the oldest cities in the world and lies 30 km south-west of Jerusalem. It is now the city of Hebron (al-Khalil), and in it is the cave of Machpelah, in which Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and their families were buried.

With the death of Saul, David found that there was no point in his remaining in Ziklag and that it was better for him to return to his homeland and his people. But as was his custom, he took no decision except after inquiring of the Lord, so he asked Him whether he should go up to one of the cities of Judah, and the Lord answered him yes. Then he asked to which city he should go, and the Lord answered him that he should go to Hebron. We see here David seeking God before everything, in peace as in war, because he had become accustomed to seek Him always.

Take care to seek God's counsel before any work, and God will answer you in different ways, such as through your father of confession, or through the Holy Bible, or in any other way. Whatever you desire in the matter, make sure through prayer that God agrees to it.

entries.section: (1) David's reign over Judah and his blessing of Jabesh Gilead

paragraphs.text: David went up to Hebron with his two wives Ahinoam and Abigail, who had been the widow of Nabal the Carmelite. As for his wife Michal, the daughter of Saul, she was still with Phalti, to whom Saul had given her (1 Sam 25:44).

entries.section: (1) David's reign over Judah and his blessing of Jabesh Gilead

paragraphs.text: David cared for his companions who had accompanied him during Saul's pursuit of him, so he brought them and their households to Hebron and the cities and villages dependent on it.

entries.section: (1) David's reign over Judah and his blessing of Jabesh Gilead

paragraphs.text: Jabesh Gilead: a city on Mount Gilead east of the Jordan, now called "Wadi Yabis." It seems that they had a strong relationship with the tribe of Benjamin, from which King Saul came, for they did not join the tribes of Israel in fighting against this tribe when it sinned in the matter of the Levite's concubine (Judg 20, 21), and now they care for Saul's body, and Saul may have cared for them during his reign.

The elders of the tribe of Judah gathered to David in Hebron as representatives of the tribe and proclaimed him king over their tribe. These elders knew that David had already been anointed by Samuel during Saul's lifetime, so it was natural that he be installed officially after the death of Saul.

The men of Judah told David of what the people of Jabesh Gilead had done, an action that showed courage and loyalty, for they risked their lives and went to where the bodies of Saul and his sons were and took them down from the wall of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them to disgrace them (1 Sam 31:10-12), and carried them to their city, where they buried them.
Thus David was anointed king in three stages:
1- He was anointed king secretly in the house of his father Jesse by the hand of Samuel (1 Sam 16:13).
2- He was anointed king over the tribe of Judah in this verse.
3- He was anointed king over all the tribes of the children of Israel (ch. 5:3). In this he is a type of Christ, who was anointed king three times:
1- From eternity (1 Tim 6:15, Rev 17:14).
2- On the Cross, by paying the debt that was upon us, He reigned over everyone who believes in Him and saved them from the hand of the devil.
3- In the Kingdom of Heaven, when He reigns forever over the hearts of those who believe in Him.

entries.section: (1) David's reign over Judah and his blessing of Jabesh Gilead

paragraphs.text: David sent a blessing and prayer for good to the people of Jabesh Gilead for what they had done with the bodies of Saul and his sons, and promised that he too would repay them for their kindness.

How beautiful that David began his reign by blessing and encouraging his people and not by blame or punishment. When a person begins his work or his meetings, it must be with gentleness and encouragement. Likewise, he made use of the enthusiasm of the people of Jabesh Gilead, who loved Saul the former king, and he did not reject them because Saul had been his enemy, but with wisdom he tried to win them in order to use their enthusiasm and energy in his new kingdom. It is good for a person to make use of all the energies around him, and with love to encourage everyone and win all.

entries.section: (1) David's reign over Judah and his blessing of Jabesh Gilead

paragraphs.text: David comforts them over the death of Saul and asks them to be strong like mighty men, and tells them that he has become king over the tribe of Judah, and perhaps by this he is inviting them to submit to him.

entries.section: (2) Ishbosheth's reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: Ishbosheth: the fourth son of Saul, who did not die in the war with the Philistines, while his other three brothers died. He is Eshbaal mentioned in (1 Chr 8:33), and the name was changed to Ishbosheth because of their hatred of the name Baal, which is a pagan god.

Mahanaim: the meaning of its name is two camps, and it lies east of the Jordan and north of the River Jabbok. There Jacob saw the host of angels and called it Mahanaim, referring to two camps, that is, his wives and children and the host of angels. It lies on the border of the territory of Gad and Manasseh and is divided into two parts, one belonging to Gad and the other to Manasseh, and Gad's part was given to the children of Merari, so it became a city of refuge (Josh 21:38). Abner was seeking to keep his position as commander of the army, so when Saul was killed in the war he took Ishbosheth and came to the city of Mahanaim on the east bank of the Jordan, where he proclaimed him king over the rest of the tribes of Israel, and he took that town as the capital of the kingdom. Abner knew the weakness of Ishbosheth's character, as shown by Ishbosheth's not taking part with his father in the battle against the Philistines, or perhaps he fled from the battle, and so Abner would become the real head of the kingdom, especially as he was a relative of King Saul, being his cousin (1 Sam 14:50). Thus Abner began to be hostile to David after he became king, and he wanted to seize Judah also, as shown by his fighting against it several times throughout the seven years in which David reigned in Hebron.

entries.section: (2) Ishbosheth's reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: Gilead: a city in the plains of Gilead east of the Jordan.
The Ashurites: what is meant is the tribe of Asher (the Asherites). Jezreel: a city in the mountains of Judah.

The kingdom of Ishbosheth included several regions, among them Gilead, the lands of Jezreel, the tribe of Asher, the tribe of Ephraim and the tribe of Benjamin, in addition to the rest of the tribes except the tribe of Judah.

entries.section: (2) Ishbosheth's reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: Ishbosheth was forty years old when he was proclaimed king over Israel, and he remained in his reign only two years, then he was killed by his servants as will come in (ch. 4), and the tribe of Judah did not submit to him, but remained steadfast in following David.

Ishbosheth was 35 years old at the death of Saul his father, and David remained king five years in Hebron, then Abner brought about this division when Ishbosheth reigned in Mahanaim. This division lasted only two years, so the kingdom is considered to extend through the days of Saul, David and Solomon, and the division took place after the death of Solomon.

entries.section: (2) Ishbosheth's reign over Israel

paragraphs.text: The capital of the kingdom of Judah, which was subject to David, was Hebron, where David reigned seven years and six months. (David's reign lasted forty years, of which seven years and six months were in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.)

Do not care for your own interest at the expense of those around you, setting up divisions and problems and disturbing others, for you will lose your own peace too, and it is the most important thing. Rather, seek peace with others as much as you can, and win those around you with love, so that you keep your peace even if the hearts of those around you have evil in them, because you are seeking the good.

entries.section: (3) War between Abner and Joab

paragraphs.text: Gibeon: a city about 8 km north of Jerusalem. The Gibeonites are the ones who deceived Joshua long ago and joined the children of Israel (Josh 10:6). After Abner made Ishbosheth king over all the tribes except Judah, he coveted taking Judah, so he declared war between himself and David's army, which was led by Joab, and they met at a pool beside Gibeon.

entries.section: (3) War between Abner and Joab

paragraphs.text: "Play": fight in single combat.

Abner called for a bloody duel between two groups of soldiers from the two armies, so that if one group won over the other, the king of the winning group would be king over all Israel, or perhaps he wanted to test the strength of the soldiers of Joab's army. (This event reminds us of what Goliath the Philistine proposed at the confrontation between the army of the Philistines and the army of Israel under Saul (1 Sam 17:8-11).)

entries.section: (3) War between Abner and Joab

paragraphs.text: Abner noticed the weakness of the two sides' inclination to fight, so he proposed choosing a team of twelve men from each side to carry out the duel, a team of the men of the tribe of Benjamin, subject to Ishbosheth, for Saul was of the tribe of Benjamin, and the other team of David's men, picked out from among the two armies in preparation for the confrontation.

entries.section: (3) War between Abner and Joab

paragraphs.text: Helkath-hazzurim: the field of swords, where the swords reaped the lives of the soldiers.

The commanders' proposal for the confrontation mentioned was a mad proposal with which the duelists of both sides were not convinced, so the encounter between them did not last long, for they agreed among themselves that each combatant would seize the head of the other and strike his fellow in his side, killing him quickly so that he would die without prolonged torment. That is, they did not duel, but each group killed the other, and the encounter in this form was a tragedy, so the place where its events took place was called "the field of the sword." Here we see the hardness of heart of Abner and Joab, who are like the Romans who loved the shedding of blood and made light of the lives of their followers. The soldiers of both sides felt that their lives had no value, so they agreed that each group would kill the other.

entries.section: (3) War between Abner and Joab

paragraphs.text: The duel produced no solution, for the twenty-four fighters of both sides fell without any display of fighting skill by either side to show the superiority of one side over the other. When the two armies saw that the matter had not been decided in this way, a fierce battle took place between them, which ended in the defeat of Abner's army before David's men.

entries.section: (3) War between Abner and Joab

paragraphs.text: Joab, Abishai and Asahel: the three commanders of David, who are the sons of "Zeruiah," David's sister on his mother's side.
"As a wild roe": the male gazelle that runs swiftly in the wilderness.

The inspired text tells us here of another tragedy that took place between Asahel, the brother of both Joab and Abishai, and Abner, the commander of Ishbosheth's army. The three brothers were leading David's companies, and Asahel was swift of foot like a gazelle, so he ran after Abner, turning neither to the right nor to the left, in order to overtake him and kill him. This was without consulting his two brothers, that is, it was a rash impulse on his part to deliver Judah and David from Abner.

Recklessness and rashness lead to needless pitfalls, for sometimes ambition that is not well considered brings misery and wretchedness to the one who rushes toward it without wisdom. Good intentions alone are not enough unless they are accompanied by wisdom and sound planning.

entries.section: (3) War between Abner and Joab

paragraphs.text: Abner looked behind him and saw the one who was following him in order to overtake him, and knew that it was Asahel, so he asked him in disapproval, "Art thou Asahel?" (The disapproval here is because he saw that Asahel by this deed was being rash and that this pride of his would not be to his benefit.)

entries.section: (3) War between Abner and Joab

paragraphs.text: "Take thee his armour": take spoil.

Abner advised him to look for a warrior who would be his equal in experience, so that he might fight with him and take spoil from him, and not expose himself to the danger of a duel with a trained commander, who was Abner himself, but Asahel refused the advice and continued his pursuit of Abner.

entries.section: (3) War between Abner and Joab

paragraphs.text: "Smite thee to the ground": kill you.
"How then should I hold up my face": I will be in a critical position in which I cannot defend my stand.

Abner repeated his advice to Asahel, asking him to stop pursuing him, or else he would face him and kill him in self-defense against his recklessness. He also made him understand that if he killed him, he would be blamed by his elder brother Joab and would not be able to justify his act before him. He was not afraid of Asahel, but he feared that he would kill him and a clash would occur between him and Joab.

entries.section: (3) War between Abner and Joab

paragraphs.text: The hinder end of the spear: the rear of the spear, the end of the shaft of the spear.

Asahel did not want to accept the advice and turn back, so Abner was compelled, in defense of himself, to face him and strike him in the belly until the shaft of the spear came out behind him, and he died on the spot. Everyone who passed the place where Asahel fell stood still, remembering this painful event of a brave young man in the prime of his life, dear to his brothers and to everyone. But Asahel erred in that he relied on his swiftness in running and did not rely on God, forgetting Abner's skill in war, so God allowed Abner to kill him.

entries.section: (4) The halting of the fighting

paragraphs.text: Joab and Abishai sought to pursue Abner to avenge their brother Asahel, whom Abner had killed, and the pursuit continued until sunset, and in their pursuit they had come to a hill near one of the villages of Benjamin on the way of the wilderness surrounding Gibeon, which is called the hill of Ammah.

entries.section: (4) The halting of the fighting

paragraphs.text: Abner's aim in reaching one of the villages of Benjamin was that the men of the children of Benjamin might join him to strengthen his army and reorganize its ranks. This is in fact what happened, for the men of Benjamin were eager to join him, defending out of their feelings Ishbosheth the king, who was of their own tribe.

entries.section: (4) The halting of the fighting

paragraphs.text: "The latter end": the end of the civil war, if it continues.

Abner warned Joab that if the war continued it would become a civil war in which many of the children of Israel would die, and he invited him to make peace. Abner did not call for the halting of the war except when a great number of his army had been killed and he himself was exposed to death, though he was the one who had begun it and made light of the lives of the soldiers whom he had asked to duel. So he is selfish, thinking of himself, and he made light of the lives of others.

entries.section: (4) The halting of the fighting

paragraphs.text: Joab swore to him that he was certain that the cause of this ill-fated war was his proposal, made in the morning of that same day, that two teams from the two sides should duel, for if he had not done that, the soldiers of both parties would have gone their own way and those futile battles would not have occurred. By this he held him responsible for this war.

entries.section: (4) The halting of the fighting

paragraphs.text: Joab responded to Abner's call despite his having laid the blame for the war on him, and blew the trumpets as a signal to the men to stop the fighting, so his men stopped pursuing the soldiers of the tribes of Israel, and the war between the two sides ended.

May you seek peace, and if a quarrel or enmity occurs with someone, take care to remove it in order to keep your peace and the peace of others. This is not weakness, but strength, to seek after peace.

entries.section: (4) The halting of the fighting

paragraphs.text: After the fighting, which took place west of the Jordan, stopped, Abner and his men marched all night in the desert lands west of the Jordan, then crossed the Jordan to its east bank and walked in the mountain passes until they reached the capital of Ishbosheth's kingdom, which is "Mahanaim."

entries.section: (4) The halting of the fighting

paragraphs.text: Joab also stopped pursuing Abner and his men, and a count was made of the two sides, and it was found that the number of dead from Joab's army was nineteen soldiers in addition to Asahel, while the loss in the men of Abner's army was much heavier, reaching three hundred and sixty dead. Joab agreed to stop the war because he knew David's desire to stop the civil war, and that he did not want to obtain the kingdom by fighting Ishbosheth and Abner, and also because David had promised Saul that he would preserve his descendants.

entries.section: (4) The halting of the fighting

paragraphs.text: Joab's soldiers carried the body of their brother Asahel and buried him in his father's tomb in Bethlehem, then continued their march all night until they reached Hebron, the residence of their king David, the next morning. Abner pledges allegiance to David as king

entries.section: (1) The names of David's sons

paragraphs.text: When David became king over the tribe of Judah, his position began to grow stronger, despite clashes between him and the rest of the tribes under the leadership of Abner. These clashes increased over five and a half years, and increased further after Abner made Ishbosheth the son of Saul king over the rest of the tribes for two years. But victory was David's, and his position grew stronger with the passing of the years, while on the contrary the followers of Ishbosheth gradually weakened, for the following reasons:
1- The weakness of Ishbosheth's character compared with Saul his father or Jonathan his brother.
2- The people's love for David and their admiration of him for his personality and his strength in wars, and their knowledge that he was the true king whom God had anointed.

3- David relied on God, while Ishbosheth and Abner depended on material strength. The clashes continued a long time because of Abner's stubbornness; on the other hand, David did not want to attack Ishbosheth and his descendants, because he had promised Saul his father not to cut off his descendants (1 Sam 24:20-22). Abner is a type of Satan, and David is a type of Christ and the children of God. Although the power of the devil seems enormous, represented by the ten tribes, God gives victory to His children and protects them, so their strength increases, while the end of the devil is eternal destruction. David waited seven and a half years until all the tribes submitted to him, preceded by many years since God's anointing in his father's house, yet David grew gradually stronger and greater. So do not be troubled if God's blessing or His answer to your requests is delayed, but hold fast to Him in spiritual striving by refusing sin and carrying out the commandment, for in the end you will receive many blessings and your relationship with God will grow stronger.

entries.section: (1) The names of David's sons

paragraphs.text: Polygamy was permitted in the Old Testament because of the immaturity of God's people, but in the New Testament God restored what He had established from the beginning of creation, namely the union of one man with one woman so that they become one flesh (Gen 2:24). David begot six sons from his several marriages during the period of his reign in Hebron, and the inspired text here gives us all their names. The first (the firstborn) was Amnon, who wronged his sister (ch. 13), and his brother Absalom killed him because of it (ch. 13:29), and his mother was Ahinoam of Jezreel, whom David married after Michal was taken from him.

entries.section: (1) The names of David's sons

paragraphs.text: Geshur: a city lying east of the Jordan between Hermon and Bashan.

The second son is "Chileab," whose name appears as "Daniel" in (1 Chr 3:1), and his mother was Abigail, who was known for wisdom and good conduct in the story of David with Nabal the Carmelite, and it seems that he died in David's lifetime. The third son is "Absalom," who tried to seize the kingdom from his father and fought him, and was killed, and David returned to his kingdom (chs. 15-19). He was the son of the daughter of the king of "Geshur," whom David married to strengthen his friendship with her father. She was a pagan, but perhaps she joined the faith after her marriage to David. Absalom was killed when he attacked his father David and his men (ch. 18:14, 15).

entries.section: (1) The names of David's sons

paragraphs.text: The fourth son is "Adonijah," who proclaimed himself king in the last part of his father's life (1 Kgs 1:11), as being the firstborn, since his elder brothers had all died, but his father appointed Solomon to succeed him on the throne. He was the son of Haggith. The fifth son is "Shephatiah the son of Abital," and no further details about him are given in the inspired text.

entries.section: (1) The names of David's sons

paragraphs.text: The sixth son is "Ithream by Eglah." No additional details about him are given in the inspired text either. All of these were born to David in Hebron, apart from those who were born to him afterwards in Jerusalem (1 Chr 3:5).

entries.section: (2) Abner's anger at Ishbosheth

paragraphs.text: "Made himself strong" for: was zealous for.

In the battles that broke out between the supporters of the house of Saul and the supporters of the house of David, Abner, the commander of Saul's army and his kinsman, defended his house bravely, trying to establish the kingdom for Ishbosheth the son of Saul.

entries.section: (2) Abner's anger at Ishbosheth

paragraphs.text: Rizpah the daughter of Aiah: Saul's concubine, who guarded the bodies of her two sons whom the Gibeonites hanged (ch. 21:8-11). Concubine: a female slave whom her master marries.

The system of concubines was in force in that era, and Saul had a concubine named "Rizpah," whom Abner tried to add to his concubines to strengthen his position and authority in the kingdom. When Ishbosheth learned of it he was displeased and rebuked Abner, because by this he had wronged Saul his father.

entries.section: (2) Abner's anger at Ishbosheth

paragraphs.text: A dog's head: the head of a dead dog, worthless.

Abner was greatly troubled by Ishbosheth's rebuke, for he considered it contempt for him, as though he were the head of a dead dog, and a false accusation by Ishbosheth that he was a supporter of David by his wronging the house of Saul in taking his concubine. He reminded Ishbosheth of his great deeds toward the house of Saul, from his leading the army in the days of Saul, then his making Ishbosheth king and defending him against David, so how could he demand of him today to return the concubine as if it were a sin and a great fault that Abner had committed. Perhaps Ishbosheth was afraid, when Abner married Saul's concubine, that Abner would set himself up as king, and this fear confirms that he was far from God and so thought evil of people.

It is noticed that Ishbosheth could not answer Abner with a single word, because he had become king by the power of Abner and not by the power of God. Whoever depends on people submits to them and they humiliate him, but whoever trusts in God remains strong however much people change.

entries.section: (2) Abner's anger at Ishbosheth

paragraphs.text: Dan: the new name which the tribe of Dan gave to "Laish" after they took the place, at the farthest northern border of the kingdom of Israel.
Beersheba: a city at the extreme south of Palestine, about 45 km south of Hebron.

Abner swore with the formula of imprecation common in that era, which means that the Lord should do evils to him if he did not carry out his decision to abandon Ishbosheth and support David, whom the Lord had chosen and anointed king in place of Saul, so that the kingdom would be transferred from the house of Saul and handed to David, to reign over all the tribes of Israel from the farthest north of the land to the farthest south.

Abner relied on his own strength in transferring the kingdom to David and forgot that he was merely a man and that God is the One who orders the lives of His children. So God used him and he agreed with David, but before David reigned over the tribes Abner died (v. 27). Power and ordering belong to God and not to weak human beings.

God permitted Ishbosheth's rebuke of Abner and Abner's anger at him so that the whole kingdom would be transferred to David. So do not be troubled by the strength of the wicked and their resistance to you, for however long it lasts, God is able to turn it at the right time to your good.

entries.section: (2) Abner's anger at Ishbosheth

paragraphs.text: Ishbosheth could not answer Abner because of his great fear of him, for he was the power that protected him, especially since Abner had threatened to take the kingdom from him.

entries.section: (3) David recovers Michal

paragraphs.text: "Whose is the land?": that is, the land of the tribes is under my authority, so says Abner.

"Saying, Make thy league with me": he declares that the people of the tribes said to Abner, "Would that you make a covenant with David so that we may follow him." The truth is that it was Abner who wanted to make a covenant with David to secure David's forgiveness of him and to become a follower and one of his commanders.

After Abner's anger at Ishbosheth, he decided to remove him from the kingship and make David king over all the tribes, so he sent to David declaring his readiness to make a covenant with him and to make him king over all the tribes.

entries.section: (3) David recovers Michal

paragraphs.text: "See my face": come to meet me.

David agreed to what Abner offered him, but he stipulated that Abner should not come to him to conclude the treaty until his first wife Michal was returned to him. Saul had taken her from him and given her as wife to Phalti the son of Laish (1 Sam 25:44).

entries.section: (3) David recovers Michal

paragraphs.text: David loved his wife Michal and desired her return as his wife, so he decided to send also to Ishbosheth, because Michal was living with the tribes belonging to Ishbosheth's kingdom, and he asked him to return his former wife Michal to him. This was a wise action by David, so that it would not be said that he had exceeded the authority of King Ishbosheth in this matter.
David asked for Michal for the following reasons:

1- Because he loved her and was faithful in taking her back as his wife when the opportunity came to him, and whoever is faithful in his house is the one who deserves to be entrusted with the kingdom (1 Tim 3:5).
2- By returning Michal he announces before the tribes his kinship to Saul, and so draws their hearts to him, especially the tribe of Benjamin, when he reigns over all.

3- It shows that he was not eager for the kingship and leadership, but for the ordering of his house and the doing of justice before everything, for it would have been easy for him to take her back after becoming king by his royal authority.
4- It is a restoration of David's dignity, which makes the tribes respect him.
But the first reason is the most important of the reasons, and it may be the only reason.

entries.section: (3) David recovers Michal

paragraphs.text: Phaltiel the son of Laish: a man from the village of "Gallim," one of the villages of the tribe of Benjamin, near Gibeah.
Ishbosheth heeded David's request so that no dispute with him would arise, for he knew the strength of David and his men, and he brought Michal to send her to him.

entries.section: (3) David recovers Michal

paragraphs.text: Bahurim: a village on the road from Jerusalem to the Jordan, near the Mount of Olives.

Phaltiel, Michal's husband, was a loving and faithful husband to her, and since he could not disobey the king's command, he went out to escort her, weeping over parting from her, and kept following her steps until Abner rebuked him, ordering him to stop walking after her and return to his house, so Phaltiel obeyed and returned to his house.

Trust in the love of God, who restores your rights to you if you have been wronged, however long the time and however late His answer, for He never forgets you, and in the long time you wait He teaches you and makes you grow in knowing Him, so you find the salvation of your soul, as happened with David, who waited a long time until the whole kingdom submitted to him.

entries.section: (4) Abner proclaims David king over all the tribes of Israel

paragraphs.text: "In times past": for a long time until now.

Abner, as a wise man, did not want to make a treaty with David without returning to the elders of Israel so that they would share in the decision and it would become a strong decision, so he reminded them of their desire, for a long time until now, that David be king over them. "Now then do it," for since this was your desire, carry it out by setting him up as king over you, for this desire of yours agrees with the divine will in choosing David as savior of his people from the Philistines and from the other enemies. It is understood from this that the tribes desired to make David king over them, but Abner did not respond to their desire because he thought of himself ruling the kingdom through the weak Ishbosheth, until God permitted the problem between him and Ishbosheth, and so he carried out the people's desire and the will of God by making David king.

Here Abner's wisdom shines forth. After his example, every ruler or leader ought not to act on his own opinion alone but to share his decisions with his people or those who work with him, and so ensure their support for him in carrying them out and the success of his plans. So pay attention to the opinion of those around you and involve them in your decisions, even if you give up some of them to put them at ease and secure their response, so that they rejoice with you in all that you do.

entries.section: (4) Abner proclaims David king over all the tribes of Israel

paragraphs.text: "Spake in the ears of": addressed them or spoke in their presence.

After Abner addressed all the tribes, he addressed the tribe of Benjamin in particular, for it was the tribe from which Saul came, to persuade them to accept David, who was of the tribe of Judah, as king, and not to be partisan for the house of Saul. Abner was able to persuade them because he was a Benjamite like them. After Abner gained the support and agreement of all the tribes of Israel, and especially the tribe of Benjamin, he went to Hebron, the seat of David's kingship, to tell him of everyone's agreement to his reigning over them.

entries.section: (4) Abner proclaims David king over all the tribes of Israel

paragraphs.text: Abner came to Hebron accompanied by a delegation of twenty men, perhaps representatives of the elders of Israel, to meet David, who welcomed them and celebrated the meeting with them by making a feast for them. It is obvious that during the meeting they informed him of the collective decision of all the tribes.

entries.section: (4) Abner proclaims David king over all the tribes of Israel

paragraphs.text: Abner told David that as soon as he left him he would go and call all the heads of the people and their helpers to come to him, to make a covenant with him and declare their acceptance of him as king, so that his reign would be founded on the collective desire of the people and would be carried out in an official manner. David permitted him to leave, and he left in peace.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: Joab was absent from Hebron because he and his soldiers were fighting some hostile peoples, and he returned with abundant spoil from this war, and the time of his return was after Abner had left David.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: When Joab returned, one of his men told him of the meeting that had taken place between Abner and King David, and how he had met with a welcome from the king and left after the meeting in peace.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: Joab was a strong personality and the head of the army, and had familiarity with David because he was his sister's son. When he heard of Abner's meeting with David and his leaving him in peace, he was very angry, because Abner had been hostile to David for many years with Saul and had tried to kill him, then divided the kingdom after Saul and gave the larger part to Ishbosheth the son of Saul. So Joab went in to David and rebuked him severely because he had not killed Abner and had sent him away in peace.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: "To deceive thee": to flatter you and cajole you with words of praise and deceive you.

And he told the king that he should know that he had come to flatter you and deceive you, so as to learn your secrets and capabilities, so that he could return and plan to take the kingdom from you for the sake of Ishbosheth the son of Saul. This shows the wickedness of Joab and his evil opinion of Abner; he is not wise, loving and forgiving like David, for he accused Abner of spying without any right.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: Well of Sirah: the name of a well about 6 km from Hebron.

Joab went out from David angry and sent, without the king's knowledge, men to overtake Abner and lure him to return again to Hebron, on the pretext of agreeing with the king or with Joab on some matters that had not been covered in his first talks with the king. Abner had reached in his journey a place with a well called the well of Sirah when Joab's messengers overtook him.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: Abner responded in good faith to the request of Joab's messengers and returned to Hebron, and Joab was waiting for him at the gate of the city. He took him aside in the gate, pretending that he wanted to speak with him privately, but he suddenly drew his sword and killed him treacherously, in revenge for his killing of Asahel his brother.

Joab had another purpose in killing Abner, which was his fear of his rivalry with him in the future for the command of David's army. This shows us how self-love leads a person to commit terrible evils.

It is noticed that Joab killed Abner at the gate of the city of Hebron and not inside it, because Hebron is one of the cities of refuge, and it is not permitted to kill a person in it by way of blood revenge. For Abner had killed Asahel, yet Joab did not take revenge for his brother. Joab's killing of Abner was treachery, for if he wanted to fight him he should have dueled him, and by this treachery he transgressed the Mosaic Law, which says, "Cursed be he that smiteth his neighbour secretly" (Deut 27:24). God permitted the death of Abner because he had wronged David much, whether in his pursuit of him in the days of Saul, or his dividing the kingdom and his clashes with David, and so that no one would think that Abner was the one who made David king, for it was God who made him king.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: As soon as David learned what had happened, he immediately declared his innocence and the innocence of his kingdom from this treacherous killing.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: "Let it rest on the head of Joab": let him bear the guilt of killing Abner, upon Moab and his sons.
One that hath an issue: this is one of the unclean diseases in the Law.
Leper: one afflicted with vitiligo.

David was not content with clearing himself, but cursed Joab and called down upon him and upon his house diseases and evils as recompense for his deed, so that there would always be among his household those sick with various kinds of issues, leprosy and paralysis, and those killed by the enemies, and the poor in constant need of necessary food.

David's curse was like a prophecy of the evils that would befall Joab and his descendants as the fruit of his wronging Abner. It is known that the descendants of evildoers often grow up wicked like their fathers, and so suffer the same woes that the fathers suffered, but if the sons reform their conduct, God has mercy on them and removes His wrath from them (Ezek 18:10-18).

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: Thus Joab and his brother Abishai took vengeance for the killing of their brother Asahel by the hand of Abner during the war, but this vengeance was an evil, unjustified act, because Abner had warned Asahel more than once against following him and asked him to keep away from him, so his killing of him was in self-defense and during the war, whereas the killing of Abner was deceit and treachery. This verse makes clear that Abishai took part in deceiving Abner to go with Joab alone, so that Joab could kill him treacherously.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: "Gird you with sackcloth": put on sackcloth, that is, coarse clothes, as a girdle, which is what is worn on the waist and extends downward, as an expression of great grief, because a person is distressed when this coarse clothing touches his skin.

David declared a period of mourning for the killing of Abner, and asked the people to show all signs of grief, which in that era consisted of tearing clothes, wearing sackcloth and striking the face. He also ordered an official funeral to be arranged, and David walked at the front behind the bier, taking part in the funeral procession of Abner. David grieved for Abner because he was killed treacherously, and he had been a commander in fighting and destroying the pagans as God commanded.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: Abner was buried in Hebron, the capital of David's kingdom, in his honor, and David wept at his grave and the people were moved by him and wept too. This shows the extent of David's forgiveness and his love for those who are hostile to him, especially if they seek peace.

It is noticed that David did not remove Joab from the command of the army although he knew that what he had done was a great wrong, because of the strength of Joab's position. It was not wise to punish him at this time lest disturbances occur, but he received his recompense afterwards at the hand of Solomon by the command of David his father. So David is just even to his sister's son Joab, once he had sinned (1 Kgs 2:31).

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: David lamented Abner with a beautiful poem, denouncing the manner in which this warrior and great commander died, an evil trick by which a simple person might die who is lured by cunning.

May you appreciate the virtues of the one who is hostile to you or wrongs you, and try to forgive him however great his mistakes, and remember his good deeds and great works after his death. This is true love, which wrongs no one and forgives all offenses.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: "Wicked men": the wicked and treacherous.

Among what David said in his lament was that Abner's death was like the death of the noble: he was not bound like a criminal sentenced to death, but he fell at treacherous, wicked hands, as thieves kill an innocent person. These words of lament moved the people, and they went back to weeping for Abner.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: "So do God to me, and more also": I become deserving of severe divine punishment.

David's companions tried to make him eat something because he had not taken any food since the beginning of the day, but he refused to taste food until sunset, although the time was still early for sunset, and David called down a curse on himself if he took anything until the sun went down. David's fast was for the following reasons:
1- Grief for Abner.
2- Rejection of the evil done to Abner by Joab and his brother Abishai.
3- Offering fasting and prayer for the departed, as was done by the people of Jabesh Gilead (1 Sam 31:13).

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: The people saw and heard what David had done because of the death of Abner, the weeping, the lament and the fasting from food, and they were comforted by this conduct of his, and were pleased with the duty of condolence he performed for Abner, for Abner was a great commander in the eyes of all the people.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: David's actions confirmed to everyone that he had not instigated the killing of Abner, and indeed that he did not know what Joab was plotting to do treacherously to this great man.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: David's men tried to console him in his deep grief over the killing of Abner, but he told them that Abner deserved all this lament because he was truly a great man, and his fall is considered a grave loss for his people.

entries.section: (5) Joab kills Abner

paragraphs.text: David spoke with wonderful humility before his servants and counselors, declaring his weakness before the strength of Joab and Abishai, the sons of Zeruiah his sister. They were strong and had no little control and domination in the kingdom, so David asked God to intervene to repay them for their evil and to preserve his kingdom in truth and justice. Solomon later killed Joab, while Jaasiel, one of the sons of Abner, became chief of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr 27:21). The killing of Ishbosheth

entries.section: (1) Ishbosheth's servants kill him

paragraphs.text: "His hands were feeble": he felt weak and lost control of matters.

Abner was the real manager in the kingdom of Israel, not Ishbosheth, who was only a nominal king, and Abner was a politician and a strong military commander. When the news of his death reached the kingdom of Israel, Ishbosheth felt that the support of the kingdom was gone and sensed his weakness without him, and the people of the tribes subject to him were afraid because they had become without a commander to protect them and were exposed to punishment from David for their rebellion against him and their following of Ishbosheth. But David was a gentle and forgiving man, so he did no evil and did not punish the tribes. We note that the name of Ishbosheth is not mentioned in this verse, but the inspired text says "Saul's son," in contempt of him and because he had lost his strength, that is, Abner.

entries.section: (1) Ishbosheth's servants kill him

paragraphs.text: "Captains of bands": heads of military companies.
Beeroth: a city in the tribe of Benjamin, 15 km north of Jerusalem. It was originally one of the cities of the Gibeonites, and the tribe of Benjamin took it.

Among the men of war belonging to Ishbosheth there were two heads of military companies named "Baanah" and "Rechab," the two sons of a man named Rimmon, from the town of Beeroth, which belonged to the tribe of Benjamin.

entries.section: (1) Ishbosheth's servants kill him

paragraphs.text: The Beerothites are the inhabitants of the town of Beeroth, and they were a mixture of Gibeonites and Benjamites. When Saul was angry with the Gibeonites (ch. 21:1), the people of Beeroth fled to a town called "Gittaim," fleeing from Saul's persecution of them. They remained there until the time of the writing of this book.

entries.section: (1) Ishbosheth's servants kill him

paragraphs.text: "Lame of his feet": crippled.

Jonathan the son of Saul had a son named "Mephibosheth," who was five years old when Saul and Jonathan were killed in their last battle against the Philistines in Jezreel. The child's nurse was afraid that the Philistines would harm him, so she picked him up to flee with him to any safe place, but as she ran the child fell from her to the ground and his feet were injured, and he became lame to the end of his life.

Mephibosheth is mentioned here because he and Ishbosheth were the ones left of the descendants of Saul, and Mephibosheth was not fit to be king because of the weakness of his feet, and also because this is a preparation for the good that David would do to him afterwards (ch. 9:1-9). That is, with the killing of Ishbosheth there is no one left for Saul to reign on his throne.

entries.section: (1) Ishbosheth's servants kill him

paragraphs.text: Baanah and Rechab sensed Ishbosheth's weakness after the death of Abner, so they thought of a plot to kill him and bring this news to David, so as to receive a great reward from him, such as becoming commanders in his armies. They forgot that David was a loving and forgiving man who hated evil, and that he had killed the one who brought him news of the death of Saul and Jonathan (ch. 1:16). So they planned to kill their king Ishbosheth, and for this to be done at midday when he was asleep and at a time when no one expects harm to befall the king because it is daytime.

entries.section: (1) Ishbosheth's servants kill him

paragraphs.text: "The plain": the plain beside the Jordan.

These two brothers were assigned to grind wheat and distribute it to the soldiers, so their entering the house was a customary matter that aroused no suspicion. When they reached where the king was lying, they found him deep in sleep, so they struck him in the belly and he died at once. Then they cut off his head and left from there in flight, with no one aware of them, and walked the rest of the day and all night through the plain beside the Jordan, heading for Hebron.

entries.section: (1) Ishbosheth's servants kill him

paragraphs.text: The two brothers came to David in Hebron with the severed head, and presented it to him, saying that it was the head of Ishbosheth the son of Saul, his enemy who had pursued him all the days, trying to seize him and kill him, and that God had avenged him on Saul and his descendants, for He permitted them to kill his son who was competing with him for the kingship over the people of Israel. But God was not pleased with the treachery and evil they did to their king, and He used their evil to accomplish His will in David's reigning, and they should not have wronged their king, for God has different ways of carrying out His will.

Do not do evil to please people or in seeking your own interest, and do not forget that God watches all the deeds of human beings and repays them for them. Always remember that God sees you, so that you do what pleases Him.

entries.section: (2) David kills the murderers of Ishbosheth

paragraphs.text: David's reaction to this event was contrary to what the two murderers "Baanah and Rechab" expected, for David declared that the living God was the One who had redeemed him out of all adversity, and not the arm of a human being, as these two murderers thought that by killing Ishbosheth they were establishing the kingdom for David.

entries.section: (2) David kills the murderers of Ishbosheth

paragraphs.text: "Gave him a reward for his tidings": I killed him in return for these tidings, for which he thought he would be rewarded well. David recalled the story of the Amalekite man who thought that by bringing him the news of the death of Saul he was coming to David with good news that would please him greatly, and David commanded that he be killed in "Ziklag" (ch. 1:15, 16), so his killing was the recompense he deserved for what he thought was pleasing good news, while its effect on David was completely the opposite.

entries.section: (2) David kills the murderers of Ishbosheth

paragraphs.text: "Take you away from the earth": kill you.

The deed of the Amalekite man was less criminal, for Saul had been severely wounded and was about to fall into the hands of the Philistines, and yet David considered him condemned and deserving of death. How much more, then, what these two persons committed of conspiracy and treachery by their sinful assault on Ishbosheth, whom David in his love described as a righteous man, for they stabbed him while he slept in his bed. David sentenced them to death, as they had done to the life of an innocent person, for it would not have been just for their recompense to be less than the Amalekite's.

David enjoyed the simple outlook with which he saw the virtues of his enemies, so he praised Saul in his lament and here describes Ishbosheth as a righteous man. May you see the virtues of the one who wrongs you so that you love him and make excuses for him in his mistakes, and so live by the commandment of Christ, that is, love of enemies.

entries.section: (2) David kills the murderers of Ishbosheth

paragraphs.text: David commanded his soldiers and they killed the two men, because he wanted not to defile his kingdom with acts of treachery, and to declare that his reigning is not accomplished by betrayal and treachery but by the power of God. So they cut off their hands, which had killed an innocent person, and cut off their feet, which had entered the chamber of the innocent man to carry out their crime, and hanged their bodies in a place frequented by many people, the pool of Hebron, so that everyone would see the consequence of transgression and betrayal, and as proof of David's love for Saul and his descendants and honor to Ishbosheth because he was a king and the son of a king. David decided to bury his head in the tomb in which Abner had been buried before in Hebron, the capital of David's kingdom at that time.

Ishbosheth and Abner differed and quarreled, and the days passed and both were buried in one tomb in Hebron. May we remember death so that we live in peace with those around us and forgive whoever wrongs us, because death will bring us together and we take nothing from this world.
David as king over all Israel and his victories over the Jebusites and the Philistines

entries.section: (1) David as king over all Israel

paragraphs.text: "We are thy bone and thy flesh": we are your relatives, for he is of the tribe of Judah and they are the descendants of the brothers of Judah.

After the events mentioned in the two preceding chapters of the killing of Abner, the commander of Ishbosheth's army, and then the killing of Ishbosheth himself, none of Saul's descendants remained alive except Mephibosheth his grandson, who was lame in his feet and therefore unfit to take the kingship, besides Abner's effort to hand the kingdom over to David. So the elders of Israel from the eleven tribes came to David in Hebron, declaring their kinship to him and therefore their submission and their acceptance of his being king over them.

entries.section: (1) David as king over all Israel

paragraphs.text: "Leddest out and broughtest in Israel": you led the armies outside and inside Israel.

They acknowledged before him that he had been leading their armies successfully during the reign of Saul, whether outside the country or inside it, and they also acknowledged what they had heard from Samuel, that the Lord would take the kingdom from Saul and give it to another better than he (1 Sam 15:28), and that all the events confirm that he is the one chosen by the Lord to reign over His people and shepherd them.

entries.section: (1) David as king over all Israel

paragraphs.text: The heads and leaders of the people came to Hebron to pledge allegiance to David, and he made a covenant with them before the Lord that he would govern his people according to the divine Law and be faithful in shepherding them, and in return the people pledged to obey him and be faithful to him. All the tribes anointed him to be king over Israel.

This is the third anointing of David. The first was secretly in his father's house in the lifetime of Saul (1 Sam 16:13), and the second was the anointing by the men of Judah in Hebron (ch. 2:4) after the death of Saul to be king over them.
God prepared David to be king by the following:
1- He taught him patience and endurance when he endured Saul's wrongs and his pursuit of him.
2- He taught him humility when he humbled himself before Saul, the king rejected by God, and did not seek the kingship for himself.
3- He taught him detachment when he lived driven out in the mountains and valleys and dwelling among the enemies during Saul's pursuit.

4- He experienced faith and reliance on God, who rescued him from the hand of Saul and from the hand of the Philistines and all who were hostile to him, until in the end He established him king over all Israel.
5- He taught him not to avenge himself, in his forbearance with Saul, who tried to kill him, and his endurance of Abner and Ishbosheth.

entries.section: (1) David as king over all Israel

paragraphs.text: David's age when he took the kingship was thirty years, and he remained king for forty years, reigning over Israel until he died at the age of seventy. The age of thirty is the age of maturity among the Jews, at which a man's opinion is taken into account, and it is the same age at which Joseph became ruler of Egypt and at which Christ began His ministry.

entries.section: (1) David as king over all Israel

paragraphs.text: The exact total length of his reign is forty years and six months, divided into two periods. The first is the period of his reign over the tribe of Judah only, and the seat of his rule during it was in Hebron, and its length was seven years and six months, beginning from the death of Saul until the death of Ishbosheth the son of Saul. The second period, thirty years, was when he reigned over all the tribes of Israel, and the seat of his rule in it was the city of Jerusalem.

When God wishes and the time is fulfilled, He restores your rights to you and makes everyone submit to you. David waited long years after being anointed king by the hand of Samuel until his reign over all the people was completed. So be patient and continue in your prayers until you receive your rights, and do not forget that your first and most important right is the Kingdom of Heaven, so care for repentance and the growth of your relationship with God before any material thing, and God will remove your sins from you however long the time, and will make your faith grow so that you enjoy fellowship with Him.

entries.section: (2) Victory over the Jebusites

paragraphs.text: The Jebusites: a tribe of the Canaanites who dwelt in Jebus, which is Jerusalem.

"Except thou take away the blind and the lame": the blind and the lame among the Jebusites are able to repel you, for they are stronger than the men of your army. In this there is a challenge and mockery of David and his army.

Jerusalem: its name was formerly Salem or Shalem, that is, king of peace, and from it came Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God (Gen 14:18). It lies on five mountains, among them Mount Zion and Mount Moriah, and rises about 700 meters above sea level and lies about 22 km west of the Dead Sea. It lies north of the tribe of Judah and near the tribe of Benjamin. It was anciently called Jebus after the Jebusites, its inhabitants, and although Joshua killed its king among the five kings (Josh 10:13-26), the Jebusites returned and took possession of it, and the tribe of Judah burned most of it, yet the Jebusites did not leave it but continued to dwell in the high, fortified places in it, while the Benjamites dwelt in the lower parts (Josh 15:36). After the eleven tribes joined the tribe of David in a united kingdom that David ruled, David decided to move the capital of his kingdom from Hebron to Jerusalem, where the Jebusites were living, so he had to fight them in order to take their city Jerusalem, which they called Jebus. The Jebusites were fortified in their land and fully confident of its impregnability, that no one could invade it, so they mocked David when they heard his decision to fight them, saying their phrase famous at that time, which means that the blind and the lame in their city were stronger and mightier than the men of his army and than he himself. The meaning of their saying was that these blind and lame would be the ones to defend the city and were enough to prevent him from entering it, so they showed him his weakness so that he would draw back from fighting them. David chose Jerusalem to be the capital of his kingdom for the following reasons:
1- Its central location among the tribes.
2- Its fortified location, because it is built on mountains, so it is hard to fight against.
3- The Jebusites lived in it, so it did not belong to any of the tribes, and thus he did not take a city from any tribe, and so does not become subordinate to any tribe.

4- It was adjacent to the tribe of Benjamin and some Benjamites lived in it, and by this he won the affection of this tribe, from which Saul came, so that peace would be established in his kingdom. It also falls within the tribe of Judah, so by this he pleased the tribe of Judah as well, which is his own.

entries.section: (2) Victory over the Jebusites

paragraphs.text: David succeeded in taking the city despite the claims of its inhabitants the Jebusites, and David called the city "the city of David."

The following verses relate the details of David's taking it. The stronghold of Zion mentioned lies in the south-east of Jerusalem; it is a high mountain in which the Jebusites fortified themselves, and David took it, then built a temple for the Lord on Mount Moriah, and the name Zion widened to express all of Jerusalem.

entries.section: (2) Victory over the Jebusites

paragraphs.text: David wanted to kindle the enthusiasm of his men, so he set a reward for whoever crossed through the water channel into the land of the Philistines, and reached the position of the Jebusite guards of the walls and fought them and defeated them. The guards were neither blind nor lame, but they said that as a challenge and mockery of David. The setting of a reward is not mentioned in this verse, but it is mentioned in (1 Chr 11:6), namely that whoever does that will be chief and commander.

David's saying that the blind and the lame are hated of his soul means the Jebusites in general. David hated them for their idolatry and for the challenge and contempt they showed toward his person and toward the people of the Lord, and David's saying about the lame and the blind became a proverb that people repeated. They say, "No blind or lame shall enter the house of the Lord," that is, there is no longer a Jebusite to enter the house of the Lord, or it is forbidden for any pagan like the Jebusites to enter the house of the Lord. The word Jebusite means trodden under foot, so it is a type of Satan, whom Christ trod down by His Cross, and Christ is the descendant of David and David is a type of Him, and Christ achieved this victory over Satan, as David triumphed over the Jebusites, in order to give this power of His to everyone who believes in Him, so that he treads down the power of Satan and drives him out of his life.

entries.section: (2) Victory over the Jebusites

paragraphs.text: After David took the city he called it the city of David, and he built it up and built many houses in it extending from the wall of the city to its middle.

entries.section: (2) Victory over the Jebusites

paragraphs.text: David's standing grew ever more brilliant and prosperous, and God was the secret of his strength, for He is the God of hosts, who sends His angels to help and support His children.

Do not be troubled by the threats of the wicked if they exalt themselves over you and mock you, for the Lord is with you, so no one can prevail against you. Be firm in your faith, holding fast to God's commandments, and you will succeed in the end like David.

entries.section: (3) Hiram helps in building a house for David

paragraphs.text: Hiram king of Tyre: he reigned 34 years over the kingdom of Tyre, and he had friendly relations and friendship with both David and Solomon.

Hiram king of Tyre was a friend of David, so he sent him much timber with skilled carpenters and masons to help him in building a great palace for himself. Tyre was distinguished by the presence of cedar trees, strong in their wood, and by carpenters skilled in the craft of woodwork. Here the blessings of God to His striving children appear, for He supported David in driving the pagans out of Jebus, then rewarded him with Hiram's gifts.

entries.section: (3) Hiram helps in building a house for David

paragraphs.text: David saw and became certain that the Lord was the One working to establish his kingdom and also the One working to magnify his kingdom, because of His love for His people and His desire to make them happy. Whoever pleases the Lord, He gives him favor in the eyes of those around him, so they are at peace with him and even try to win his affection.

It is beautiful of David to attribute the credit for all that he came to of greatness and exaltation to the Lord, who supported and strengthened him. Let us humble ourselves before the Lord so that we may have spiritual insight to discern that all the success that comes to us is not the fruit of our strength or human abilities but is a grace and gift from the Lord, and so we thank Him every day.

entries.section: (4) The sons born to David in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: David took wives and concubines, as was the custom of the kings of those times, in addition to his wives that he had when he was in Hebron, who are mentioned in (ch. 3:2-5). But sadly the great number of wives did not protect David from falling into his lust for Bathsheba and committing adultery with her. Rather, what protects is chastity and the fear of God, as Joseph did (Gen 39:11-15).

entries.section: (4) The sons born to David in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: The first four are "Shammua," "Shobab," "Nathan" and "Solomon," who are the sons of Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and Shammua has another name by which he is mentioned in (1 Chr 3:5), which is "Shimea."

entries.section: (4) The sons born to David in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: "Ibhar" is also mentioned in (1 Chr 3:6, 14:5), and "Elishua," whose name appears as "Elishama" in (1 Chr 3:6), and "Nepheg" (also spelled "Nefeg"), who is also mentioned in (1 Chr 3:7 and 14:6).

entries.section: (4) The sons born to David in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: "Elishama" is also mentioned in (1 Chr 3:8), "Eliada" is also mentioned as "Eliada" in (1 Chr 3:8), and in (1 Chr 14:7) he is called "Beeliada."

"Eliphalet" or "Eliphelet" was born after the death of the son mentioned with the same name in (1 Chr 3:8 and 14:7). The First Book of Chronicles (chs. 3, 14) adds two other sons to the eleven sons mentioned here, namely Nogah and Eliphelet, and the inspired text did not mention them here because they died young.

If you have physical children, take care to bring them up in the fear of God, but the most important thing is that you acquire virtues, and love and serve those around you, and care for the salvation of their souls, for all these are your spiritual children who remain with you forever in the Kingdom of Heaven.

entries.section: (5) Victory over the Philistines

paragraphs.text: When David's kingdom began to grow and expand through the joining of all the tribes to him, the Philistines began to fear him, so they planned to fight him before the growth of his kingdom was complete and made preliminary reconnaissance movements. When the news of these movements reached David, he took refuge in a fortified place to arrange matters with his commanders.

entries.section: (5) Victory over the Philistines

paragraphs.text: The valley of Rephaim: a fertile valley between Bethlehem and Jerusalem. The Philistines spread their forces in the "valley of Rephaim."

entries.section: (5) Victory over the Philistines

paragraphs.text: As was David's custom before undertaking any move, he asked the Lord whether he should go up to confront the Philistines and whether He would give him victory over them, and the Lord answered him yes.

entries.section: (5) Victory over the Philistines

paragraphs.text: Baal-perazim: a high place north of the valley of Rephaim.
"The Lord hath broken forth upon mine enemies before me, as the breach of waters": the Lord burst upon the enemies as the rushing waters burst through everything that stands in their way.

David advanced to meet the Philistines, and the confrontation took place at a place later called "Baal-perazim," that is, the lord of breaking through, where David won a splendid victory, and as was his custom he ascribed the victory to the Lord who supported him, and His power advanced through the ranks, bursting upon the enemies, therefore the place was called "the lord of breaking through."

entries.section: (5) Victory over the Philistines
