paragraphs.text: The Philistines had carried their idols in the midst of their armies, as was the custom of peoples anciently, thinking that these gods of theirs would help them achieve victory. When the Philistines were defeated and fled, they had no time to take their idols with them in their retreat, so they left them at the place of the battle, and David and his men destroyed them and burned them with fire so that they would not be a stumbling block to the people afterwards.

entries.section: (5) Victory over the Philistines

paragraphs.text: The Philistines did not surrender after their first defeat, but waged another war to take revenge on David and his kingdom, so they massed their armies in the same place, that is, in the valley of Rephaim.

entries.section: (5) Victory over the Philistines

paragraphs.text: Mulberry trees (baca trees): a kind of tree from which a sap comes out resembling tears.
The host of the Philistines: the camp of the Philistines, where they fortify themselves.

As was David's custom, he turned to prayer to the Lord, asking whether he should fight the Philistines. The Lord was not content with answering him with approval or refusal, but also directed him to the plan he should follow to gain the victory. He commanded him not to confront them from the front as the previous time, but to circle around them until he was behind them and to hide in an area thick with trees, and when he heard the sound of regular steps like the steps of a mighty army, as if coming from the tops of the trees, then he would know that the Lord was present with him and going before him to give him victory over the army of the enemies, and he should come out of his hiding place and fight them.

The Lord is present with His children at all times as long as they seek Him. When some trials or hard circumstances surround us, let us trust that God will stretch out a helping hand to us and bring us out of distress into a broad place. We only have to call upon Him, for He is near and answers those who call upon Him.

entries.section: (5) Victory over the Philistines

paragraphs.text: Geba: a city in Benjamin on the northern edge of the kingdom of Judah, that is, north-east of Jerusalem, and it was assigned for the dwelling of the priests (Josh 21:17). Gazer: a city in the land of the tribe of Judah lying on the border of the land of the Philistines, north-west of Jerusalem.

David carried out the plan the Lord had drawn for him with all precision, so the Philistines were defeated before him and fled, and David pursued them with his army from Geba until they reached Gazer, where the children of Israel stopped pursuing them. That is, the Philistines did not flee to their land, which lies west of Jerusalem, but fled to the north-east of Jerusalem, that is, the city of Geba, to fortify themselves there, and since they found no opportunity to fortify themselves, they turned back and headed west toward their land and went by the road of the Jewish city of Gazer, which lies on the border of the land of the Philistines. The bringing of the ark to the city of David: more details of the carrying and moving of the ark are found in (1 Chr 13, 15, 16)

entries.section: (1) Uzzah touches the ark

paragraphs.text: "Chosen men": the elite, the choicest of the people.
David gathered thirty thousand of the choicest men of the people, leaders, wise men and elders, to share with him in moving the ark of the covenant to the city of David.

entries.section: (1) Uzzah touches the ark

paragraphs.text: Baale of Judah: it is the same village of Kirjath-jearim mentioned in (1 Chr 13:6), a city on the border of Judah and Benjamin lying about 14 km west of Jerusalem. The ark was there since its removal from Beth-shemesh and remained until it was moved to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.

"That dwelleth between the cherubims": the cherubim are an angelic order that was beneath the throne of God (bearing the throne) when the Lord appeared to Ezekiel (Ezek 11:22), therefore He said to David, "that dwelleth between the cherubims."

They all went to where the ark was at that time, in "Baale of Judah," in the house of Abinadab, where the ark had remained since the children of Israel recovered it from the Philistines. It was placed for a short time in Beth-shemesh, then moved to the village of Kirjath-jearim (1 Sam 6). The ark remained in the village of Kirjath-jearim throughout the lifetime of Samuel and Saul and the beginning of David's reign while he was in Hebron, that is, about 75 years.

David's purpose in moving the ark was that it should be in the capital of the kingdom, which includes the king and the high priest, and because the ark was a symbol of the Lord's dwelling in the midst of His people. The ark was called by the name of the Lord of hosts, of whom it is said, "that dwelleth between the cherubims," because His glory was manifested between the two cherubim that were on the cover of the ark of the covenant. David also intended by moving the ark that the people be bound to God's presence in their midst.

entries.section: (1) Uzzah touches the ark

paragraphs.text: Cart: a wagon drawn by animals, which here are oxen.
Abinadab: a man from the village of Kirjath-jearim who accepted that the ark of the covenant be in his house when it was sent back from the Philistines.
Gibeah: a high place in the village of Kirjath-jearim.

David and the priests of the Lord neglected the commandment concerning how the ark was to be carried when moved from one place to another, for it must be carried by the priests on their shoulders by the two staves assigned for carrying. Instead they set it on a new cart drawn by two oxen, which set out with it from the house of Abinadab, which was on a high place in the village of Kirjath-jearim, and "Uzzah and Ahio," the two sons or grandsons of Abinadab, were driving the oxen, and Ahio went in front leading the oxen while Uzzah walked behind the ark watching from behind.

entries.section: (1) Uzzah touches the ark

paragraphs.text: Fir wood (cypress): a kind of wood distinguished by its durability and pleasant smell.

Harps (the oud): the plural of the oud, an instrument known since antiquity, known to many Eastern peoples and found depicted on Egyptian tombs, and still used today with some developments in it. It is a box with several strings, whose number ranges between 4 and 10 according to the type. David mastered playing it and its use spread among the children of Israel, and it was used in the rites of worship and on occasions of joy and feasts. Psalteries: a musical instrument in the shape of a triangle with four strings, played with the fingers. Timbrels: the plural of the tambourine, called in Egypt the "riqq." It consists of a membrane of animal skin stretched around a wooden frame in which small bells are fitted, and it makes a sound when struck.
Cornets (the harps): the plural of the harp, one of the ancient musical instruments.
Cymbals: they resemble the "cymbals" now used in our churches. They are two round plates of brass, which ring when one is struck against the other. The Hebrews used them in the rites of worship.

The procession of the ark was splendid, for David and the representatives of the people walked in the height of their happiness and joy, dancing and playing the musical instruments made of fir wood, among them harps, psalteries, timbrels, cornets and cymbals.

entries.section: (1) Uzzah touches the ark

paragraphs.text: Nachon's threshingfloor: it is the same one called the threshingfloor of Chidon in (1 Chr 13:9). The threshingfloor is a level rocky ground on which they thresh grain to separate the chaff from it (a threshing floor). Nachon is the name of a person who owned a threshingfloor near Jerusalem.
"The oxen shook it": the oxen were unruly, that is, they stumbled and then rushed on quickly.
"The Lord had made a breach upon Uzzah": He struck him and put him to death.

It happened during the journey that the oxen suddenly became unruly, when they had reached the threshingfloor of Nachon in the middle of the road from Baale of Judah to Jerusalem. The oxen stumbled because of the roughness of the ground, and Uzzah feared that the ark would overturn and fall to the ground, so he put out his hand to steady the ark. This act aroused the anger of the Lord, and He put him to death at once.

God was not unjust in striking down Uzzah, because he was a Levite and knew that it is not right for anyone to touch the ark, but that it must be carried by the priests with two staves put through the rings of the ark. He must have understood this, because the ark was in his father's house, which had it for more than 70 years, so he had learned that no one may touch the ark. But it seems that he had become accustomed to the sight of the ark and its service, so he rushed without care lest it fall to the ground. It would have been better for Uzzah to insist on its being carried on the shoulders of the priests, and if priests were not available, then on the shoulders of the Levites, without anyone touching it.

We note that God permitted the cart drawn by the cows to go from the land of the Philistines to the lands of the children of Israel in peace, and the cattle did not become unruly. But here God permitted the oxen to become unruly, because the Jews know how the ark is to be carried by the priests. Sadly David forgot to consult God about how to move the ark, so what happened happened.

entries.section: (1) Uzzah touches the ark

paragraphs.text: "Was displeased": he was affected by the death of Uzzah, who had taken care of the service of the ark for many years, but at the same time he was not objecting to God's command, because he knew that what happened was a carelessness on Uzzah's part in touching the ark. With the sudden death of Uzzah the joy of the people turned to sorrow, and David was distressed by the change of the situation and the clouding of the serenity of the occasion, and he called the place where Uzzah died "Perez-uzzah," that is, "the breach of Uzzah," because of his being put to death by the Lord. This name continued to be given to the place to the day of the writing of the book.

entries.section: (1) Uzzah touches the ark

paragraphs.text: "Was afraid": he felt the awe and majesty of the ark to the point of trembling before it, because God is a mighty God and jealous for His holy things.

David realized that dealing with the ark requires complete precision in following what the Lord had legislated concerning it, because the Lord is a God jealous for His Law, and he, that is David, is a human being prone to error who might neglect to adhere to all that the presence of the ark in his city and under his possession requires, and he had seen the consequence of that before him in the Lord's putting Uzzah to death. Perhaps he wrote Psalm 15, "Lord, who shall abide in thy tabernacle?" at that time.

entries.section: (1) Uzzah touches the ark

paragraphs.text: David was afraid to move the ark to his city and asked a man named Obed-edom to keep the ark in his house. He was from the Philistine city of "Gath" and was living at that time on the road between the threshingfloor of Nachon and Jerusalem, and he was originally a Levite and was appointed afterwards to guard the ark (1 Chr 13:13). This shows the faith of Obed-edom, by which he surpassed David the prophet, for he accepted that the ark be in his house, and his faith overcame his fears, and he saw fit to adhere to the rites of reverence for the ark that the Law prescribes, trusting in God's blessing that he would receive.

The tender God is also the fearful and just One, so may you bow down before His sanctuary with reverence when you enter the church, then stand in your place and offer repentance and ask for His mercy and thank Him because He has granted you to enter His house, and He will reveal His secrets to you and give you joy in His presence with you, so that your heart rejoices in truth.

entries.section: (2) Moving the ark from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David

paragraphs.text: Obed-edom the Gittite: he was called the Gittite perhaps because he was from the town of Gath-rimmon, which was in the portion of Dan in the south and was given to the sons of Kohath (Josh 19:45, Josh 21:24), especially as Obed-edom was of the Korahites, descendants of Kohath (Num 16:1). The ark remained in the house of Obed-edom three months, and its presence in the house was a cause of blessing for him and for all his household. This was the natural reward for Obed-edom's faith, which distinguished him from the rest of the Jews, whose fear overshadowed their faith.

entries.section: (2) Moving the ark from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David

paragraphs.text: David learned of God's blessing upon the house of Obed-edom, so he went to him to take the ark from him, and commanded that a great procession be arranged to move it to his city Jerusalem, and everyone was glad to do this noble work. Here the humility of David appears, who learned from his previous mistake in leaving the ark in the house of Obed-edom out of fear of God, who punishes those who do not adhere to His Law, and he learned the humility of faith from Obed-edom, so he went to his house and asked him to take the ark to Jerusalem to be a blessing to the capital of the kingdom.

entries.section: (2) Moving the ark from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David

paragraphs.text: Whenever the bearers of the ark had gone six paces, for this time they carried the ark on the shoulders as the commandment requires, they would sacrifice an ox and a fatling, in atonement for their previous mistake in the way of carrying it, and as an expression of their thanks to the Lord and a celebration of the moving of the ark.

entries.section: (2) Moving the ark from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David

paragraphs.text: David was dancing with all enthusiasm in the procession of the ark, as an expression of his joy in the Lord and in the holy task he was performing, and he was wearing a linen garment, of the kind that the priests wore during the service and that those adhering to the Law wore on holy religious occasions. David took off his robe, which is the outer garment that represents grandeur, so the ephod, which represents purity, appeared, as he moved with joy and danced before the ark, declaring his humility and his joy at God's consenting to dwell in their midst and to live in the city of David to bless them, and showing his repentance for his neglect and shortcoming in not moving the ark quickly to his city Jerusalem. David sang Psalm 30 as an expression of his joy at the moving of the ark of God.

entries.section: (2) Moving the ark from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David

paragraphs.text: In their march, while carrying the ark, they used, in addition to the musical instruments mentioned before, trumpets and shouting as an expression of their great spiritual joy.

entries.section: (2) Moving the ark from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David

paragraphs.text: The procession reached the city of David, and the inhabitants of the city were looking out from the windows to watch the great procession. Michal, David's wife, also looked out from the window of her house and saw her husband the king leaping and dancing with joy. She did not like this conduct and considered it vulgar, lowering the dignity of the king and his majesty, for she believed in herself that the king must keep his dignity and grandeur at all times, therefore the king was lowered in her eyes. She was attached to the glories of the world and external grandeur.

Nothing of the grandeur of the procession caught Michal's attention except David's conduct. How much we also do like her when we criticize the conduct of others and their way of speaking or expression without caring about the content of what they say. So do not hasten to criticize, but look at the good conduct and good intention in people so that you benefit from everyone, and do not condemn the innocent as Michal did.

entries.section: (2) Moving the ark from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David

paragraphs.text: David had prepared a tent in his city to place the ark inside, so they set it in the midst of it.

This is different from the tabernacle of meeting, which at that time was in Gibeon (1 Chr 16:39). David and the people offered burnt offerings and peace offerings as an expression of their joy at the moving of the ark to the capital of the kingdom, and of their thanks to the Lord who permitted this work to be completed in peace. David wrote Psalm 30 at this time.

In (1 Chr 16:37-43) the inspired text mentions that Zadok the high priest and the rest of the priests remained in Gibeon to serve the tabernacle of meeting and offer the sacrifices, while the singers were appointed to serve the ark in Jerusalem. That is, the tabernacle of meeting with all its contents, the altar of brass, the altar of incense, the lampstand and the table of the showbread ... all this remained in Gibeon, and the ark alone was placed temporarily in a special tent in the city of David. The priest Abiathar served the ark in Jerusalem, and this arrangement continued until the days of Solomon, when Zadok alone became high priest, and he built a temple for the Lord and placed in it the ark and all the contents of the house of the Lord (1 Kgs 2:26, 27).

entries.section: (2) Moving the ark from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David

paragraphs.text: At the end of the assembly, after the offering of the sacrifices and burnt offerings, David prayed for the people and blessed them before sending them away, giving each one of them a loaf of bread, a cup of wine and a cake of dried figs as a sign of a fellowship of love among them. Bread, wine and figs were among the customary offerings to the Lord presented in His tent, and figs are among the trees that are widespread in the region. After that each one departed to his city, having taken part in the celebration of the return of the ark of the Lord into the midst of Jerusalem.

entries.section: (3) Michal rebukes David for his dancing

paragraphs.text: Handmaids: the plural of handmaid, that is, a female servant.

After the great celebration ended, David also returned to bless his household as he had blessed the people. His wife Michal came out to meet him with disdain, reproaching him for the appearance in which he had shown himself before his people, without honor and without dignity, for he had taken off his robe and begun to leap and dance as the rabble of the people and the foolish among them do. In her contempt for David she said that his appearance was foolish before the maidservants who were looking from the windows and the servants who were on the road.

entries.section: (3) Michal rebukes David for his dancing

paragraphs.text: Her saying "How glorious was the king of Israel to day" means that his appearance was contemptible and foolish.

David was angered by her words and answered her that he was dancing and leaping before the Lord and not to put on a display before everyone, and that this dancing of his was only to express his joy in the Lord and his acknowledgment of His great work with him in choosing him as king for his people after rejecting her father Saul and his descendants. This dancing was like worship and joy for God and an honoring of Him, and not like the dancing of fools. The great God deserves this honor, and God chose him because he honors Him and submits to Him, whereas Saul God rejected because he was proud against Him. Thus he rebuked her for her lack of concern to honor God and her preoccupation with appearance and human grandeur, but there is no honor for any human being before God. This is the feeling of the humble David.

entries.section: (3) Michal rebukes David for his dancing

paragraphs.text: David said to her that before the Lord he feels his lowliness and the smallness of his rank, but among the servants he remains respected and glorified, for God exalts the humble and honors him and glorifies him before all his people.

entries.section: (3) Michal rebukes David for his dancing

paragraphs.text: Michal was barren and bore no children throughout her life, and perhaps this was a punishment, and barrenness was considered by the Jews a disgrace, because every woman hoped that the awaited Messiah would be born of her. The Holy Bible mentions in (2 Sam 21:8) that Michal had five children, but the truth is that they were the children of Merab her elder sister, who had died, and Michal adopted her five children and raised them, so they were ascribed to her, as Joseph was ascribed to Leah or to Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant, as a mother, because Rachel had died (Gen 37:10).
To the degree that you humble yourself before God and before people, God exalts you in the sight of all and gives you grace and spiritual awe, so that people respect you and love you.

David's desire to build a house for the Lord and his prayer. The events of this chapter probably took place after chapter eight, that is, after David finished his wars, but it is mentioned here because it is connected with the moving of the ark mentioned in the previous chapter.

entries.section: (1) David's desire to build a house for the Lord

paragraphs.text: Nathan the prophet: a prophet who lived in the time of both kings David and Solomon and recorded their lives (1 Chr 29:29 and 2 Chr 9:29). He was faithful in conveying God's word frankly without fear of the king's person, yet he also spoke with respect and esteem for David even while rebuking him.

A house of cedar: the cedar is the evergreen tree of Lebanon, and its fruit resembles the fruit of the pine. Its wood is good and has an aromatic smell, and it was used in building palaces and the masts of ships and in making statues.
Curtains: pieces of cloth from which the tent is made.

Hiram king of Tyre had supplied David his friend with cedar wood to build a house for himself (ch. 5:11), and David settled in it, as it was considered a royal palace. All things around him were quiet and settled, whether internally after the extinction of the family of Saul, which had been competing with him for the rule, or externally from the surrounding peoples such as the Philistines and others. It grieved David to dwell in a palace built of cedar wood while the ark of the Lord was in a tent of cloth, so he expressed to Nathan the prophet, his contemporary, his desire to build a house for the Lord no less splendid, if not more so, than his own house. This shows David's humility in resorting to telling Nathan the prophet about building a house for the Lord. He did not say to himself, "I am also a prophet, so why should I ask another prophet?" that is, he also forgot his position as a king.

entries.section: (1) David's desire to build a house for the Lord

paragraphs.text: Nathan did not consult the Lord about David's desire, but expressed to him his own opinion about it, approving this desire of his and assuring him that the Lord would work for the success of this endeavor, because the Lord had supported him in all his ways before.

entries.section: (1) David's desire to build a house for the Lord

paragraphs.text: Since Nathan hastened and agreed to David's desire to build the house of God of cedar, God spoke to him the same night to speak to David and ask him, "Shall you build me a house?" By this God commends David's desire, but shows him that He had dwelt in a tent among His people since the days of Moses, Joshua and the judges, and had not asked any of the judges, that is, after the people settled in the Promised Land, to build Him a house. The appropriate time for building a house had not come, neither in the days of the judges nor in the days of David.
We note that God spoke to Nathan and did not speak to David, for two reasons:
1- Because Nathan was the one who hastened and agreed to David's desire, since it was logical and a beautiful spiritual desire, without consulting God, so God made known to him his mistake.

2- To establish humility in David's heart, for although he was a king and a prophet, he needed to hear the voice of God through another prophet, in addition to His informing him through Nathan, as we shall see, that it would not be he who would build Him a house, but his son.

God also postponed the building of a house for Himself to declare that He had not given them victories over the enemies so that they would build Him a house, for He has no need of a house of stones and wood, but rather wants to reign over the hearts of His children. Although it was Solomon who built the house of the Lord, his father David was greater in God's sight and his heart was like the heart of God.

entries.section: (1) David's desire to build a house for the Lord

paragraphs.text: The sheepcote: the pasture of the sheep.
"From following the sheep": from tending the sheep.

The Lord did not want to frustrate David or make him doubt that He was displeased with him, therefore He did not permit him to build the house, so the Lord enumerated to him His kindnesses to him, which show His love for him. Indeed He began His following speech about him by calling him "my servant David," a title by which the Lord calls His chosen prophets who are faithful to Him. Then He followed that by reminding him of those kindnesses, which consisted in making him king over his people after he had been merely a shepherd of sheep, in addition to supporting him in all the works he did, giving him victory over all the hostile peoples and removing from him those who troubled him and his rivals, and giving him a name and renown among his people and the surrounding peoples also, so that he became one of the great men of history.

entries.section: (1) David's desire to build a house for the Lord

paragraphs.text: The children of wickedness: the wicked peoples.

After the Lord had enumerated His kindnesses to David, He mentions here His works, the works of the Lord, for the sake of His people. After the people had been wandering in the earth with no homeland, He gave them a homeland to dwell in, the land of Canaan, and established them in their homeland, so they dwelt safe and secure, no longer enslaved and humiliated by another people as they had been in Egypt.

entries.section: (1) David's desire to build a house for the Lord

paragraphs.text: God shepherded His people anciently. Whenever the pagan peoples attacked them, with the Lord's permission because of their departing from His way, God would raise up "judges" to deliver them by their means from their enemies, and in the time of David God gave His people rest and gave them quiet and stability. This is at the level of the whole people; as for David himself, the Lord tells him that He will bless his family, so that it remains in the forefront even after his death, as will come in the following verses.

entries.section: (1) David's desire to build a house for the Lord

paragraphs.text: "Which shall proceed out of thy bowels": your son born of you.

The Lord foretold him that when the time came for his departure from the earth and he died as his fathers died, his son who came from his loins would take the kingdom after him, and the Lord would support him and establish him on the throne of the kingdom. He said "thy seed" and did not say "your son," because He does not mean only the building of the house by the hand of Solomon, but also Christ, who will build the house that lasts forever, which is the Church.

entries.section: (1) David's desire to build a house for the Lord

paragraphs.text: The Lord made clear to him that his son who would take the kingdom after him was the one charged with building the house of the Lord, for Solomon the son of David is the one who built the temple of the Lord. The Lord also promised that the kingdom of Judah would remain and all its kings would be from the house of David forever. This means, through the true and everlasting kingship of the Lord Jesus Christ for ever and ever, as is said in (Lk 1:32-33), "and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David: and he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end."

entries.section: (1) David's desire to build a house for the Lord

paragraphs.text: "If he commit iniquity": if he turns aside.
The rod of men: the enmities of the children of men and their transgressions.
The stripes of the children of men: the woes of diseases and crises that afflict a person.

God continues His words about Solomon and makes clear that He will look upon him as a son, so He will shepherd him and support him with special care, and the king is bound to God as to a father in a strong relationship. But the full meaning applies to Christ, who is His Son in essence and not by adoption as in the case of Solomon. Then He continues His words about Solomon and makes clear that He will treat him as a compassionate father treats his son, so if he turns aside from the straight way He will use disciplinary means with him, whether by exposing him to the troubles of human beings or to crises and afflictions, and this discipline will be for his good so that he may know his mistake and correct his way. But, says the Lord, I will not reject him or cast him off as I rejected Saul and took the kingdom from him and from his descendants, and so cleared the way for you. This was fulfilled with Solomon when he set up idols to please his wives, but he returned and repented and renounced all the riches of the world in the Book of Ecclesiastes. And when the sons of Solomon, King Rehoboam or those after him, sinned, He left them two tribes, and the kingdom of Judah continued after the kingdom of Israel, which had split off from it, for many years.

If some afflictions meet us in our life, let us not meet that with grumbling, but let us examine ourselves lest we have turned aside from upright conduct and God has permitted us some warnings to be for us an awakening to correct our course.

entries.section: (1) David's desire to build a house for the Lord

paragraphs.text: After your departure from this worldly life you will see with your spirit your house and your kingdom secure in progress and advancement, and the kingship will continue in your house a long time, in which all the kings of Judah will be of your descendants. This promise was fulfilled partially concerning David and his descendants, but the full fulfillment takes place in the person of the Lord Christ, who came in the flesh from the descendants of David to reign over the spiritual Israel, which is the believing people of God from all the nations, as an everlasting king with an everlasting authority that does not pass away.

entries.section: (1) David's desire to build a house for the Lord

paragraphs.text: The faithful servants of the Lord convey His message with all faithfulness and truthfulness. So did Nathan, and he told David all the words of the Lord which he heard from Him in the vision.

This is the mission of the servants of the Lord, which they are careful to perform with all faithfulness and truthfulness, namely conveying to the believers the Lord's message to them complete, without addition or omission, so that they may straighten their way and correct the course of their life in a manner that pleases the Lord.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: "Sat": that is, he rested a little to collect his thoughts and then knelt or bowed down, or the opposite: he began with prostration, and when he grew tired of the length of prayer he sat and completed his prayer. The sitting is not meant literally, but rather settling and being present before God.

David entered the tabernacle of meeting and appeared before the Lord prostrate and prayed the following prayer: You have done great things with me, my God, which I do not deserve. Who am I but a simple shepherd of sheep, the son of an ordinary man from the common people, so how did You raise me to this position to be king over Your people?! We note in David's words that he was not angry or grieved because God refused to let him build Him a house, but on the contrary he felt God's great favor to him in all his life and His favor to his descendants in that He would permit his son to build the house of the Lord.

Before we ask more of the Lord in our prayers, we must first thank Him for all the kindness and care with which He has flooded us in our life. Therefore our Church, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, places the prayer of thanksgiving at the beginning of every ritual service.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: "The manner of man": a wish that every person desires.

You were not content, my God, with these graces which You have poured out upon me, but You reassured me about what will happen in the future and for a long time to my descendants, and this is a wish that every person desires, to be reassured about the future of his children and grandchildren after him.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: "Thou, Lord GOD, knowest thy servant": You know what is in my heart.

I find myself unable to express my thanks and my acknowledgment of the favors with which You have flooded me, and the promises You promised me and my descendants. You know what is in my heart, for You are the searcher of hearts and the tester of thoughts, and You know my weaknesses and my mistakes.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: You did these great kindnesses which You promised would be for me and my descendants after me in honor of Your word, which is Your promises to me, and You informed me of them and made me know them.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: Truly You are a sole and unique God in Your greatness, and there is no God besides You, and we learned that from what we heard from Your prophets and from our fathers, who saw Your works and experienced Your love for Your people and Your care for them.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: "Terrible things": the plagues with which Pharaoh and his people were struck.

There is no nation on earth like Your people, whom You chose from among all the peoples, and You walked with them to rescue them and save them, and You gave them a distinguished place among the peoples, and their fame spread among them as the people of the Lord Jehovah, the mighty God of Israel.

David draws the attention of the people of Israel to the great works the Lord did for them, His awesome and fearful works such as the plagues with which Pharaoh and his people were struck, and the fear of the peoples of Canaan of His people whom He rescued from Egypt and drove out nations before them.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: You, Lord, chose Israel as a people special to You and established them forever apart from the rest of the peoples. This was in fact fulfilled despite Israel's fall and dispersion throughout the world by captivity, for Israel according to the flesh ended with the coming of Christ, so those who belong to Him, that is, the believers in Him, became the new people of Israel, whom the Lord will establish in the faith to the end.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: And now, Lord God, let Your promises be established forever with me and with my house, according to the word which You spoke to Your servant Nathan, so fulfill to us Your promises, and even if I sin or the members of my house sin, forgive us.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: David prays that the name of the Lord remain great and glorious in all generations, so that everyone may know that the God of Israel is the Lord of hosts; he also prays that He keep his house established before Him so that it does not become extinct.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: David said, because of Your grace to me, Lord, and Your promise to build me a house and establish it forever, I pray this prayer to You and thank You from all my heart.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: David declares his confidence in God's promises which He gave him by the mouth of Nathan, then asks Him to begin by giving blessing to him and to his house so that it remains blessed forever.

May we trust in God's promises so that they push us to every good work, and not be shaken if afflictions meet us, for God's promises must be fulfilled. We only persevere in prayer and striving and trust that He will complete His work in us.

David's victories and his administrative organization. (1) David's victory over the Philistines and the Moabites (vv. 1-2) 1 And after this it came to pass, that David smote the Philistines, and subdued them: and David took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines. 2 And he smote Moab, and measured them with a line, casting them down to the ground; even with two lines measured he to put to death, and with one full line to keep alive. And so the Moabites became David's servants, and brought gifts.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: The reins (Metheg): the bridle used with the horse, and what is meant here is control over.

The mother city (Ammah): that is, the capital, which is "Gath," the most important of the Philistine cities and close to the children of Israel, which had a fortified hall in which the chiefs of the Philistines gathered to plan attacking the children of Israel. Among the wars that David fought against the neighboring peoples and won was his war against the Philistines. It was not the first of the wars with them, for he had fought them before and defeated them, but they continued attacking the children of Israel, so this time he crushed them and subdued them and took the city of "Gath," the greatest of their cities, and by this the power of the Philistines was greatly weakened.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: "Measured them with a line": the line was the means of measuring anciently, whether of lands or, here, of men lined up in a single row.
"Casting them down to the ground": he made the Moabites lie on the ground beside one another or sit on the ground in a single row.
"With two lines measured he": that is, he took two thirds of the Moabites.
"With one full line": that is, a third of the Moabites.

There was friendship between David and the Moabites when he entrusted his father and mother to them when he was fleeing from the face of Saul (1 Sam 22), but it seems that wrongs, treachery and hard conduct occurred from the Moabites, so David was compelled to discipline them so that they would not be a source of continual trouble for the children of Israel. He seized the captives and measured them with two lines, that is, after he put them in a single row on the ground, he measured with a line, then the same length of line again, and the remainder was equal to one line, so by this he divided the Moabites and killed two thirds and kept a third alive.
It is implicitly understood that he killed the violent and stubborn fighters and kept alive the elders, women and children.

By this David broke the power of the Moabites, so they became servants subject to him, bringing gifts, that is tribute, whether of silver or gold or the produce of the field or sheep or anything of their products. David fulfilled the prophecy of Balaam, "a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab" (Num 24:17).

David took the capital of the Philistines and broke the mighty men of Moab, so the land submitted to him. So be strong in your striving against the lust that dominates you or the sin into which you repeatedly fall .. hold fast to God with many prayers and fasts and give up anything that feeds this sin, and God will give you victory and subject your body and spirit to Him, so that you live in peace.

(2) David's victory over the king of "Zobah" (vv. 3-8) 3 David smote also Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates. 4 And David took from him a thousand and seven hundred horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: and David houghed all the chariot horses, but reserved of them for an hundred chariots. 5 And when the Syrians of Damascus came to succour Hadadezer king of Zobah, David slew of the Syrians two and twenty thousand men. 6 Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus: and the Syrians became servants to David, and brought gifts. And the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went. 7 And David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadadezer, and brought them to Jerusalem. 8 And from Betah, and from Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, king David took exceeding much brass.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: Hadadezer the son of Rehob: he is the king of Zobah.

Zobah: one of the kingdoms of Aram, lying north of Damascus and extending from Hamath in the west to the river Euphrates in the east. It is a wide kingdom and includes several small kingdoms, all under the control of Hadadezer.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: Some regions of the kingdom of Zobah declared rebellion against their king Hadadezer, so he went to fight them to restore his authority over them. There was continual hostility between Israel and the kingdom of Zobah, so David seized this opportunity and attacked them from behind at Hamath and defeated them (1 Chr 18:2).

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: "Houghed the chariot horses": he commanded that their hamstrings be cut so that they become unfit for war.

In that war David captured huge numbers of enemy soldiers, reaching 20 thousand footmen and 1,700 horsemen, besides the chariots, most of which he destroyed and only 100 chariots were left, which is a small number not fit for war but used for transporting goods. David also commanded that the hamstrings of the horses be cut so that they become unfit for war.

It is mentioned in (1 Chr 18:4) that he took "a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen." The "thousand" here in the Second Book of Samuel means a thousand chariots, and the seven hundred horsemen mean seven hundred commanders of cavalry units, and the unit is ten horsemen, so the number of horsemen is seven thousand as stated in the Book of Chronicles. The omission of "chariot" here is customary for brevity, so the conclusion is that David captured 20 thousand footmen and seven thousand horsemen and took a thousand chariots.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: Syria of Damascus: one of the small Aramean states. The Arameans possessed this city at the time of the rise of the kingdom of Israel, and it lies in the land of Aram, which extends from Lebanon to the Euphrates and from the Taurus mountains to Damascus and beyond.
There was friendship between the king of Damascus and the king of Zobah, so the king of Damascus went to help Hadadezer against David, but David defeated him and killed 22 thousand of his soldiers.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: David appointed over the cities of Syria of Damascus what are known today as "military governors," so as to be safe from their rebelling against him and so that they would collect the tribute for him, and the Arameans submitted to his authority.
The secret behind all David's victories and successes and his deliverance from the plots of his enemies was the power of God supporting him.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: Shields of gold: the shield is a sturdy metal disc used by the warrior to protect himself from the arrows that the enemy shoots. The shields of the soldiers of Hadadezer were of gold, or of wood overlaid with gold.
Betah: an Aramean city also called "Tibhath" as in (1 Chr 18:8). It exists now under the same name and lies between Aleppo and the Euphrates.

Berothai: a city in northern Palestine, now the village of "Brinan," which lies 10 km south-west of Baalbek, and is called Chun as it appears in (1 Chr 18:8). David took the golden shields that the Arameans use in war, and he also took from the two Aramean cities of "Betah" and "Berothai" exceeding much brass, and brought these precious spoils to Jerusalem.
All these quantities of gold and brass David afterwards handed over to his son Solomon to use in building the temple.

God's power supporting you cannot be overcome by anyone, however much the wicked gather against you. So do not be troubled by any threats, but remember the name of your God and beseech Him, and He will deliver you and protect you from all evil.

(3) The king of Hamath congratulates David on his victories (vv. 9-12) 9 When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had smitten all the host of Hadadezer, 10 Then Toi sent Joram his son unto king David, to salute him, and to bless him, because he had fought against Hadadezer, and smitten him: for Hadadezer had wars with Toi. And Joram brought with him vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and vessels of brass: 11 Which also king David did dedicate unto the LORD, with the silver and gold that he had dedicated of all nations which he subdued; 12 Of Syria, and of Moab, and of the children of Ammon, and of the Philistines, and of Amalek, and of the spoil of Hadadezer, son of Rehob, king of Zobah.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: Toi king of Hamath: one of the Hittite kings, king over Hamath.
Hamath: a small kingdom neighboring Zobah.
Joram: he is called Hadoram in (1 Chr 18:10), and he is the son of Toi.

The news of Hadadezer's defeat before David reached Toi king of "Hamath," and for him it was happy news, since there was enmity between him and Hadadezer caused by previous wars between them. Toi sent his son Joram to David to congratulate him on his victory, to inquire about his well-being and to pray for blessing for him, and he carried with him precious gifts, which were vessels of gold, silver and brass. David's acceptance of the gift shows that he was a man of peace and did not want war without cause.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: Syria (Aram): they dwelt in Mesopotamia and then dispersed westward to many places. When we read in (1 Chr 18:12) Edom instead of Aram, that is because there was a treaty between Aram and Edom, so when David defeated them, the writer of the Second Book of Samuel wrote Aram as the more important in this alliance, and the writer of the Book of Chronicles wrote Edom because it was the more important in his view.

Moab: they dwelt east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea (v. 2). The children of Ammon: they dwelt east of the Jordan north of Moab. The news of the victory over them is mentioned in (ch. 10). The Philistines: they dwelt south of the children of Israel and east and south of the Mediterranean Sea, and the victory over them is mentioned in (ch. 5:17-25, 8:1). Amalek: they dwelt south of the children of Israel and the Philistines and north of Sinai. The news of the victory over them is mentioned in (1 Sam 30). Hadadezer: the victory over him is mentioned in (vv. 3, 4). The gifts that Joram presented to David, he set apart, together with the spoils he took from the peoples he fought, for the Lord, and kept them so that Solomon his son might use them in making the requirements of the house of the Lord, the vessels and their accessories, as well as the requirements of constructing the building itself and adorning it. The inspired text mentions some of the peoples who were the source of David's spoils and those who gave him gifts, namely: Aram, Moab, the children of Ammon, the Philistines, Amalek, Zobah.
Thus we see how David prepared for his son Solomon, and helped him, in building the temple of the Lord, by the following:
1- He fought the peoples who troubled the people of God and defeated them, so peace prevailed, which helped Solomon to build the house of the Lord.
2- Accepting gifts and establishing good relations with the surrounding peoples who respect the people of God, and this establishes peace for the kingdom of God.
3- He prepared the building materials that Solomon would need to build the house.

Just as David took care to prepare for the building of the house of the Lord by collecting gold, silver and brass, may we care not only for building our churches but even more for reverence and respect when entering them and during the prayers, so that we feel the presence of God and enjoy His work in us.

(4) The administrative organization (vv. 13-18) 13 And David gat him a name when he returned from smiting of the Syrians in the valley of salt, being eighteen thousand men. 14 And he put garrisons in Edom; throughout all Edom put he garrisons, and all they of Edom became David's servants. And the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went. 15 And David reigned over all Israel; and David executed judgment and justice unto all his people. 16 And Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the host; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder; 17 And Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, were the priests; and Seraiah was the scribe; 18 And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the executioners and the runners; and David's sons were priests.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: The valley of salt: south of the Dead Sea, also called the Sea of the Arabah. It is one of the places to which rainwater gathers in winter carrying a large quantity of salt, and when the water evaporates in summer the salt remains in the form of sheets.
A monument: a pillar or wall set up to remind of important things.

David set up a memorial monument on the occasion of his victory over the Arameans and his killing of 18 thousand of them in the "valley of salt," to be a witness to the great work of God with His people and a declaration before the hostile peoples reminding them of the power of the God "Jehovah," the God of Israel, who stands behind the victories of His people and does not permit anyone to harm them or challenge them. It is mentioned in (1 Chr 18:12) that the victory was over Edom, and as we mentioned, there was an alliance between Aram and Edom, so each book mentions one of the allies. The Book of Chronicles also mentions that the victor was Abishai, and this does not contradict what is mentioned here, because Abishai was one of David's military commanders.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: Just as David organized the administrative aspects in Aram and appointed "military governors," so he also did in Edom, so as to ensure the stability of the region under his authority, so the Edomites submitted to David and paid him tribute. The inspired text repeats once more the Lord's support of David in all that he turns to of works, whether military or organizational.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: David was truly a ruler chosen by his people; all the tribes pledged allegiance to him and declared their loyalty to him. He was a just ruler who showed partiality to no one in governing, neither he nor the judges appointed by him, so the people lived under his leadership in stability and security.

entries.section: (2) David's prayer

paragraphs.text: David appointed officials to the main ruling positions in the state as follows:
Joab: supreme commander of the army, which is equivalent to a minister of war and commander-in-chief today, so he organizes his armed forces to be ready to face any external aggression.

Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud: recorder, who records the official decisions issued by the state and the laws and regulations that the king decrees, in addition to recording the important historical events in the life of the kingdom and the king, of wars and victories.

Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar: two heads of the priests who shared the service of the Lord. The first, "Zadok," for the service of the tabernacle of meeting, which was still in "Gibeon," while "Ahimelech" was for the service of the ark of the covenant of the Lord, which David had moved to Jerusalem. This appointment showed David's concern for the spiritual service for the sake of his people.

Seraiah: to organize the state's accounts and supervise the collection of tribute and organize the censuses. Benaiah the son of Jehoiada: commander of the royal guard and head of the infantry battalions under the command of Joab, the commander of the army.

The executioners: they are the keepers of security and guards of the king, and they also carry out the sentences of flogging on the guilty. In the time of David they were of the Cherethites, that is, the original inhabitants of Judea, and they used foreign executioners such as the Cretans so that they would not show partiality in sedition or sentences to any person because of kinship.

The runners: they are the foot soldiers; Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was their head in the days of King David. David's sons: what is meant here is not their being anointed to the priesthood or performing its rites, because that was limited to the descendants of Aaron and the tribe of Levi, while David and his sons were of the tribe of Judah. So the intended meaning of priests here is that they were counselors to their father, constantly attending him, and he describes them figuratively here as priests because priests are mediators between the people and God, just as David's sons were helpers to him and mediators between the people and him, that is, they cared about the problems of the people and met with their father to solve them. So the word priest here means a servant and mediator and not the Aaronic priesthood.

May every father and mother and servant or official in any place organize his responsibilities and involve others with him in them, and follow them up with patience, encouragement and firmness, so that he enjoys peace and growth in his spiritual and social life. David and Mephibosheth

entries.section: (1) Honoring the descendants of Saul

paragraphs.text: When a person's affairs are settled, he often forgets God and the doing of good. David, however, with his great heart, once he was settled began to seek to do good even to the one who had been most hostile to him, King Saul. He did not forget the covenant he had made with Saul (1 Sam 24:20-22), and likewise with his son Jonathan, to care for their descendants (1 Sam 20:12-17). Out of his love for Jonathan he sought to fulfill his promise, and so he asked those around him whether anyone of the house of Saul was still alive.

Because David was a king appointed by God, he did not act like the other kings of the world, who destroy the offspring of the kings before them. And here we see how the love and care that Jonathan had sown toward David, and his protecting him when Saul wanted to kill him, God repaid to him through David's care for his son Mephibosheth.

Do not forget your covenants with God and with people. If God is faithful in His covenant with you to care for you, why are you negligent in your covenants and in keeping His commandments? He loves you, so renew your covenants with Him to the measure that suits you, in specific exercises; and if you tend to forget, write down your covenants with God and with people so that you may carry them out.

entries.section: (1) Honoring the descendants of Saul

paragraphs.text: David's men set about searching for someone who could tell them news of the house of Saul and who of them remained alive. They came to a servant of the house of Saul whose name was “Ziba,” and they ordered him to come before David, who asked him whether he was “Ziba,” and he answered that he was.

entries.section: (1) Honoring the descendants of Saul

paragraphs.text: The king asked him whether anyone of the house of Saul was still alive, that he might show him kindness. Ziba answered him that there was a son of Jonathan who was lame in both feet (he is Mephibosheth, who was mentioned in ch. 4:4).

Every good deed we do for others is in truth directed to God Himself, as the Lord Christ said: “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me” (Mt 25:40).

entries.section: (1) Honoring the descendants of Saul

paragraphs.text: Lo-debar: a place in Gilead, called Debir in (Josh 10:38), and now known as Umm ad-Dabar, south of Wadi al-Arab, east of the Jordan.

David asked him where he could find this son, and he answered that he was in the house of “Machir the son of Ammiel,” in the land of Gilead. This man was noble in hiding Mephibosheth with him so that no one would harm him, and he must have done so out of loyalty to Saul. He was also loyal to David, for he honored David and his men when they came to Mahanaim in flight from his son Absalom, who had risen in revolt against him (ch. 17:27-29).

entries.section: (1) Honoring the descendants of Saul

paragraphs.text: David sent messengers to the house of Machir to bring Mephibosheth from there to him in Jerusalem. Saul had other sons and grandsons, such as his sons by Rizpah and his grandsons by Merab (1 Chr 8:33), but Ziba did not mention them. We do not know Mephibosheth's feelings when he was summoned: was he afraid of some harm intended for him by David, or did he believe what he had heard from Ziba, that David wished to do him good? In any case, he had to go to David.

entries.section: (2) David's meeting with Mephibosheth

paragraphs.text: Mephibosheth came to David and showed his great respect and submission to him, for he bowed down before him and declared his complete readiness to obey him, saying, “Behold thy servant!”

entries.section: (2) David's meeting with Mephibosheth

paragraphs.text: Saul thy father: a grandfather is counted as a father to his grandchildren.

David reassured him and made him understand that his purpose in bringing him was to show him kindness, in faithfulness to his friendship with his father Jonathan. Mephibosheth did not know of the friendly relationship that had existed between his father and David, for he was only five years old when his father died. David also promised to restore to him all the lands of his grandfather Saul, which had passed to David after the death of Ishbosheth and the return of Michal to him as wife. And to honor him further, he ordered that he should eat his food at the king's table as one of his own household.

entries.section: (2) David's meeting with Mephibosheth

paragraphs.text: Mephibosheth had not expected this generous treatment from David, and he could do nothing but bow down a second time in thanks and appreciation, for he had thought himself a nobody after the kingship had departed from the house of Saul, and he likened himself to a dead dog, which has no strength and no use.

Long before, David had bowed down to Jonathan as heir to the throne in the days of the kingship of his father Saul (1 Sam 20:41); and now God restores honor to the humble David, so that the son of Jonathan bows down to him.

Does this expression not call for some reflection here? Is it not the very same expression, “a dead dog,” that David used when he was being hunted by Saul (1 Sam 24:14)? The days turn, and the grandson of Saul says it to David! But David had said it in great humility despite his strength and despite Saul having fallen into his hands, whereas Mephibosheth says it in the face of David's gifts and his love that surpasses understanding.
Be humble and thankful to everyone who honors you, for thanks is the least thing that can be offered to the generous. And thank God, who has made people honor you.

entries.section: (3) David's gifts to Mephibosheth

paragraphs.text: Thou shalt till: that is, you shall plow the land and sow it.
Bring in the fruits: that is, bring forth produce from the land.

David gave his instructions to Ziba. He first informed him that he had granted to Mephibosheth, his master, all that had belonged to Saul of agricultural lands, on condition that Ziba, the members of his household and his servants should cultivate the land and look after it so that it would yield abundant crops, providing food and the other needs for Mephibosheth and his household; and he also decreed that Mephibosheth should eat his food at the king's table. It appears from this verse that Ziba was the head of a large household, for he had fifteen sons, besides daughters, as well as twenty servants, all of whom were able to look after the wide lands that David had given to Mephibosheth.

entries.section: (3) David's gifts to Mephibosheth

paragraphs.text: Ziba promised King David that he would carry out everything he had commanded him exactly. And David added the following statement, confirming his honoring of Mephibosheth, that he should always eat at the king's table as one of his sons.

entries.section: (3) David's gifts to Mephibosheth

paragraphs.text: Micha: the son of Mephibosheth and grandson of Jonathan. His name appears as the son of “Merib-baal” in (1 Chr 8:
34), and likewise in (1 Chr 9:40), who is Mephibosheth himself.

The inspired text mentions here a son of Mephibosheth, Micha, who is mentioned again in (1 Chr 8:35-39) and (1 Chr 9:41-44) as head of a clan among the clans of Benjamin. And (1 Chr 8:40) adds that among his descendants there were mighty men of valor, strong in wars, who had many sons and grandsons. In accordance with the king's command, all the members of Ziba's household and his servants obeyed and served Mephibosheth in all the property and lands that were restored to him. This lasted for a time, and then Ziba turned against Mephibosheth afterward, as the inspired text will tell us, and falsely slandered him to the king (ch. 16:1-4, 19:24-30).

entries.section: (3) David's gifts to Mephibosheth

paragraphs.text: From that time Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem so as to be near King David, who regarded him as one of his own circle who ate at his table. The lands of his grandfather Saul that David restored to him were in Gibeah of Benjamin, and Ziba tended them and brought their produce to him. And as we learned in (ch. 4:4), Mephibosheth was lame in both feet as a result of his nurse fleeing with him and dropping him from her hand to the ground, and he remained so all his life.

Reflect on God's gifts to you, so that you may trust in His care and your heart may be at peace, and you may feel how very beloved you are to His heart; then you will reject every sin and live for Him, enjoying fellowship with Him.
David's victories over the Ammonites and the Arameans

entries.section: (1) The insult of the king of Ammon to David

paragraphs.text: The children of Ammon: they are the descendants of Lot, and they dwell east of the Jordan River, and there were many wars between them and the children of Israel. Nahash, their king, was a friend of David because of the hostility of both toward Saul. Nahash king of the Ammonites, who had been hostile to the children of Israel, died; Saul had confronted him and defeated him (1 Sam 11). After his death his son Hanun reigned in his place.

entries.section: (1) The insult of the king of Ammon to David

paragraphs.text: It seems that Nahash king of the Ammonites had done some good to David, perhaps when David was fleeing from Saul; so when Nahash died, David sent messengers to console his son Hanun, who reigned after him.

entries.section: (1) The insult of the king of Ammon to David

paragraphs.text: Hanun's counselors suspected the messengers of David and told the king that they had come to spy out the land and learn its fortifications so that David might attack him, and that the purpose of their visit was not consolation.

entries.section: (1) The insult of the king of Ammon to David

paragraphs.text: Buttocks: the hinder part of the body, from behind.

Hanun rushed without wisdom after his counselors, and he insulted David's messengers and despised them by shaving off half of their beards and cutting off their garments from behind up to the buttocks, to mock David and his people.

entries.section: (1) The insult of the king of Ammon to David

paragraphs.text: David's messengers were in great shame at the insult that had come upon them, and they sent to David to tell him what Hanun had done to them. King David was greatly displeased at this foolish conduct on the part of Hanun, and he sent them new garments and told them to remain at Jericho until their beards had grown again, and then to return to Jerusalem.

Do not rush after any counsel you hear, however close the counselors may be to you, for they may sometimes lack wisdom. Examine the matter, seek God's guidance, and return to your father and spiritual guide, and you will always act wisely.

entries.section: (2) David's victory over the Ammonites

paragraphs.text: They stank before David: David hated them because of what they had done.
Beth-rehob (Aram): a small Aramean state near Hamath, in the upper Jordan valley in northern Palestine, near Dan.

Aram-zobah or Zobah: a small Aramean state west of the Euphrates, which belonged to King Hadadezer (ch. 8:3). Maacah: this is Aram-maacah, a small Aramean state east of the Jordan near Mount Hermon. Tob: a region east of the Jordan.

The children of Ammon felt that their insult to the messengers whom David had sent must have angered him and that David would surely punish them, so they prepared armies for the war that David might wage against them. Since they were weaker than David in military strength, they hired soldiers from the surrounding Aramean peoples, and the numbers of those soldiers were as follows:

20 thousand footmen from Beth-rehob and Zoba, a thousand men from Maacah, and 12 thousand men from Tob. And in (1 Chr 19) we find other details about the preparations of the king of the Ammonites, namely that he hired a large number of horsemen and war chariots, and that the king of Maacah went out himself to fight with him.

entries.section: (2) David's victory over the Ammonites

paragraphs.text: David took note of the Ammonites' preparation of armies, so he in turn commissioned the commander of his army, Joab, to summon the chosen, mighty men of war to meet the armies of the children of Ammon and those with them.

entries.section: (2) David's victory over the Ammonites

paragraphs.text: The children of Ammon arranged their ranks according to a plan they had devised to surprise David's armies with: the Ammonites drew up at the entrance of their capital “Rabbah” to meet David's armies if they came from the north, while the Arameans drew up in the plain east of the Dead Sea to confront David's armies if they came from the south.

entries.section: (2) David's victory over the Ammonites

paragraphs.text: Joab found two parties ready to attack him, the hired Arameans from the north and the Ammonites dwelling in Rabbah from the south. So he drew up his plan to match the plan that the children of Ammon had laid down: he also divided his army into two parts, each part facing a part of the enemy's armies. He himself led the chosen, that is the strongest, part, which had to face the hired Arameans because they were the stronger party, while he assigned his brother Abishai to command the part that had to face the Ammonites.

entries.section: (2) David's victory over the Ammonites

paragraphs.text: Joab agreed with his brother Abishai that each of them would watch the other's position in the battle, so that if the fighting position of one of them was in danger, the other would come to his aid.

entries.section: (2) David's victory over the Ammonites

paragraphs.text: Joab encouraged his younger brother Abishai, stressing in his words the need to endure and to fight with courage for the sake of the victory of their people and the preservation of its honor among the nations, and in defense of the land that the Lord had given them. They must strive as far as they were able, and the Lord would complete the rest.

If the forces of the enemy devil attack us and we feel that the war against us is fierce, let us strive and resist him, firmly grounded in faith in the word of the Lord, who gave us authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy.

entries.section: (2) David's victory over the Ammonites

paragraphs.text: Joab attacked the Arameans, and with God's help the Arameans were afraid of him and fled. This terrified the children of Ammon, for if the mighty Arameans had fled, what would the armies of the children of Israel do to them? So they were very afraid and fled before them.

entries.section: (2) David's victory over the Ammonites

paragraphs.text: When the news of the flight of the Arameans before David reached the Ammonites, their allies in the war, their morale weakened and they were certain that they could not stand alone after the Arameans' withdrawal from the field of battle. So they too decided to withdraw before Abishai and retreated into their city “Rabbah of Ammon” in order to reorder their ranks, for after a year they attacked the children of Israel, as is recorded in (ch. 11). And when Joab saw that the enemies had scattered and fled from the fight, he returned rejoicing in the victory to Jerusalem, and perhaps David sang at that time Psalms 2, 20, 21, and 110.

entries.section: (3) David's victory over Hadadezer

paragraphs.text: The Arameans did not accept the defeat that the people of Israel had inflicted on them, so they decided to gather their military forces again and to bring other Aramean states into their ranks so as to increase the numbers of their armies.

entries.section: (3) David's victory over Hadadezer

paragraphs.text: He brought out the Arameans beyond the River: he placed them at the front of the armies because of their courage.
Aram beyond the River is the name by which the Hebrews called Aram-naharaim (Naharaim, “the two rivers,” referring to the Tigris and the Euphrates). Helam: a place east of the Jordan.
Shobach: the commander of the army of Hadadezer, king of Aram-zobah and the greatest of the kings of the Arameans.

Hadadezer was the leader of the effort to reconstitute the armies. He had previously fought a battle against David in which he was also defeated (ch. 8:3), so he sought vengeance for his earlier defeats before David. He therefore summoned the Arameans dwelling between the Tigris and the Euphrates and placed them at the front of his armies because they were famous for courage and strength, and he appointed “Shobach,” the commander-in-chief of Hadadezer's army, to lead them, and these armies drew up at “Helam.”

entries.section: (3) David's victory over Hadadezer

paragraphs.text: The news of the movements of the Aramean armies and their preparations reached David, so he decided to lead the army of Israel himself and to take the initiative in the war. He crossed the Jordan River and came with his armies to “Helam,” and the two parties made ready for battle.

entries.section: (3) David's victory over Hadadezer

paragraphs.text: Once again the Lord gave victory to Israel: David slew the soldiers of seven hundred chariots, each chariot carrying ten soldiers, and he also slew 40 thousand horsemen and footmen, as well as “Shobach” the commander of the enemy's armies.

It is mentioned in (1 Chr 19:18) that he slew 40 thousand footmen, while here it is 40 thousand horsemen. Each writer saw the part most important in his view and ascribed the whole to it: in 2 Samuel the forty thousand are ascribed to the horsemen although they were of both horsemen and footmen, and the opposite in the First Book of Chronicles, which ascribes them to the footmen.

entries.section: (3) David's victory over Hadadezer

paragraphs.text: When it became clear to the Aramean kings, who had originally joined under the banner of their supreme king Hadadezer, that they had not the strength to stand against the people of Israel, they made peace with them, by which they acknowledged submission to Israel, and no longer responded to any request from the Ammonites to ally with them in any wars against the children of Israel. And by the victory over the Arameans and their subjection to the children of Israel, the borders of David's kingdom extended to the Euphrates, fulfilling God's promise to Abraham that his descendants would possess the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates (Gen 15:18); and what is meant by the Nile is the seasonal river east of the wilderness of Sinai, that is, west of the Philistines, whom David defeated.

If troubles multiply upon you, or many gather against you, do not be alarmed, for your God is stronger than all the world and is able to deliver you and give you victory over them. Hold fast to Him with much prayer and persistence, and you will receive His power, which is able to do all things.
David's sin with Bathsheba

entries.section: (1) David's successive victories over the children of Ammon

paragraphs.text: After the year was expired: after a year had passed.
At the time when kings go forth to battle: at the time of the year when kings usually go out to wage wars, which is spring or summer, when the weather is suitable.
Rabbah: the capital of the children of Ammon, situated on the Jabbok River, a tributary of the Jordan.

When David saw that the children of Ammon were not submitting to him like the rest of the surrounding lands, and that they were trying to renew their strength and prepare for war, he decided, a year after fighting them and the Arameans, to wage a third war on the children of Ammon, to discipline them and break them completely, so that they would no longer think of stirring up war against the children of Israel again. He put Joab at the head of the army, together with the men of war from all the tribes of Israel, and they destroyed their cities and lands and besieged their capital “Rabbah.” This time David did not go out to war with his army but remained in Jerusalem.
Thus David triumphed over the enemies surrounding the kingdom of the children of Israel and subdued them in seven wars, which are:
1- The war against the Jebusites.
2- The war against the Philistines and their allies alone.
3- The war against the Moabites.
4- The war against Hadadezer.
5- The war against Edom.
6- The war against the children of Ammon and Aram.

May you put an end to everything connected with sin, and keep nothing that reminds you of it, lest Satan use it against you in your time of weakness; and give up anything that binds you to sin, however dear it may be to you.

entries.section: (2) David's adultery

paragraphs.text: This chapter and the next speak of the great sin into which David fell, which left an evil mark upon him and upon his house. After David had eaten his midday meal and rested a little, he rose to walk a while on the roof of his house, and he saw a woman of surpassing beauty bathing in a place near his house; and when his eyes fell upon her, he desired her in his heart.

David abandoned his striving with his army and gave himself over to idleness, and so he fell into sin. Perhaps this gives us a strong lesson to continue always in our striving, to avoid what is unbecoming to the children of God, and to shun the idleness that may be an open door to practices that do not please the Lord.

entries.section: (2) David's adultery

paragraphs.text: Bathsheba the daughter of Eliam: she is also called “Bath-shua the daughter of Ammiel,” as is recorded in (1 Chr 3:5); her first son died and the second was Solomon.

David asked those around him who this woman was, and he was told that she was Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite. He was one of the heroes of David's army (ch. 23:39), and was originally a pagan of the sons of Heth but became a Jew, or his father became a Jew and so he became a Jew.

entries.section: (2) David's adultery

paragraphs.text: David sent and summoned Bathsheba to his house, and perhaps he showed his servants that he wished to inquire after her welfare because she was the wife of one of the chief commanders of his army. He was alone with her and caressed her until he slipped and lay with her. She had finished the seven days of her menstruation (her monthly period), during which she was unclean according to the Law and no one could touch her (Lev 12:1), and he supposed, according to expectation, that conception could not occur immediately after the seven days.

We must take care for true purity and not merely outward purity, and not do as David did, who was careful not to touch Bathsheba during the days of her menstruation but did what was far worse, because his heart had already been defiled within; so he caressed her until he committed adultery with her. Therefore let us train ourselves to control our senses, because through them sin enters, which defiles body and spirit together.

entries.section: (2) David's adultery

paragraphs.text: The fruit of sin soon appeared, and the woman conceived. This was a great predicament, exposing her to death by the judgment of the Law (Lev 20:10), so she sent to David to tell him of the situation that he might rescue her. Thus we see the justice of God, who permitted David to be exposed although the likelihood of conception was very slight, so that David and all generations might know the importance of vigilance and of keeping away from sin, even if it could be hidden from the eyes of people.

entries.section: (3) The failure of the attempt to cover the sin

paragraphs.text: David thought, and his thinking led him to a plan which he supposed would bring him out of this predicament. He sent to the commander of his army, Joab, to send Uriah to him, and Joab did so and sent Uriah to him.

entries.section: (3) The failure of the attempt to cover the sin

paragraphs.text: Uriah carried out the order summoning him to the king, not knowing the reason for it. David told him that, because of his trust in him and his knowledge of his ability to judge rightly the military situation of the battle raging against the children of Ammon, he had summoned him in order to ask him about the progress of the war, the welfare of Joab, and the welfare of the army.

entries.section: (3) The failure of the attempt to cover the sin

paragraphs.text: Wash thy feet: to wash after the long journey.
A mess of meat: a portion of food.

David showed great hospitality to Uriah, permitting him to go to his house and wash after the toils of the long journey, and as soon as he left him, he sent after him a choice portion of delicious food so that he and his wife might eat. But in reality this honor was not for Uriah; David's aim was that he should spend the night with his wife, so that people would think that Bathsheba's child was Uriah's, and thereby he would hide his sin.

entries.section: (3) The failure of the attempt to cover the sin

paragraphs.text: Uriah did not wish to go to his house to sleep there, but spent his night in one of the rooms set apart for the lodging of the royal guard, which were beside the gate of the royal palace.

entries.section: (3) The failure of the attempt to cover the sin

paragraphs.text: Some of David's men told him that Uriah had not gone to his house to sleep there, and David was bewildered by the matter and asked him why he had not taken advantage of being near his house to rest in it with his wife. David's agitation appears here because of his fear that his sin would be exposed, and perhaps this agitation was evident to those around him; for these are the inevitable results of sin.

entries.section: (3) The failure of the attempt to cover the sin
