paragraphs.text: Uriah answered him that it was not fitting for him to lodge in his house with his wife while the ark of the covenant of the Lord was in a tent, and the soldiers of the children of Israel, whether of the tribe of Judah or of the other tribes, and Joab the commander of the army, were all lodging in tents they had pitched in the open field near the battlefield; so how, this being the case, could he allow himself to rest and take his ease with his wife? And he swore by the life of the king that he would not do this.

entries.section: (3) The failure of the attempt to cover the sin

paragraphs.text: David gave him leave for another day, on condition that he would let him return to the battlefield after the two days had passed, so Uriah stayed in Jerusalem another day in compliance with the king's order. We wonder here why David gave him leave for another day when Uriah was occupied with thoughts of the war, because he was an important commander among David's commanders. Of course the reason is clear: perhaps he would long to see his wife and go into his house, and there would be an opportunity for him to lie with her, and so David would hide his sin.

entries.section: (3) The failure of the attempt to cover the sin

paragraphs.text: After David had given Uriah the opportunity of another day, he noticed that he had not gone into his house, so he invited him to eat the midday meal with him, and deliberately made him drink much wine until he was drunk, and he went out from David's presence at evening. David thought that, with Uriah having lost his senses, he would long for his wife and go to his house in a state of drunkenness and lie with her; but Uriah's subconscious mind was occupied with the war and with fulfilling his duty as a commander for God's sake, so that even when he was drunk he did not return to his house but slept with the king's servants.

Sin is sinful and its results are distressing, so do not be drawn to its desire, for within its honey is poison. Keep away from every source of sin, however small it may seem, and you will live in purity and enjoy peace, and you will be able to be with God and to carry out your work successfully.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Uriah in the war

paragraphs.text: When David's attempts with Uriah failed, he thought of another scheme. He sent a written letter, sealed and closed, to Joab by the hand of Uriah, telling him in it to set Uriah in the forefront of the ranks when the battle grew fierce, and to order the rest of his soldiers to withdraw from around him so that he would receive the blows alone, be struck, and die. Here we see how cruel David was and how unjust to an innocent man who carried in his own hand the letter of his death like one carrying his own shroud, and this shows how sin drags other sins along with it.

Let us beware of the first step and be aware of how sin enters a person gradually, for as soon as one falls into a single sin, it drags after it many sins. David's sin began with a look, and then the other sins followed in its train, so that there was the sin of adultery, then murder.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Uriah in the war

paragraphs.text: Joab obeyed the king's order. When he besieged the city of “Rabbah of Ammon,” the capital of the Ammonites, he put Uriah at the head of the army in the most difficult position, opposite the strongest men of the enemy, and then ordered his men to withdraw from around Uriah and leave him alone to face the enemy forces.
The enemy's soldiers came out to defend their capital, and some of the soldiers of the army of Israel were killed, among them Uriah the Hittite.

And here we see how Joab carried out David's words with skill, not only in obedience to the king, but in order to catch him in a fault, namely murder, so that David would no longer rebuke him for killing Abner; and thus Joab shared with David in the sin of murder. For whoever falls into sin wants to justify himself by seeing those around him fallen into sin, so that his conscience may not reproach him and he may not repent.

David felt humiliated and weak before Joab and could not harm him despite his evil deeds, so he charged his son Solomon to repay him according to his deeds (1 Kgs 2:5, 6). And we note Joab's strength in rebuking David after Joab killed Absalom, when David did not speak to him for fear of him (ch. 19:5-8).

entries.section: (4) The killing of Uriah in the war

paragraphs.text: Joab sent a message to the king informing him that his orders concerning the military plans had been fully carried out, and telling him the state of the battles in progress and the remaining details of the war against the children of Ammon.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Uriah in the war

paragraphs.text: His message was oral, and he charged the messenger to observe the effect of his words on the king: if he found that the king was displeased because they had come near the wall of the city of Rabbah, he was to tell him that Uriah was among those killed. This was because Joab knew in his shrewdness that the king would understand that it was a deliberate plan to be rid of Uriah according to the king's own orders. They should not have approached the walls, because the enemy hurled huge stones to strike the soldiers besieging the city, and it would have been better to besiege it from a distance. The king might remind the messenger of the death of Abimelech the son of Gideon, who was besieging his enemies in the tower of the city of “Thebez,” when a woman cast a piece of a millstone upon him from the top of the wall and broke his skull (Judg 9:
50-54.) (Joab ordered his messenger that, if he noticed David's anger at what he reported to him.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Uriah in the war

paragraphs.text: The messenger left the field of battle and went to Jerusalem, making for the king's house, and told the king all that Joab had sent him with.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Uriah in the war

paragraphs.text: The messenger related the details of the events to the king, saying that the enemy had prevailed against them when they went out from the city into the plain to fight them there, and the soldiers of Israel launched a counterattack that forced the enemy to fall back to the entrance of the city, which brought the soldiers of Israel close to the wall of the city, and the enemy took advantage of this position to shoot arrows at them from the wall. Perhaps the messenger noticed the king's displeasure at the situation, and so he hastened to tell him of the death of Uriah.

entries.section: (4) The killing of Uriah in the war

paragraphs.text: David was relieved when he heard of Uriah's death, and the signs of anger vanished from his face. He charged the messenger with a reply to Joab, telling him not to be grieved over the killing of a number of his soldiers, for on the battlefields everyone is exposed to death. He added in his message that Joab must take courage and fight against the city strongly until the army of Israel entered it and destroyed it. Then he charged the messenger to encourage Joab and strengthen his resolve on behalf of the king.

entries.section: (5) David marries Bathsheba

paragraphs.text: The inhabitants of Jerusalem learned, from following the news of their army, that Uriah had died. Bathsheba his wife learned the news of his death, and she did what custom required of her of lamenting and weeping, regardless of her inner feeling.

entries.section: (5) David marries Bathsheba

paragraphs.text: The mourning: a period of usually seven days, like the mourning for Saul (1 Sam 31:13). After the mourning for Uriah ended and the days of grief were complete, David married Bathsheba and she bore him a son. The Lord was greatly displeased at David's falling into the sin of defilement, for it was not fitting to answer God's work on his behalf by breaking His commandments, especially since adultery had drawn him into cruelty, to the point that he killed a great and innocent commander among the commanders of his war to cover his shameful sin.

Believers must keep their purity, for they are temples of God and the Spirit of God dwells in them, so let them not anger God by an ugly deed. Is it fitting that we answer God's saving work on our behalf by breaking His commandments? God was displeased at what David did of adultery and murder for the following reasons:
1- Because God raised him from behind the sheep and made him a great king, why then should he betray God by breaking His commandments?!
2- David was greatly godly in his righteousness, so why did this great tower fall and accept a great sin like adultery?
3- God favored David with the presence of the ark in his city so that he might remember God's constant presence with him, but he neglected this and fell into his grievous sin.

4- David was an example and a model for his people because he was the king; by his falling into sin he became very small in the eyes of Joab the head of his army and in the eyes of many of his servants, who drew conclusions and understood the matter, and he made them stumble greatly.
5- David's age at that time was about fifty, which is the age of settledness, that is, without the impulsiveness of youth, so it is strange that he fell into this sin.
6- David was married to several women, so there was no need for him to look at another woman.
And by David's falling into adultery, he fell into a group of sins, which are:
1- He forgot that he was the Lord's anointed, consecrated to His service by leading his kingdom, so it was not right for him to submit to evil desires.

2- He neglected the sense of the importance of fighting for God's sake; for if he had grown old and could not go out, he should at least have prayed for the fighters and not sought in his selfishness his own pleasure.
3- He wronged this woman and drew her into sin, for she may have been affected by his position and feared to oppose him.
4- He betrayed one of his military commanders by assaulting his wife, especially since he was a foreigner who had become a Jew, and so was exposed to severe stumbling.
5- The sin of adultery drew him to the sin of murder in order to hide his crime, so he killed an innocent man.
6- Most important, he broke the Law of God and became condemned to death.
7- Laxity toward the evil look and the wicked thought, which led him to complete fall into adultery.
8- Idleness and slackness: after he had eaten he rose to walk on his roof, and so he became exposed to falling into sin.
The humility of the Christ is shown in His being pleased to be born of the descendants of Bathsheba, who committed adultery with David (Mt 1:
6), to declare that He came to save adulterers and sinners by His redemption of them on the Cross.
David's punishment, and then his capture of Rabbah of the children of Ammon

entries.section: (1) Nathan's rebuke of David

paragraphs.text: The Lord sent Nathan the prophet to David after a period since his sin of not less than a year, for Bathsheba his wife had borne him a child, who lived for a time, as will come in (vv. 14, 15). This shows that God teaches the prophets to be humble: although David was a prophet, He did not speak to him directly but sent another prophet to him to rebuke him, to declare to him the voice of God, and to call him to repentance. Nathan related to him a case for David to judge between two men, one very rich and the other poor, living beside him. Most likely Nathan took David aside while he was giving his opinion on this case, in order to reveal his sin to him through it so that he would repent. This is the fitting way of reproving others: that it be in private, lest we embarrass them before people.

entries.section: (1) Nathan's rebuke of David

paragraphs.text: Nathan went on to recount the case, saying that the rich man had very many flocks, but the poor man had nothing except one ewe lamb, and he cared for it until it grew up in the midst of his household. It was dear to him, sharing his food, and he loved it like his daughter.

entries.section: (1) Nathan's rebuke of David

paragraphs.text: He spared to take of his own flock to dress for the wayfaring man: he was unwilling to slaughter one of his own sheep to cook a meal for the guest.

Nathan completed the rest of the case, saying that it happened that the rich man received a guest, and he was unwilling to take one of the many sheep he owned to slaughter it and prepare a meal for the guest, but with all cruelty seized the one ewe lamb that the poor man owned and slaughtered it to honor his guest with it.

entries.section: (1) Nathan's rebuke of David

paragraphs.text: David was greatly moved when he heard the case on which Nathan asked for his judgment, and he was very angry at what the rich man had done and issued a severe sentence against him. He swore by the living God that the man should be put to death for the monstrousness of his crime and should restore the lamb fourfold according to the Law (Ex 22:1), because this man had no pity on the poor man. Thus David's anger against this man appears: he went beyond the limits of the Law, which was to fine him by restoring four times what was stolen, to killing him because he was a hard-hearted man. And this was indeed fulfilled in David: just as Uriah the Hittite died, four of David's sons died, namely the son of Bathsheba (the child of sin), Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah. And just as David committed adultery with Bathsheba, Amnon committed adultery with Tamar his sister, and Absalom with his father's concubines. God forgave David and did not put him to death because he offered repentance from the depth of his heart and was not ashamed to confess before Nathan the prophet.

entries.section: (1) Nathan's rebuke of David

paragraphs.text: Nathan, like the other prophets of God, did not fear to confront King David with the word of the Lord which He had charged him to deliver to him, despite its harshness. He rebuked him, declaring to him that he was the rich, hard-hearted man mentioned in this case, and reminded him that God had taken him from his father's house to be king over Israel, and had rescued him many times from Saul's pursuit of him, and had given him as an inheritance the servants of Saul and all his house and his wives, that is Michal the daughter of Saul, and everything that was his passed to him. He was not content with making him king over the tribe of Judah only, but made him king over all the tribes of Israel; and if this was not enough for him, and he wanted more, He would have given him that too. This speech shows Nathan's courage in rebuking David, because by it he exposed himself to David's anger, so that he might order him killed; but he was laying down his life when he obeyed God and rebuked David.

entries.section: (1) Nathan's rebuke of David

paragraphs.text: After that Nathan confronted David openly with his sin, which was his despising of God's commandments and his killing of Uriah with the sword of the children of Ammon, that is, plotting with Joab to kill Uriah by placing him in the face of the battle to die, and afterward taking Bathsheba, with whom he had committed adultery and who had conceived.

And here David understood that the case Nathan had presented to him was his own story: he was the rich man with the many cattle, which signify his many wives, and he had seized the one ewe lamb of the poor man, that is Bathsheba, the only wife of Uriah the Hittite.

At last David awoke from the hardness of heart and the spiritual blindness that had covered him after his fall into adultery and murder. Despite David's righteousness, his negligence made him fall into the gravest of sins; and it is the nature of sin, when it increases, to deprive a person of his spiritual sense, so he remained a whole year without repentance until Nathan the prophet roused him. The Holy Bible mentions this shameful sin of David for the following reasons:
1- It does not flatter the saints but shows their weaknesses, so that we may be encouraged however much we fall.
2- Let us thank God, who keeps us when we see others, especially the strong, fall.
3- Let us be encouraged, if we fall into sin, to repent like David.
4- We learn the depth of repentance, whatever our sins may be, so that we press on with power in the way of God.
5- A declaration of humanity's need for the Christ the Savior, for all are exposed to falling, even the saints.

6- Acceptance of divine discipline if He allows it, so that our repentance may be complete, as happened with David through the death of his infant son and Absalom's driving him out of the kingdom, in addition to many other troubles.

God uses parables with you to rouse you to repent of your sins, so do not neglect them as though they were ordinary stories. Benefit from the events that pass over you, such as the death of one of your loved ones, or a problem that happens to you or to someone you know, so that it may be a means of your repentance; then God will accept you and remove your sins from you, however heavy they may be.

entries.section: (2) God's punishment of David

paragraphs.text: The sword shall never depart from thine house: the stability of peace in his house will be shaken, so there will be quarrels and troubles among the members of his family, and his descendants will kill one another.
And now the Lord has decreed to punish you with the following:

First: as you handed Uriah over to be killed, the sword will work to shake the peace in your house (God does not cause evils but permits them to occur). This punishment was fulfilled afterward: Absalom killed his brother Amnon (ch. 13) and then launched a coup against his father (ch. 15). It was fulfilled also in Solomon's killing of his brother Adonijah, and likewise many harsh wars arose afterward against the kingdom of Judah, and finally its people were taken captive to Babylon; and before the captivity, the sons of the last of the kings of Judah, of the descendants of David, namely King Zedekiah, were killed by Nebuchadnezzar, who killed his sons before his eyes.

entries.section: (2) God's punishment of David

paragraphs.text: The second punishment that God permitted for David was the rising of evil against him from his own house, through Absalom's taking the kingdom from him and driving him out of it (ch. 16:8). The third punishment was the assault on his wives, and this was fulfilled by his son Amnon's assault on his sister Tamar (ch. 13) and then Absalom's lying with his father's concubines and the announcing of this before the people, that is, it would be “in the sight of this sun” (ch. 16:21), meaning that he declared before all his seizing of the kingdom from his father.

entries.section: (2) God's punishment of David

paragraphs.text: David committed his sin with Bathsheba and worked to have her husband killed, all of this in secret, but the Lord declares to him that He will carry out his punishment openly.
The following appears in God's punishment of David:
1- God's justice and His showing no partiality to anyone, whatever his worldly position or his nearness to God.
2- The evil influence of the head of a family upon it: after David sinned, his children were affected, so Amnon committed adultery with his sister and Absalom killed his brother.

entries.section: (2) God's punishment of David

paragraphs.text: After Nathan confronted David with his sin, he felt it and repented of it, and acknowledged his guilt before the Lord Himself and in the presence of the man of God Nathan, and he wrote the fifty-first Psalm, which begins with the words “Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness.” ...... And since Nathan judged that his confession had come from sincere repentance, he told him, by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, that God had forgiven him: although his sin deserved the punishment of death according to the Law, God spared him from death because of his repentance of it. It is clear that this is a picture in the Old Testament of the sacrament of confession: just as a person confesses before his father of confession and his sin and its punishment, which is death, are lifted from him, so God lifted from David his sin and its punishment because of his confession before Nathan the prophet, who is a type of the father of confession.

entries.section: (2) God's punishment of David

paragraphs.text: The whispers of the guards must have passed on the matter of David's sin and made it a subject of gossip, so the rumors spread and perhaps reached his enemies. Here they saw David, the man godly in the Lord's eyes, collapse before sin, and they showed their malicious joy over him. Therefore, although God removed David's sin from him and spared him from death, He punished him, as Nathan declared to him, with three punishments, and the fourth is that the child who would be born of Bathsheba would die, because he was the fruit of sin.

If the door of repentance is open to you however grievous your sins, like the sin of David, why do you delay? Rise, hasten to your father of confession so that you may escape eternal destruction, regain your peace, and enjoy fellowship with God.

entries.section: (3) The child of adultery and the birth of Solomon

paragraphs.text: Nathan departed from the king's presence and returned to his house. Then the child that the wife of Uriah the Hittite bore to David fell sick, and the sickness grew severe upon him.

entries.section: (3) The child of adultery and the birth of Solomon

paragraphs.text: David fasted, prayed, and humbled himself before the Lord that the child might be healed, and instead of lying on his royal bed, he slept on the ground as a form of austerity and humbling before God. What increased David's humbling was his feeling that the child's sickness was discipline from God for his adultery and murder.

entries.section: (3) The child of adultery and the birth of Solomon

paragraphs.text: The chiefs of his people and the men close to him tried to raise him from the ground to sleep on his bed and to seat him with them at the table to eat of the delicious royal food, but he did not wish to lessen his humbling before the Lord; most likely he ate only meager foods for austerity and humbling before God. Thus we see the practice of fasting clearly in the depths of the Old Testament, which the children of God now practice in His Church.

entries.section: (3) The child of adultery and the birth of Solomon

paragraphs.text: The child died on the seventh day of his illness, and the members of the king's household were at a loss how to tell him the sad news, for how great was his grief when the child was sick, and how much more it would increase if he learned of his death. He would surely be shocked on hearing the news and would deprive himself of food and rest more than before.
And we note that God permitted the death of the child to declare that there is no gain from sin, but every gain that comes from it must pass away.

entries.section: (3) The child of adultery and the birth of Solomon

paragraphs.text: David sensed, from the movements and whispers of his men, that an important event had taken place, so he concluded that the child was dead, and he asked them whether the child was dead, and they were obliged to tell him the truth.

entries.section: (3) The child of adultery and the birth of Solomon

paragraphs.text: Contrary to what the members of his household expected, David behaved with complete calm on hearing the news. He ended the signs of his humbling, rose, washed, and anointed himself with perfume to regain his refreshment, and put on his royal garments instead of the austere ones he had worn during the mourning. He went to the house of the Lord, where he prayed and worshiped, thanking the Lord in every circumstance, even for the death of his son, and then he returned to his house and ate the usual royal food.

David's conduct shows his complete submission to the divine will, and this is what every true believer ought to do, thanking the Lord in every circumstance and in all things, offering the Lord praise and worship.

entries.section: (3) The child of adultery and the birth of Solomon

paragraphs.text: David's men were astonished at his conduct and were bewildered as to what the matter could be, so they dared to ask him how it was that he grieved and humbled himself while the child was still alive, and when he died he rose and resumed his normal life and abandoned all signs of grief!

entries.section: (3) The child of adultery and the birth of Solomon

paragraphs.text: David made them understand that he had humbled himself before the Lord that his son might be healed while he was still alive, being certain that the Lord was able to grant him healing however severe the illness. Although Nathan had told him that the child would die, he did not lose his hope in God's mercy and continued to pray.

entries.section: (3) The child of adultery and the birth of Solomon

paragraphs.text: David added that his son had died and there was no longer any opportunity to ask for God's mercy in his healing, so his thought turned to the eternal life to which his child had gone before him, and he would follow him when God willed. Thus a group of virtues appears in this great man David the prophet, which are:
1- His faith in God's mercy, so he hastened to Him with many prayers that his son might be healed.

2- His inclination to austerity and humbling before God in many spiritual practices, such as fasting accompanied by prayers, with all that it includes of abstaining from food, bodily comfort and splendid clothing.
3- David's reliance on God and acceptance of His will, however contrary to his desires.

4- David's attachment to eternal life, which influenced his life and made him feel a stranger in the world although he was a great king, so that he said, “I am a stranger in the earth: hide not thy commandments from me”
(Ps 119: gimel 19), which made him cling to prayer and to meditation on the Law of God.

Be sure that your prayers, your fasts and your humbling before God are very precious in His sight, for this means your faith and your love for God more than all that is in the world. He accepts this spiritual striving of yours, and even if He does not give you what you asked, He will give you manifold more in your life, keep you, and give you a great place in the heavens.

entries.section: (3) The child of adultery and the birth of Solomon

paragraphs.text: Solomon: a name meaning peaceful or peacemaker.

David comforted Bathsheba on the death of their son, and then he went in to her and she bore him a son whom he named Solomon, as a prophecy of the peace that would prevail in the time of his reign, and the Lord would give him rest from all his enemies. The Lord loved Solomon because of His foreknowledge of the glorious works he would do in the future when he took the throne of the kingdom, and the Lord sent a message to David by the hand of Nathan declaring another name for Solomon, Jedidiah, that is “beloved of Jehovah,” declaring His love for him.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: The royal city: the high part of the city of Rabbah in which the king dwells.
The city of waters: the lower part of Rabbah, the capital of the kingdom, which was watered by the Jabbok River, one of the tributaries of the Jordan, and so had abundant water.

Joab was fighting the Ammonites, and during that time David fell into his sin. The Holy Bible mentions it in detail because it does not hide the sins of the saints, and then it returns here in this verse to complete the events of the war with the Ammonites.

And we note that the Holy Bible is not bound by historical sequence, because it is a spiritual book concerned to show the spiritual meanings so that we may apply them in our lives. So it mentions in this chapter that Bathsheba bore a son, who grew and died, and then she conceived and bore Solomon. Then it returns and tells us about the war with the Ammonites, although the war had ended before the events mentioned in this chapter, that is, the death of the child of adultery and then the birth of Solomon. Joab attacked the capital of the children of Ammon, called Rabbah, which was in two parts; he took the lower part, called the city of waters, and cut off the water from the upper part, called the royal city, in which the king dwelt. Then he besieged the royal city and it began to fall before him, so he sent to David to give him the good news of the fall of the capital of the children of Ammon and asked him to hasten with an army to enter this capital himself, so that the honor of capturing it would be his and not Joab's. Thus God rouses David and restores him to his proper position as a king and military leader working for God's sake, not giving in to the sin and evil into which he had fallen. For repentance and life with God raise a person from sin and restore him, with head held high, to a new life with God.

And we note that Joab spoke sharply to David in calling him to fight and take the city, saying, “Come thou... lest I take the city, and it be called after my name.” But he also shows his loyalty to David in wanting David's name to be called upon the city; and so we ought to imitate Joab, ascribing all power and success to God and not to ourselves.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: David carried out Joab's request, so he gathered the rest of his army and set out toward “Rabbah,” entered it and captured it.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: A talent of gold: equal to about 8 kg.

David took the crown of their king, which was of gold, heavy in weight and set with precious stones, and put it on his head as a declaration of the extending of his authority over the Ammonites. He and his men also took very great spoil from the defeated city “Rabbah.” Most likely, because of the weight of the crown, two of David's men lifted it and placed it on his head for a short time as a declaration of his greatness and his possession of the children of Ammon, and then they lifted the crown from his head.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Harrows: an agricultural implement, a cart with toothed wheels for cutting the stalks of wheat and barley.
The brickkiln: the furnaces in which mud bricks, that is raw ones, are burned.

In view of the Ammonites' harassment of and attack upon the children of Israel more than once, at the hand of Nahash their king (1 Sam 11) and the mockery by his son Hanun of David's messengers (ch. 10), in addition to the hardness of heart of the Ammonites, who clung to pagan gods to the point of offering their children as sacrifices and burning them to please them, David was compelled, contrary to his custom, to be harsh with them. He killed them by passing harrows and saws over their bodies after he had thrown them on the ground, and killed them with axes, and killed some of them in brick furnaces, to be burned and tormented by the blazing fire, perhaps so that this would make the rest of the pagan peoples fear God, abandon the worship of idols, and fear to fight against the people of God.
Although God had commanded not to be hostile to the Ammonites, because they are the descendants of Lot, relatives of the people of God (Deut 2:
16-23), yet because of the Ammonites' immersion in pagan worship and their repeated assault on the people of God, David was compelled to attack them and kill them.

God is very merciful to everyone who repents and returns to Him, but He is just in punishing the wicked who reject Him, destroying them with eternal destruction. So take advantage of the opportunity of this life to hasten in repentance to God, and you will escape eternal torment.

Amnon rapes his sister and Absalom kills him (1) The rape of Tamar and her expulsion (vv. 1-18:) 1 And it came to pass after this, that Absalom the son of David had a fair sister, whose name was Tamar; and Amnon the son of David loved her. 2 And Amnon was so vexed, that he fell sick for his sister Tamar; for she was a virgin; and Amnon thought it hard for him to do any thing to her. 3 But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah David's brother: and Jonadab was a very subtil man. 4 And he said unto him, Why art thou, being the king's son, lean from day to day? wilt thou not tell me? And Amnon said unto him, I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister. 5 And Jonadab said unto him, Lay thee down on thy bed, and make thyself sick: and when thy father cometh to see thee, say unto him, I pray thee, let my sister Tamar come, and give me meat, and dress the meat in my sight, that I may see it, and eat it at her hand. 6 So Amnon lay down, and made himself sick: and when the king was come to see him, Amnon said unto the king, I pray thee, let Tamar my sister come, and make me a couple of cakes in my sight, that I may eat at her hand. 7 Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, Go now to thy brother Amnon's house, and dress him meat. 8 So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house; and he was laid down. And she took flour, and kneaded it, and made cakes in his sight, and did bake the cakes. 9 And she took a pan, and poured them out before him; but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, Have out all men from me. And they went out every man from him. 10 And Amnon said unto Tamar, Bring the meat into the chamber, that I may eat of thine hand. And Tamar took the cakes which she had made, and brought them into the chamber to Amnon her brother. 11 And when she had brought them unto him to eat, he took hold of her, and said unto her, Come lie with me, my sister. 12 And she answered him, Nay, my brother, do not force me; for no such thing ought to be done in Israel: do not thou this folly. 13 And I, whither shall I cause my shame to go? and as for thee, thou shalt be as one of the fools in Israel. Now therefore, I pray thee, speak unto the king; for he will not withhold me from thee. 14 Howbeit he would not hearken unto her voice: but, being stronger than she, forced her, and lay with her. 15 Then Amnon hated her exceedingly; so that the hatred wherewith he hated her was greater than the love wherewith he had loved her. And Amnon said unto her, Arise, be gone. 16 And she said unto him, There is no cause: this evil in sending me away is greater than the other that thou didst unto me. But he would not hearken unto her. 17 Then he called his servant that ministered unto him, and said, Put now this woman out from me, and bolt the door after her. 18 And she had a garment of divers colours upon her: for with such robes were the king's daughters that were virgins apparelled. Then his servant brought her out, and bolted the door after her.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Absalom: the third son of David, born in Hebron; his mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur. Tamar: the full sister of Absalom, whom Amnon, her half brother, raped.

The punishments with which David had been warned began to be fulfilled. The beginning of the painful events was Amnon's rape of his sister Tamar. Absalom the son of David had a beautiful sister whose name was Tamar, and Amnon, her half brother, felt a lustful passion toward her.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Vexed ... sick: he was distressed in spirit, and his heart became constricted and choked to the degree of physical illness.
Hard: impossible.

Amnon's desire for Tamar was so pressing that it became an illness that took away from him the desire to engage in any activity, and he was at a loss how to reach what he sought, for Tamar was a virgin, and the customs of that age required that virgin girls live in a private dwelling, the house of the women, away from mixing with any of the men of the family; moreover, he could not marry her because she was his sister, and the Law forbids that. We wonder at Amnon's giving himself over to his lust for his sister, and perhaps his father David's sin with Bathsheba encouraged him to rush into this evil lust, for the sins of fathers can cause children to stumble and push them into evil.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Amnon had a cousin close to him, Jonadab the son of Shimeah, who is the same as “Shammah” mentioned in (1 Sam 16:9); the Scripture describes him as very wise). We shall see later that his wisdom was of the stumbling, evil kind.(

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Jonadab noticed the leanness and weariness that Amnon was in, which increased day by day with no apparent cause, for he lived the life of the sons of kings and lacked nothing. So he asked him the reason, and he told him of his lust for Tamar: he felt that he loved her to the point of madness and could not restrain himself from her.

Satan is able to fabricate within a man or a woman an emotion toward another, and he justifies it as a need that a person cannot resist, in matters that are unlawful, that is, the love of a married man for another woman, or of a girl for a person who does not wish to marry her or where there are obstacles preventing it. So be watchful, my brother, because your enemy Satan has the power to persuade you and arouse you emotionally; do not give in to him as long as that is against the commandment... It is a fabricated feeling: resist it from the beginning and you will surely triumph by the grace of the Christ. And expose it to your father of confession and not to an evil friend, lest he lead you astray.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Jonadab gave him evil counsel to achieve his desire. He advised him to feign illness and lie on his bed, and his father would surely come to ask about him; then he should pretend to be sick and without appetite for food and ask his father to charge his sister Tamar to cook food for him with her own hands, so that perhaps his appetite would open and he would take to the food she prepared for him.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Amnon carried out the evil plan that his cousin had devised for him. He pretended to be ill, and the rest of the matters went as Jonadab had devised: the king came to ask about him, and Amnon asked him to allow his sister Tamar to come to him and cook food for him to eat from her hands.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: David did not perceive any evil intention behind this request of Amnon, so he simply granted it and asked Tamar to go to Amnon's house to prepare food for him. If only David had prayed to God to rescue him and his children from evil! For prayer above all protects a person from many troubles, especially since a virgin sister's staying with her half brother was not a customary thing at that time.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: The pan: a vessel in which cakes and food are prepared.

She emptied what she had prepared of food into a vessel and presented it to him, but he refused to eat in the presence of the servants and ordered everyone to go out, on the ground that he had no appetite in the presence of the servants, and perhaps he could eat quietly with his sister alone.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: After the servants had gone out, Amnon asked Tamar to bring him the food while he was lying in his bed so that he might eat from her hand, and Tamar took the food she had prepared and brought it to Amnon's chamber.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: She approached him in innocence and presented the food to him, but he did not take it from her; rather he seized her, asking her to lie with him and do evil.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Tamar was taken by surprise by this evil request, and she implored him not to harm her by assaulting her, telling him that the people of God are a holy people and do not commit such deeds, which are contrary to holiness, and she entreated him not to do this ugly deed to her.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Tamar went on, explaining that if she lost her purity she would lose her honor and shame would come upon her and she would not be able to face people. As for him, he would be in the eyes of all as one of the wicked and despised and would be rejected. And to find a way out of the situation, she asked him to put his wish to marry her to the king, who would grant him his wish (although the marriage of half brothers and sisters was forbidden by the Law (Lev 18:9), Tamar offered this idea hoping to escape the predicament so that the matter would be put before the king, who would do what he saw fit, and in this way she would rescue herself from this rape). Most likely she was in a remote chamber and could not cry out because no one would hear her; she was a pure woman, obedient to her father and humble, working with her own hands although she was a princess.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Despite Tamar's entreaties and her making him aware of the consequence of this deed, he did not heed her advice but overpowered her and obtained his wicked desire from her. This shows that there was a struggle and resistance on Tamar's part, but Amnon, by his bodily strength, was able to overcome his poor sister.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: After he had obtained his desire, his love for her turned to intense hatred, greater than the love with which he had loved her, and his hatred for her overrode any human feelings, for he ordered her, in this state of grief and distress, to arise at once, leave the place and go far away. This shows the falseness of the lustful emotional feelings from which some suffer; rather, whoever is immersed in lust is a selfish, hard-hearted person who does not know love, because love is giving and not taking, and one who cannot control himself is a selfish person who deceives himself that he loves when he has not known true love.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Tamar said to him that there was no cause for his sending her away, for she had not been a cause of what had happened, and she explained to him that his sending her away was a greater evil than the evil he had done to her by his sin. But Amnon did not wish to listen to her in this either; rather his heart hardened and he increased in his evil to the point of ordering his servant to put her out and bolt the door after her. This shows the extent of his cruelty: he did not apologize to her for what he had done or have pity on her, for she had lost her virginity and was exposed to conceiving, and she had nothing with which to defend herself, especially since this expulsion took place immediately after the fall.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Tamar, like the other virgin princesses, wore a garment of many colors, showing that she was a virgin princess. The servant carried out his master's order and brought her outside and bolted the door after her.

(2) Absalom kills Amnon (vv. 19-29:) 19 And Tamar put ashes on her head, and rent her garment of divers colours that was on her, and laid her hand on her head, and went on crying. 20 And Absalom her brother said unto her, Hath Amnon thy brother been with thee? but hold now thy peace, my sister: he is thy brother; regard not this thing. So Tamar remained desolate in her brother Absalom's house. 21 But when king David heard of all these things, he was very wroth. 22 And Absalom spake unto his brother Amnon neither good nor bad: for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had forced his sister Tamar. 23 And it came to pass after two full years, that Absalom had sheepshearers in Baal-hazor, which is beside Ephraim: and Absalom invited all the king's sons. 24 And Absalom came to the king, and said, Behold now, thy servant hath sheepshearers; let the king, I beseech thee, and his servants go with thy servant. 25 And the king said to Absalom, Nay, my son, let us not all now go, lest we be chargeable unto thee. And he pressed him: howbeit he would not go, but blessed him. 26 Then said Absalom, If not, I pray thee, let my brother Amnon go with us. And the king said unto him, Why should he go with thee?

27 But Absalom pressed him, that he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him. 28 Now Absalom had commanded his servants, saying, Mark ye now when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and when I say unto you, Smite Amnon; then kill him, fear not: have not I commanded you? be courageous, and be valiant. 29 And the servants of Absalom did unto Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons arose, and every man gat him up upon his mule, and fled.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: In expression of her intense grief at the loss of her honor, Tamar put dust on her head and tore the garment of many colors that she was wearing, which was a sign of the virginity she had lost, and she put her hand on her head as a sign of deep grief and of her awareness of the calamity that had befallen her (as women do to this day), and she began to cry out in a loud voice, lamenting her state and the misery she would suffer. She did all this as she was going to the house of her brother Absalom.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Regard not this thing: do not think much about this matter.
Remained desolate: depressed, withdrawn into herself.
Tamar reached Absalom's house, and he perceived, with his shrewdness and through her words crying out about the calamity that had struck her, and he asked her whether Amnon had assaulted her.

Absalom wanted to lighten the matter for his sister, so he asked her not to think much about what had happened and to leave the matter to him ... Tamar lived in the house of her brother Absalom, depressed and withdrawn into herself, meeting no one.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: The news of what had happened reached David and he was greatly distressed, but he took no action against his son Amnon. This was another error on his part, like Eli the priest (1 Sam 4), and other calamities resulted from it, the details of which will come in later verses.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Absalom hated his brother Amnon in his heart, but he did not show his anger; he kept it within him until the right opportunity should come, when he would end his temporary silence and avenge himself and his sister.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Sheepshearers: those who shear the wool of the sheep.
Baal-hazor: its place is now “Jebel al-Qusur,” 4.5 miles northeast of Bethel and fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem.

After two years the opportunity that Absalom had been waiting for to take his revenge came, for he was shearing his sheep, and the time of shearing sheep was considered a happy occasion on which feasts were held, because wool was a source of wealth, and Absalom invited his brothers to his feast.

Hatred and the desire for revenge remained hidden in Absalom's heart, and they led him to the sin of murder. The children of God must not allow anger to lodge in their hearts, lest it lead them to greater sins by which their lives are ruined. May you not go to sleep on any day before forgiving the one who has wronged you, so that God may forgive you your sins as you say in the Lord's Prayer; for if you do not forgive him, God will not forgive you. And if thoughts of resentment and anger against him fight you, pray earnestly to God to lift this war from you and strengthen your weakness.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Absalom went himself to invite his father the king and some of his men to his feast.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: The king excused himself from going, he and his men, so as not to burden his son Absalom with special preparations to receive him, and despite Absalom's pressing, David did not wish to go, but he blessed him. This shows Absalom's cunning, for he made it appear a feast at which his father was supposed to be present, so that Amnon would not suspect anything.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Then Absalom asked the king to allow Amnon to go with him, as the heir to the throne, since he was the eldest of David's sons, so that he would attend on behalf of the king. At first the king saw no need for his son Amnon to go, because this too would cause Absalom trouble with special preparations, as a representative of the king. But in the face of Absalom's pressing, the king sent Amnon with him, and the rest of his brothers.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: When Amnon's heart is merry with wine: when his consciousness is gone and he is carried away by intoxication from much wine. The opportunity that Absalom had planned for doing away with Amnon came, and he ordered his servants that when they saw that the wine had affected Amnon's consciousness, they were to kill him at once and fear nothing, for he was responsible for the killing and it was he who commanded them to do it, so they would bear no guilt; and he encouraged them and removed from them all fear or dread of attacking the heir to the throne. This shows the extent of Absalom's evil: he concealed the hatred in his heart for two years, which is a long time, in order to take revenge on his brother Amnon, and then how he persuaded his servants to kill Amnon and that they bore no responsibility, although his words were wrong and God would hold them to account for it, and the king too could punish them. For evil blinds a person's eyes and tries to deceive others.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: The servants carried out Absalom's order and killed Amnon, and the rest of the brothers were terrified as they saw their eldest brother killed, so they mounted their mules and fled quickly from the place.

(3) David's grief and Absalom's flight (vv. 30-39:) 30 And it came to pass, while they were in the way, that tidings came to David, saying, Absalom hath slain all the king's sons, and there is not one of them left. 31 Then the king arose, and tare his garments, and lay on the earth; and all his servants stood by with their clothes rent. 32 And Jonadab, the son of Shimeah David's brother, answered and said, Let not my lord suppose that they have slain all the young men the king's sons; for Amnon only is dead: for by the appointment of Absalom this hath been determined from the day that he forced his sister Tamar. 33 Now therefore let not my lord the king take the thing to his heart, to think that all the king's sons are dead: for Amnon only is dead. 34 But Absalom fled. And the young man that kept the watch lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold, there came much people by the hill side behind him. 35 And Jonadab said unto the king, Behold, the king's sons come: as thy servant said, so it is. 36 And it came to pass, as soon as he had made an end of speaking, that, behold, the king's sons came, and lifted up their voice and wept: and the king also and all his servants wept very sore. 37 But Absalom fled, and went to Talmai, the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son every day. 38 So Absalom fled, and went to Geshur, and was there three years. 39 And the soul of king David longed to go forth unto Absalom: for he was comforted concerning Amnon, seeing he was dead.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: The news reached David, but in an exaggerated form, for they told him that Absalom had killed all his sons, whereas Amnon alone had been killed. The king grieved greatly, tore his garments and lay on the ground, and all his men shared his grief and tore their garments, and this shows the signs of the intense grief into which the king and those with him fell.
We must not be carriers of every piece of news we hear without verifying its truth, for we may cause griefs or pains to others without real cause.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: This hath been determined: he planned this matter.
Let not my lord the king take the thing to his heart: let the king not grieve this intense grief.

Jonadab was present with the king and was aware of the beginnings of the matters and of what had happened at the feast, for it was he who had advised Amnon of the plan to rape Tamar, so he tried to persuade the king that Amnon alone had been killed, and not the rest of his brothers, and that Absalom had been harboring evil against him since he assaulted his sister Tamar. This shows the extent of Jonadab's deceit: he is the source of the evil yet conceals his evil, and he is a type of Satan, who works in the hearts of people so that they become enemies to one another and then hides himself as though he had done nothing.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: The young man that kept the watch: in ancient times kings appointed persons of keen sight to observe whether there were movements of enemies around the city.

After Absalom took his revenge and killed Amnon, he fled lest the king kill him. The watchman who observed any movements around the king's palace was performing his duty, and he saw a large number of people walking along the side of the mountain, and Jonadab said to the king, “Behold, the king's sons have come” alive from Absalom's feast, as I told you.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: When Jonadab had made an end of speaking to the king, his sons arrived, and no sooner did they meet their father than they wept bitterly, and the king and all his men wept in grief for Amnon.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Geshur: it lies east of the Jordan River between Hermon and Bashan.

Absalom fled to his grandfather “Talmai,” king of Geshur, the father of his mother Maacah, to take refuge with him from the face of David his father. He welcomed him because he was his grandson, and he stayed with him for three years because he was in great fear of his father's punishment.

entries.section: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

paragraphs.text: After a long period had passed since this event, David was comforted over the death of his son Amnon and longed to go himself to Geshur to bring Absalom back to his house, but he could not, because he knew that if he did this, people would accuse him of injustice among his sons and of laxity in applying the penalty of the Law to take the right of the slain son. This shows the tenderness of David's heart and his forgiveness and fatherly compassion.

If David resembled God in his compassion and forgiveness toward sinners, however great their evil, may you understand this so that you forgive others however great their evil, since God is so compassionate toward you.
David allows Absalom to return to Jerusalem

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: The king's heart was toward Absalom: always thinking of him and longing for him.
Joab was close to David and well informed about his affairs, and he sought to bring Absalom back for the following reasons:
1- Because he knew how much David loved Absalom and longed to see him.
2- He expected that Absalom must surely return, so he wanted to win the love of David and Absalom by being the intermediary in his return.

3- He knew how much the people loved Absalom, so he expected that he would become king after his father; but his being far from the people of God could stir doubt among the people whether they would choose Absalom or his elder brother Adonijah.
4- Joab knew of David's anger against him for killing Abner, so by bringing back Absalom, the killer of his brother, and David's pardoning him, David would forgive Joab and he would win David's love.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: Tekoah: a village south of Jerusalem about 20 km from it. The ruins of the same name are found in its place to this day.

In the village of “Tekoah” there was a woman renowned for wisdom and sound reasoning in speech and in presenting matters, so Joab sent for her to charge her with a task, and he asked her to pretend grief, wearing mourning clothes and not anointing herself with perfumes, so that she would appear as a woman grieving for a dead person dear to her.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: Put the words in her mouth: he taught her what she would say to the king.
He asked her to seek to appear before the king and speak to him with the words he had taught her.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: Help, O king: crying to the king for help in some matter.
The woman went in to the king and bowed down before him, crying to him to help her face a problem that tormented her and kept her sleepless.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: The king asked her the reason for her deep grief, and she told him an imaginary story, as Joab had instructed her, to use as a parable that applied to David and his two sons Amnon and Absalom.

The story began by saying that she was a widow whose husband had died and left her two sons, who quarreled while working in the field where there was no one to part them, and the quarrel developed into a struggle with the hands, and one struck the other and killed him.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: The men of the Law judged the killer of his brother to death, according to what the Law decrees, and asked the mother to hand over her son the killer so that the sentence of the Law might be carried out on him. The woman went on to present the matter, saying that if she did so and handed over her other son to be killed, they would thereby quench the light of her life, meaning her remaining son, the killer, who was the only son left to her; and her husband's name would be blotted out from the earth, for he would have no descendants left with the death of both sons, and her husband's inheritance would pass to others of the sons of the clan.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: The woman skillfully used her power of reasoning and persuasion, so that David was moved by her words and felt her problem, and he reassured her and asked her to be calm, saying he would issue instructions to the men of her clan to pardon her son the killer in consideration of her circumstances.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: The woman realized that King David's exempting her son involved a breaking of the divine commandment (the Law), so she called down upon herself that she should bear the guilt of transgressing the commandment and that David and his throne should be guiltless of this offense. She based this on the Law, which allows the pardoning of a killer in some circumstances out of mercy (Deut 19:4, 5).

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: David assured her of his protection of her from anyone who confronted her and insisted on handing over her son, and told her to bring him to the king, and he would command him not to molest her.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: The revenger of blood: the nearest relative who demands the blood of the slain.
There shall not one hair of thy son fall to the earth: no one shall touch him with harm.

The woman asked him to confirm his promise to her with an oath so that this promise would be made firm and the members of her clan would cease to demand that she hand over her son, lest the revenger of blood add to the calamity of the killing of one of the two sons the new calamity of killing the remaining son, and her pain and weariness be doubled and her misery increased.
David wanted to set her heart completely at rest, so he granted her request and swore to her by the living God that no one would be able to harm her other son in any way or touch him with harm.

May you use wisdom in your speech with others to persuade them and win them and call them to carry out the mercy you desire or any good work, and not use commands or rebuke, which are rejected most of the time.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: Here the story that was taken as a parable of David's position toward Absalom came to an end, with the woman obtaining the required promise from which there is no going back, namely the pardon of the killer. So she decided to prepare to enter into the real subject, and she asked the king to permit her to continue speaking so as to disclose to him a certain thing, and he permitted her.

Whoever has authority over others should be patient in listening to their cases, allowing them to explain the details of their complaint, and listen to them with all deliberation and attention, so that his judgment in the end may be fair.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: The woman began to make use of the king's pardon of her son (in her invented story), saying to him that if he had pardoned her son out of mercy for his mother, why had he not taken account of the wish of his people to justify another person in a similar matter (she meant that the majority of the people of Israel loved Absalom and justified his killing of his brother). And why did he insist on keeping the killer son (she meant Absalom) in exile, although what applied to my son, and your oath that you would not allow anyone to harm him, applies also to your son? Your insistence on not forgiving him makes you guilty before God, because you swore that no one would harm my son, and this is your son, so how can you not forgive him?! And because David was a wise man, he could understand the wisdom of this woman who spoke in a parable.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: The wise woman gives the king here a profitable sermon: that all must die and return to the earth like water spilled on the ground that cannot be gathered up again; so if you are grieved over Amnon, death is the destiny of every living person.

God Himself devises means, gives graces, and works in the heart and mind of the offender so that he returns to Him and He pardons his offense, so that he does not remain far from God's care). By these words the woman means that if God does this with all mercy toward the sinner, and this is His dealing with erring human beings, then all the more should David pardon his son and call him back from his exile and restore him to himself. The woman took advantage of her knowledge that the people loved Absalom and that David himself loved him and longed for his return (ch. 13:39), but feared that he would be unjust in forgiving the killer.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: I have come to you, O king, and presented to you this matter of pardoning Absalom, although the people were frightening me, saying that the king would not listen to my entreaties; yet I dared to come and gave the example of the mother and her two sons, so that perhaps you might be convinced by my mediation and pardon your son.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: In the end the woman summarizes her story, by which she means it to be a parable calling David to forgive Absalom, and she says to him: all my hope is that you listen to me and do me justice against the revenger of blood who seeks to kill my other son and to remove my name and my son's name from the people of God and from the inheritance of the holy land that He gave to His people. All this moved David to forgive Absalom.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: May the final decision of my lord the king concerning the pardoning of his son Absalom be another comfort to me, as your first word was about the killer of his brother in the field. You have pardoned my son because you saw that it was good, and you are the best at discerning between good and evil because you are sent by God to serve His people; so may your judgment in the case of Absalom also be for the good of your people, and may the Lord support you and bless your steps.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: The king understood the hints the woman was making, which applied to him and his son Absalom, and that her aim in the end was that the king should review his position toward his son Absalom. He also understood that there must be a planning mind behind this woman, moving all of this, so he asked her not to conceal a matter about which he would ask her, and the woman showed her readiness to answer what he would ask.

And we note David's readiness to bring Absalom back because he loved him, although the story the woman told did not apply entirely to Absalom, for he was, for example, not an only son but had many brothers... but David longed to see his son.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: The king concluded that Joab, who was the person best informed about the king's circumstances and his longing for Absalom (v. 1), was the one who had urged her to what she did and said, so he asked her whether it was Joab who had prompted her in what she said, and the woman answered with an oath that what the king had concluded was correct, and she confirmed to him that Joab was indeed the one who had charged her with what she said.

entries.section: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

paragraphs.text: None can turn to the right hand or to the left from ought that my lord the king hath spoken: without addition, omission or distortion.
To fetch about this form of speech: so as not to approach the subject directly.

The woman added that Joab did not wish to confront him himself directly with the words, so he charged her with the matter. Then she praised the intelligence and discernment of the king, who concluded from the story she had invented that he was the one meant by it, concerning his position toward Absalom, and that by this wisdom of his he was like the wisdom of the angels, to whom the Lord gives the grace of knowing many things that human beings do not know.

This woman, by her wisdom and good words, was able to win David and he agreed to her request; so may you use the right time and praise others and offer them good words founded on prayers, that God may give you wisdom in winning them, and you will be at peace with those around you.

entries.section: (2) David permits Joab to bring Absalom back to Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: I have found grace in thy sight: I have found acceptance of my person from you by your honoring me.

The king was convinced that he must change his position toward Absalom, which in fact he longed to do inwardly, so he summoned Joab, who was the true intermediary between him and his son, and asked him to bring his son to Jerusalem.

entries.section: (2) David permits Joab to bring Absalom back to Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Joab rejoiced because the king accepted his mediation, so he bowed down before him in expression of his thanks, repeating the statement that the king's acceptance of his mediation showed his great trust in him, and that this was an honor to his person in which he took pride.

entries.section: (2) David permits Joab to bring Absalom back to Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Joab went to Geshur to bring Absalom in fulfillment of the king's order, and took him with him back to Jerusalem.

entries.section: (2) David permits Joab to bring Absalom back to Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Absalom returned to Jerusalem, the capital of King David, but the king decided to deprive his son of seeing him, as a proof to the people that he was still displeased at what Absalom had done before in killing his brother Amnon, and also as a message to Absalom that he was still displeased at his killing his brother Amnon, so that he would humble himself and repent.

entries.section: (2) David permits Joab to bring Absalom back to Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Absalom was beautiful and more handsome than all the sons of his people, and he was praised and extolled by all the people, for his whole body was marked by beauty.

entries.section: (2) David permits Joab to bring Absalom back to Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: After the king's weight: units of weight equal to 8 grams.

Hair was a sign of Absalom's handsomeness, so besides the perfumes with which he anointed it, he cared for it with all care, and out of his great admiration for it he cut it only once a year, being compelled to, because it was very thick and made a weight on his head. He used to boast of it and weigh it, and its weight reached about 1.5 kilograms, especially since it was anointed with oils and perfumes, and he even put gold filings on it so that it would shine, as a kind of luxury and display.

entries.section: (2) David permits Joab to bring Absalom back to Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Absalom had three sons and one daughter, whom he named after his aunt Tamar, and she was beautiful like her father, her aunt and her grandfather David (1 Sam 16:12).

Absalom was preoccupied with his beauty, so he departed from purity of heart and life with God, and his end was regrettable, as we shall see in the following chapters. So do not be preoccupied with your beauty, your position or your possessions, for they are all passing and will distract you from the salvation of your soul, so that you depart from God and fall into many sins. And if God has given you something, thank Him for it.

entries.section: (3) Absalom's attempt to see the king

paragraphs.text: After Absalom's return from Geshur he did not meet his father even once for two whole years. His deprivation of meeting his father for two years, in addition to the long period he spent in Geshur, which was three years, affected his psychology and was reflected in his behavior toward his father, as will come in the next chapter. He did not benefit from this long period in repentance and humility, but his heart was filled with pride, jealousy and envy, and he sought to take the kingdom from his father, as will appear in the next chapter.

entries.section: (3) Absalom's attempt to see the king

paragraphs.text: Absalom was distressed by the long deprivation of meeting his father and of being received in the royal palace as one of his sons, so he thought of turning to Joab to mediate for him in his request to see his father. But Joab refused to mediate this time, and despite Absalom's pressing, Joab continued to refuse and did not go to Absalom; perhaps he knew that David would probably refuse for the sake of justice and so that the people would not stumble, and Joab did not wish to embarrass himself.

entries.section: (3) Absalom's attempt to see the king

paragraphs.text: Absalom resorted to a trick so that Joab would come to him, and he ordered his men to burn the barley crop in Joab's field next to his own, in order to provoke Joab so that he would come to him protesting the burning of his field, and Absalom's men carried out this order.

entries.section: (3) Absalom's attempt to see the king

paragraphs.text: His trick succeeded, for Joab was angry at the burning of his field and went to Absalom, asking and raging why he had burned his field!

entries.section: (3) Absalom's attempt to see the king

paragraphs.text: Absalom justified his deed by saying that it was his trick to provoke him to come to him, since he had refused to come to him more than once, and he wanted to send a message by him to the king asking him the reason for permitting him to return to Jerusalem without permitting him to meet him; it would have been better to leave him in Geshur with his grandfather than to be in Jerusalem deprived of seeing his father. He charged Joab to ask the king to permit him to see him, and if the king still considered him guilty of anything, to let him kill him, for that was better for him than to continue in this situation. By this Absalom showed his love and longing for David, to stir his father's feelings toward him, relying on his compassion and fatherhood, although Absalom was evil and did not love his father, as will appear later.

entries.section: (3) Absalom's attempt to see the king

paragraphs.text: Joab conveyed Absalom's wish to the king, and the king's heart softened toward his son and he agreed to permit him to see him. So Absalom came to his father and bowed down before him in a bow of respect and reverence, and the king rose from his seat and embraced his son with intense longing and kissed him.
How beautiful was David's fatherhood and forgiveness. May we have pity on sinners that God may have mercy on us, and perhaps by our pity we may draw them to repentance.
Absalom's revolt against his father

entries.section: (1) Absalom wins the people to his side

paragraphs.text: After Absalom had won the favor of his father King David, he began to carry out his plans to seize the kingdom from him. He surrounded himself with displays of grandeur and went about in a procession in a chariot, like a prince and crown prince, with horsemen on horses before him and runners running ahead to clear the way for him, announcing his passing through the place. He had learned this from his pagan grandfather, his mother's father, the king of Geshur. David, however, was humble and rode on a mule, as God had commanded in the Law. Absalom ran after displays of grandeur, while David endured many afflictions, and in the end reigned over his people and remained humble.

entries.section: (1) Absalom wins the people to his side

paragraphs.text: Absalom would go early in the morning to the gate of the city, where the judges held their sessions to judge the people's cases. He would meet those who had cases and would flatter them, pretending to appreciate their problems and trying to draw close to them and get to know them by asking which tribe they belonged to, and they would answer his questions, glad of his interest in them. When he heard the problem of one of them, he would assure him that the right was on his side and that he was not in the wrong in anything, and he would say the same thing to his opponent if he also came. Then he would cast doubt on the justice of the judges whom the king appointed, accusing them of injustice, partiality and corruption in judgment, and so he led them to hate the king and weakened their trust in him.

entries.section: (1) Absalom wins the people to his side

paragraphs.text: Absalom claimed before them that if he sat on the seat of judgment, he would do justice to every man who had a suit.

entries.section: (1) Absalom wins the people to his side

paragraphs.text: He dealt with those who came for judgment in a manner that made them feel his humility as well as his sympathy with their problems. If any of them tried to bow down to him out of respect for his position as a prince, he would not let him bow down, but would raise him up, draw him near, and kiss him.

entries.section: (1) Absalom wins the people to his side

paragraphs.text: They come for judgment: they appear before the judges to have their cases heard.
He stole the hearts of the men of Israel: he won their hearts to himself, and they loved him.
Such was his conduct toward everyone who came for judgment from all the tribes of Israel, and by it he drew their hearts to himself and they loved him.

Do not be a hypocrite and deceive others, showing affection and love in order to achieve your own purposes. Rather, be sincere in showing good feelings, so that you may reveal to them the Christ who dwells in you and win them to Him.

entries.section: (2) Absalom plots a coup against his father King David

paragraphs.text: Forty years after Samuel anointed David king, Absalom began to take an actual step to seize the kingdom. He claimed to his father that he had a vow to the Lord that he must fulfill, and asked him to allow him to go to Hebron to worship the Lord and offer sacrifices. This was merely an outward pretense; in truth he was preparing to stir up a rebellion against his father starting from Hebron, organizing his movement there, far from his father. The people of Hebron were the first over whom David had reigned when he reigned over the tribe of Judah only (2 Sam 5:5) after the death of Saul, and they were distressed by David's later move to Jerusalem, which belonged to the tribe of Benjamin. In addition, Absalom had been born there and had lived the beginning of his life there, so he must have had friends there and relationships with them.

entries.section: (2) Absalom plots a coup against his father King David

paragraphs.text: David did not object to allowing his son to go to Hebron to worship and offer sacrifices. On the contrary, he was glad of it, because it meant that his son was drawing near to God, and he blessed him with a prayer for his safety, and Absalom set out for Hebron.

entries.section: (2) Absalom plots a coup against his father King David

paragraphs.text: From Hebron Absalom sent his men throughout the land and gave them instructions that when they heard the sound of the trumpets, they were to spread among the tribes that this meant that Absalom was reigning in Hebron, so that they would make the whole people believe that Absalom had officially become king over the land.

entries.section: (2) Absalom plots a coup against his father King David

paragraphs.text: To complete his plan of seizing power without any right, he invited two hundred of the notables of the people to a feast he held in Hebron, and they accepted his invitation in good faith, not knowing that by this he wanted to make the people believe that he was supported as king by the leaders of the people. He also wanted to keep them away from Jerusalem so that they would not help the king against him, and likewise to weaken his father's morale, as he would feel that the leaders had left him and become supporters of Absalom. Besides, he was preparing the plan to convince them to accept him as king in place of his father.

Beware of pride, for it drags its owners into many troubles and makes them like the blind, so that they fall into various sins. Guard against it by submitting to your spiritual father, learning from those around you, and attending to your repentance every day, so that you live in humility.

entries.section: (3) David learns of Absalom's rebellion and leaves Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Giloh: a village in the hills of Judah, about 8 km northwest of Hebron.

Absalom sent for a wise man named Ahithophel, summoning him from his town "Giloh," where he was at that time offering sacrifices. This Ahithophel was originally a counselor to David, but sadly he betrayed his lord David and joined Absalom. Confusion spread through the land: some welcomed Absalom as king and some held fast to David as king, because Absalom's affability toward the people had led many to accept him, in addition to the organized propaganda for him in all the tribes.
In their betrayal of David, Absalom and Ahithophel are a type of Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Christ and sold Him.

entries.section: (3) David learns of Absalom's rebellion and leaves Jerusalem
