paragraphs.text: The news of Absalom's rebellion reached David from his loyal men, and that he had declared himself king and many had rallied around him.

entries.section: (3) David learns of Absalom's rebellion and leaves Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: David understood, by his experience and the wisdom God had given him, that the situation was serious, so he ordered his men to leave the city of Jerusalem, lest Absalom destroy it and kill them and everyone in Jerusalem. Perhaps he remembered at that time God's punishment of him after his fall into adultery and murder, that the sword would never depart from his house, and so he accepted what Absalom did with humility and submission to God.

entries.section: (3) David learns of Absalom's rebellion and leaves Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: All submitted to the king's command and showed their complete readiness to carry out everything he commanded them, for they were his loyal men.

entries.section: (3) David learns of Absalom's rebellion and leaves Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Concubines: female servants with whom the king had lived.
The king left his palace in Jerusalem, fleeing outside the city with his wives and his sons, and left ten of his concubines in the house in an attempt to preserve the royal palace if possible.

entries.section: (3) David learns of Absalom's rebellion and leaves Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: All David's men and his household followed him out of Jerusalem, and they gathered at the last house in the city to cross from there to the outside of the city. During this, David said the third Psalm: "LORD, how are they increased that trouble me!" "... he that did eat of my bread (Ahithophel) hath lifted up his heel against me."

entries.section: (3) David learns of Absalom's rebellion and leaves Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: The Pelethites: they are the police and the royal guard in the present day.
The Cherethites: the infantry of the army.
The Gittites: the people of the city of Gath, one of the five great Philistine cities.

David stood at the gate of the city, and his men began to cross to the outside of it before him one by one, and with them the police, the infantry of the army, the soldiers, and the Gittites who had accompanied David during his periods of flight from Saul, had converted to Judaism, and had become loyal to David; the number of the Gittites was 600 men.

It is good to be realistic, to meet adverse situations with wisdom, and to act quickly so that no harm comes to you. Lift your heart in prayer to God and He will guide you; do not yield to illusions and wishful thinking, but ask for God's help, and you will bear the affliction and pass through it until it ends.

entries.section: (4) Ittai the Gittite insists on accompanying David

paragraphs.text: Ittai the Gittite: a man from the city of "Gath," who was the commander of the six hundred Gittite men mentioned above.

Ittai, a Philistine man from Gath, wanted to go out with David and accompany him in his flight from Jerusalem, but David did not want to burden him with the hardship of the pursuit to which he would be exposed. There was no reason for it, since he was a foreigner and far from his own country, and the matter might not concern him at all; he could stay in Jerusalem to serve the new king, for he had come to the land of Judah only a short time before, and it was not proper for him to wander about with David, for David did not know where matters would settle for him. So he asked him to return to Jerusalem and to take his six hundred Gittite men with him as well. David prayed for him, asking mercy from the Lord for the loyalty he had shown toward him, and asked the Lord to reward him with good.

We note that this account is an elaboration of what is mentioned in (v. 18); the historical order is that David told them to go back, and when they insisted on following him, they crossed to the outside of the city with the Pelethites and the Cherethites.

entries.section: (4) Ittai the Gittite insists on accompanying David

paragraphs.text: Ittai swore by the living God that he would not leave his lord but would stay with him in every circumstance, whether God willed to give him life or death. In his following of David, Ittai is a type of the Gentiles who followed Christ, while Absalom, in his rejection of David his father, is a type of the Jews who crucified Christ.

entries.section: (4) Ittai the Gittite insists on accompanying David

paragraphs.text: In the face of the determination and resolve that Ittai showed not to abandon his lord, David allowed him to cross with the people going out of Jerusalem, and he crossed, he and his six hundred men and all their little ones and their wives.

How great is this loyalty and love from Ittai, a man of foreign race! It is remarkable that David is betrayed by his son, yet is supported by strangers who loved him, just as he was supported before by Jonathan and Michal, the children of Saul, who was persecuting him. May you be loyal to every person who has shown you love, and above all be loyal to God, so that you do not betray Him by committing sin, and if you sin, return to Him quickly in repentance.

entries.section: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

paragraphs.text: The Kidron Valley: its present name is the Valley of Sitt Maryam, and it is sometimes called the Valley of Jehoshaphat; it extends from the northwest of Jerusalem to its southeast.
The way of the wilderness: the wilderness of the Jordan between Jerusalem and Jericho.

Sorrow filled all of Jerusalem, and the people were weeping over what had befallen. The king went out with his men and they came to the Kidron Valley, and all the people went out with him and passed through the wilderness of the Jordan (between Jerusalem and Jericho). And as David crossed this valley, so also Christ crossed this valley on His way to the garden of Gethsemane on the night of His sufferings (Jn 18:1).

entries.section: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

paragraphs.text: Zadok: of the descendants of Eleazar son of Aaron, and one of the two great priests in the days of David; he remained faithful to him during Adonijah's attempt to seize the kingdom.

Out of the priests' love for David and their feeling that he was the true king, Zadok and Abiathar brought out the Ark and set it down at the gate of the city, so that all the people going out of the city might pass before it, to lift their morale and give them the feeling that God was in their midst and was their helper.

entries.section: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

paragraphs.text: David preferred that the Ark remain in Jerusalem, so he asked Zadok to return it to its place, for if the Lord willed to bring David back to his kingdom, He would let him see the Ark and the tabernacle of meeting again, and if the Lord was not pleased with him, let Him do to him as seems good in His eyes. This shows how great David's concern was for the Ark: it should remain in its place and not be taken out as the sons of Eli the priest took it out in their war with the Philistines, and they were defeated and the Philistines took the Ark (1 Sam 4, 5). The Ark must stay firmly in its place, while David was merely a man: either God would be pleased with him and bring him back to his kingdom, or He would not bring him back because he did not deserve it. This was great humility on David's part.

This is a lesson for us from our teacher David: that we should always surrender our lives to the Lord so that He may accomplish His will in them according to His good pleasure, and accept with thanksgiving everything the Lord allows for us.

entries.section: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

paragraphs.text: You are a seer: full of wisdom and understanding, able to judge matters and see which is right. Abiathar: the other great priest, who conspired with Adonijah to take the kingdom for him.

Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar: they remained in Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion and used to inform David of Absalom's plans, and Ahimaaz was the first to tell David of Absalom's defeat. David asked Zadok to return to Jerusalem, together with Ahimaaz his son and Jonathan son of Abiathar, so that he might follow the course of events inside the city, analyze them with his wisdom, and send David a report on the situation.

entries.section: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

paragraphs.text: David made the two great priests Zadok and Abiathar understand that he would slow his pace in the plains of the wilderness of the Jordan, waiting for them to bring him word of the movements of Absalom and his men around the city after watching them closely, and to send him news of all the details by their two sons.

entries.section: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

paragraphs.text: Zadok and Abiathar carried out David's directions, and they carried the Ark back to its place in Jerusalem and stayed there watching for Absalom's movements, so as to inform David of everything that happened.

(6) Ahithophel joins Absalom, and David seeks the help of Hushai the Archite to defeat Ahithophel's counsel (vv. 30-37:) 30And David went up by the ascent of mount Olivet, and wept as he went up, and had his head covered, and he went barefoot: and all the people that was with him covered every man his head, and they went up, weeping as they went up. 31And one told David, saying, Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom. And David said, "O LORD, I pray thee, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness." 32And it came to pass, that when David was come to the top of the mount, where he worshipped God, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat rent, and earth upon his head: 33Unto whom David said, "If thou passest on with me, then thou shalt be a burden unto me: 34But if thou return to the city, and say unto Absalom, I will be thy servant, O king; as I have been thy father's servant hitherto, so will I now also be thy servant: then mayest thou for me defeat the counsel of Ahithophel. 35And hast thou not there with thee Zadok and Abiathar the priests? therefore it shall be, that what thing soever thou shalt hear out of the king's house, thou shalt tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests. 36Behold, they have there with them their two sons, Ahimaaz Zadok's son, and Jonathan Abiathar's son; and by them ye shall send unto me every thing that ye can hear." 37So Hushai David's friend came into the city, and Absalom came into Jerusalem.

entries.section: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

paragraphs.text: The Mount of Olives: east of the Kidron Valley, which separates it from Jerusalem.

David and his men went up the Mount of Olives, and the scene was deeply moving: David was weeping with his head covered as a sign of intense grief, and walking barefoot as a sign of abasement, and all the people accompanying him did likewise. David had not wept before during Saul's pursuit of him, but here he weeps because the betrayal came from his son, and perhaps he remembered at that time his sins of adultery and murder, so he wept in repentance, humbling himself before God.

entries.section: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

paragraphs.text: Turn into foolishness: make his counsel wrong, vain and useless.

David learned that his former counselor Ahithophel had joined Absalom's camp, so he prayed to the Lord to bring to nothing the counsel of Ahithophel that he might give to Absalom (Ps 41:11). David's goodness is shown in that he did not ask for harm to come to Ahithophel the traitor, but only for his counsel to be brought to nothing.

entries.section: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

paragraphs.text: David reached the top of the Mount of Olives and worshipped there. Hushai the Archite, one of David's counselors, had been absent from Jerusalem during that period, and when he learned of the events he went at once to David with his clothes torn and earth on his head, as a sign of intense grief, wishing to accompany his lord wherever he went.

entries.section: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

paragraphs.text: David saw that Hushai's going out with him would add nothing to the strength of his army but would increase his burdens, because he would have to provide for his needs, and Hushai was not a man of war, being a man of counsel, and it was more profitable for David to benefit from his abilities. So he asked him to return to Jerusalem and pretend to serve Absalom as he had served his father, and to give counsel that opposed the counsel of Ahithophel, and this is what in fact happened, as we shall see later. And David repeated Psalm 41: "Mine enemies speak evil of me."
God always sends help to His servants in due time, so we should pray to Him, asking for help in distress, and He is able to use whomever He wills to bring us deliverance from dangers.

entries.section: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

paragraphs.text: David assigned him a useful task and informed him that he would find in Jerusalem both Zadok and Abiathar with their two sons, and that Hushai was to watch everything that happened around Absalom and what was said in his council in conversations with his followers, and to report all that he saw and heard to the two priests, who would send it with their two sons to David. All this arrangement was for David's protection and involved no wrong to Absalom, but was an attempt to stop his evil. It will appear later how great was David's love and concern for the life of his son Absalom despite all the evil he had done against him.

entries.section: (5) The Ark of God is sent back from the field of battle

paragraphs.text: Hushai carried out David's request and returned to the city of Jerusalem, and the time of his arrival coincided with the arrival of Absalom, who entered it to take possession of it and set himself up as king over Israel. The meeting of Ziba and Shimei with David, and Absalom's entry into Jerusalem

entries.section: (1) Ziba deals treacherously with Mephibosheth

paragraphs.text: Ziba: the servant of Mephibosheth (ch. 9). Bottle: a skin vessel for keeping liquids.

Ziba came to David while he was on the Mount of Olives and presented him with a gift consisting of two donkeys, two hundred loaves of bread, bunches of grapes, a hundred cakes of figs, and a skin of wine. Ziba did this expecting David to triumph over Absalom's rebellion, so that good would come to him from David.

entries.section: (1) Ziba deals treacherously with Mephibosheth

paragraphs.text: Faint: tired.

David asked him why he had brought all this, and Ziba answered that the donkeys were for the king's household to ride on, to ease the weariness of the journey, the bread and figs for the king's soldiers to eat, and the wine for those who might grow weary from walking in the wilderness, since wine was used at that time as a remedy for some illnesses.

entries.section: (1) Ziba deals treacherously with Mephibosheth

paragraphs.text: David asked Ziba about Mephibosheth the son of Saul, and he answered him that he was in Jerusalem. Here Ziba seized the opportunity to slander Mephibosheth falsely, claiming that he was pleased with the events taking place, in the hope that the present conflict between David and Absalom would end in his favor, that is, in Mephibosheth's favor, and the people would choose Mephibosheth as king over them. The truth is that Mephibosheth was innocent of this charge and wished to come to meet David as he left Jerusalem, but Ziba deceived him and went without him (ch. 19:26).

entries.section: (1) Ziba deals treacherously with Mephibosheth

paragraphs.text: The king believed Ziba's words and was angry with Mephibosheth, whom he had honored and treated well: how could he repay kindness with evil? Therefore he issued a decree that everything he had given to Mephibosheth of possessions and lands should be given to his servant Ziba. Ziba rejoiced and bowed down in thanks to the king, and prayed for him, wishing that the king's favor toward him and care for him might continue.
David benefited from Ziba's conduct toward him in the following ways:
1 - Discipline from God: as one of his commanders, Uriah, was betrayed by David, so now Mephibosheth, to whom David had done much good, betrays him.
2 -David and his men needed the food that Ziba brought.
3 -David learned not to be hasty in his judgments on Mephibosheth, for he understood afterward that he had been wronged and that Ziba was the traitor.
Do not betray those around you and deal treacherously with them to gain quick profits, for God sees you, and you will lose later on earth and then lose your place in the Kingdom.

entries.section: (2) Shimei son of Gera curses David

paragraphs.text: Bahurim: a village near the Mount of Olives, lying between it and the Jordan River; its site is now "Ras et-Tamim."

David and his men reached the village of Bahurim, and behold, a man came out from it to meet them, Shimei son of Gera, one of the inhabitants of that village, who belonged to the tribe of Benjamin and the clan of Saul. He was gloating over what had befallen David, so he began to curse him with harsh words and to throw stones at him, he and his men, as a sign of insult and spite. Of course the stones and dust did not reach David and his men, but they were signs of hatred and gloating, because Shimei was walking on one hill and David and his men on another, with a valley separating them.

entries.section: (2) Shimei son of Gera curses David

paragraphs.text: Bloody man: a man of wars and bloodshed.
Man of Belial: a wicked man, because he is attributed to Belial, who is a pagan god.
The LORD hath returned upon thee all the blood of the house of Saul: the Lord has taken vengeance on you for those of the house of Saul who died.

What this man said was a plain expression of his gloating over David, asking him never to return to Jerusalem, which he had left, and accusing him of being a man thirsty for bloodshed. He supposed that King David was the cause of the death of Abner son of Ner and of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and therefore that he was a wicked man who had seized the kingdom from the house of Saul, and now the Lord was taking vengeance on him for those evils, taking the kingdom from him and giving it to his son Absalom, and that the misfortunes that had befallen him were nothing but a sign of the Lord's vengeance on him and on his deeds. Yet this was the opposite of the truth, for David had not killed anyone of the house of Saul, and he had fought the wars of the Lord to triumph over the pagans.

entries.section: (2) Shimei son of Gera curses David

paragraphs.text: Sons of Zeruiah: Zeruiah was David's sister and the mother of Joab and his two brothers Abishai and Asahel.

Abishai, one of David's chief commanders, was enraged by this man's behavior and described him as a mere contemptible dog of no worth, and asked the king's permission to go over to him and cut off his head. The king rebuked him and made him understand that his opinion did not agree with what the king himself saw, and that he should not work to silence Shimei, for he was only an instrument the Lord used to discipline David, because God was displeased with him on account of his sin. David was not willing then to punish Shimei, just as Christ was not willing for Peter to use his sword in defending Christ when He was arrested.

Do not be vexed with those who wrong you, but accept this from the hand of God and examine yourself, perhaps you are at fault in something toward God. Make excuses for those who wrong you and forgive them.

entries.section: (2) Shimei son of Gera curses David

paragraphs.text: David wanted to lessen the impact of Shimei's insolence on his men, so he urged them not to be surprised at his conduct: if his own son, David's son who came from his own loins, was pursuing him, it was no wonder that a man of the tribe of Benjamin and of the clan of Saul should do what he was doing in cursing and insulting him. He repeated his request to them to let the man say what he pleased, for he deserved that insult, since the Lord was the one who had allowed it.

entries.section: (2) Shimei son of Gera curses David

paragraphs.text: David hopes that God will reward him for accepting the insult, considering that it came by God's permission, and will give him mercy by forgiving his sins.

entries.section: (2) Shimei son of Gera curses David

paragraphs.text: Shimei continued to curse David and to throw dust and stones at him and his men, expressing his contempt and gloating.

entries.section: (2) Shimei son of Gera curses David

paragraphs.text: Because of the length of the journey and the intense grief of all the people, weariness overcame them, so they turned aside to a place in the wilderness of the Jordan to rest from the toil of the journey.

entries.section: (3) Hushai as a counselor to Absalom

paragraphs.text: On the other side, Absalom's advance and the men who had joined him reached Jerusalem, together with Ahithophel his counselor, and the time of his arrival coincided with the arrival of Hushai the Archite, to carry out what David had instructed him. As soon as he arrived in Jerusalem, Hushai the Archite began to draw close to Absalom, declaring his complete loyalty to him and proclaiming him king.

entries.section: (3) Hushai as a counselor to Absalom

paragraphs.text: Absalom found it strange that Hushai had left David in his crisis as he fled from Jerusalem, and he asked him the reason for his lack of loyalty to him.

entries.section: (3) Hushai as a counselor to Absalom

paragraphs.text: Hushai denied having betrayed David, and wisely claimed that he would serve the one whom the Lord and the people had chosen as king over them, especially since he was the son of his lord David and not a stranger to him, and he added that he was ready to be as loyal to him as he had been loyal to David. Hushai meant David, because he was the one whom God had chosen, but Absalom, in his pride, supposed that he was the one chosen by God.
If your intention is good, God will help you and give you favor in the eyes of others, and will use you in every good work and give you wisdom in every action.

entries.section: (4) Absalom goes in to his father's concubines

paragraphs.text: As soon as Absalom entered Jerusalem, he asked Ahithophel, who was considered the most important of the king's counselors, together with those with him, what he should do at the beginning of his reign.

entries.section: (4) Absalom goes in to his father's concubines

paragraphs.text: Ahithophel advised Absalom to lie with the ten concubines who had stayed behind and not fled with David, and had remained in Jerusalem to look after David's house. Then the people would hear and be certain that this conduct of Absalom's would anger David and would leave no room for the possibility of reconciliation between Absalom and his father, and they would work with all their might to establish Absalom as king, for otherwise, if David got hold of them, he would strike them down with a terrible blow. So there would be no going back from the rebellion they had carried out.

entries.section: (4) Absalom goes in to his father's concubines

paragraphs.text: Absalom carried out Ahithophel's advice, and they pitched a tent for him on the roof of the royal palace so that he might lie in it with David's women in the sight of all Israel, so that the people would know that the relations between him and his father had become completely strained, with no going back.

We recall here that it was from this roof that David cast an evil look at Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite and then fell with her, and now God allows him to be disciplined by his son's adultery with his concubines.

entries.section: (4) Absalom goes in to his father's concubines

paragraphs.text: It was known to all that Ahithophel was a wise and experienced man whose counsel never failed, and both David and Absalom valued his counsel very highly and regarded what he said as though it were from God. Ahithophel wanted to show Absalom's enmity toward his father, and then to have David killed by the hand of Absalom and his men, because he feared that David would be reconciled with Absalom, forgive him and return to his kingdom, and then take vengeance on Ahithophel himself, the author of the evil counsels.

Intelligence and wisdom are great gifts that divine providence grants in varying degrees, so let us use them for good and not for evil, lest we fall under judgment "when we are asked to give an account of our stewardship."
The defeat of Ahithophel's counsel

entries.section: (1) Ahithophel's counsel

paragraphs.text: After Ahithophel gave his first counsel concerning David's concubines, and Absalom carried it out, he now gives him the second counsel, concerning the war plan he advises him to follow, which was as follows: Ahithophel would choose 12,000 warriors to be under his command and would surprise David that very night. The shock of the surprise would confuse David and his men, especially as they were weary from the long journey, so the king would be alarmed and unable to lead his men, and they would flee, and then it would be easy to strike the king and kill him.

Ahithophel's counsel shows the extent of his betrayal of David, who had cared for him and looked after him for many years, for he resembles Judas Iscariot. To carry the betrayal further, he wanted to lead the army, perhaps so that he might have a greater position in the new kingdom.

entries.section: (1) Ahithophel's counsel

paragraphs.text: By the killing of David, all the people who were with him would return to Absalom and no one else would be killed, and peace would prevail. David here partly signifies Christ, of whom Caiaphas the high priest prophesied that He must die for the Jewish nation so that it might obtain salvation, and this was a prophecy from God on the mouth of Caiaphas (Jn 11:49, 50). Here Ahithophel says that by the killing of David the people would obtain peace and the ranks would unite behind Absalom, but God did not allow the death of David here, and Ahithophel's plan and counsel were rejected, as we shall see in the following verses.

entries.section: (1) Ahithophel's counsel

paragraphs.text: Absalom and all his men were persuaded by Ahithophel's counsel. In truth it was a very sound plan in every respect, for surprise always has a great effect in military tactics; and ending the fighting without bloodshed would please the people and raise Absalom in their eyes, since he did not wish to harm any of them.

May you appreciate the kindness and favor of anyone who has helped you in anything in your life, not only by giving thanks to God, but also by doing a service for him or for those around him as far as you can. But at the very least, do nothing against him, lest you be a traitor to him like Judas Iscariot.

entries.section: (2) The counsel of Hushai the Archite

paragraphs.text: Absalom asked for Hushai the Archite to be summoned, so that he might benefit from his experience as well and learn from him whether he supported the opinion of the other counselor, Ahithophel, so that all would agree on one opinion, or whether he had another point of view worthy of consideration, so that a choice could be made between the two opinions. Absalom's action was by God's ordering, because Ahithophel's plan was in fact sound and all the counselors approved it, but God allowed doubt in Absalom's heart, or he took care to add Hushai's counsel, perhaps so that the idea might be even more sound.

entries.section: (2) The counsel of Hushai the Archite

paragraphs.text: Hushai arrived and stood before Absalom, and Absalom set before him the plan Ahithophel had advised and asked him whether he supported it, so that it would be carried out, or whether he had another opinion, which he should present to him.

entries.section: (2) The counsel of Hushai the Archite

paragraphs.text: It was part of Hushai's wisdom that he acknowledged that Ahithophel's counsels had on many occasions been good and sound, because Ahithophel was one of the king's most important counselors, and he said this so that it would not be known from his opinion that he was prejudiced against Ahithophel, but he added that it was not good this time.

entries.section: (2) The counsel of Hushai the Archite

paragraphs.text: Hushai began to state the reasons for which he did not support Ahithophel's opinion. He mentioned that David's men were mighty men of war, and that they were in a state of great anger because of the events taking place, and that their anger was like the anger of a bear robbed of her cubs, which is seized by such fury that she devours everyone she meets. Moreover, David was a man of war with great knowledge and previous experience of its plans and the duties of precaution in them; he does not spend the night with his men, but chooses places that no one expects, such as digging a trench to spend the night in or hiding in one of the natural pits in case fighting breaks out between the two camps. And even if some of David's men were killed in the battle, counter-rumors could spread saying that those who were killed were Absalom's soldiers, and the morale of Absalom's army and of his followers among the people would be affected.

entries.section: (2) The counsel of Hushai the Archite

paragraphs.text: Even the brave and mighty soldiers of Absalom's army, though their hearts are strong as the heart of a lion, are struck to the core by rumors, and fear begins to spread in their hearts, because they know very well the courage of David and the heroes of his army and David's military abilities.

entries.section: (2) The counsel of Hushai the Archite

paragraphs.text: After Hushai had set out the reasons for his rejection of Ahithophel's plan, he began to give his own counsel, which was as follows:

All the tribes of Israel are to be summoned from the north of the land to the south, so that their number will be great, like the sand that is by the sea, and they will gather around Absalom to protect him on every side, and then attack David wherever he may be hiding, as the dew falls on the ground, and kill him and his men, so that not one of them is left alive.

entries.section: (2) The counsel of Hushai the Archite

paragraphs.text: Hushai goes on explaining his plan, setting out an imaginary picture that pleases Absalom's vanity. He says that if David in his flight takes refuge in some city, that city will be destroyed, as if its houses were tied with ropes and the ropes pulled, so that the houses fall and become heaps and ruins; he means that it will be easy to destroy because the army that is with Absalom is very large.

entries.section: (2) The counsel of Hushai the Archite

paragraphs.text: The good counsel of Ahithophel: that is, sound with respect to the killing of David, and the intended meaning is not that it was good in the eyes of God.

The imaginary picture that Hushai devised dazzled the minds of Absalom and his men, and displays of grandeur and pomp led them astray, as he imagined himself in the midst of tens of thousands of people surrounding him, striking down David and his followers and demolishing the cities in which they were hiding. Because he was proud, he accepted Hushai's counsel with great joy and was deceived by it, for pride blinds a man's eyes, and Absalom and his men decided that Hushai's plan was better than Ahithophel's plan. This was by God's ordering, for the sake of David's righteousness and Absalom's wickedness, and He persuaded Absalom and all the counselors of Hushai's plan in answer to David's prayer (ch. 15:31). Thus we see that with the temptation God makes the way of escape for His loving children: despite the danger of Ahithophel's counsel, God made Absalom accept Hushai's counsel and so saved their beloved David.
Man is often deceived by outward things and enticed by external appearances, so that he falls into pride and conceit and loses his goodness.

entries.section: (3) Hushai informs the priests of the counsel

paragraphs.text: In fulfillment of David's instructions, Hushai conveyed to Zadok and Abiathar, the chief priests, the details of what had taken place in the session in which Absalom and his men consulted with his counselors.

entries.section: (3) Hushai informs the priests of the counsel

paragraphs.text: As a precaution, lest Absalom turn to Ahithophel's plan and attack David that night, Hushai asked the two priests to advise David to cross the Jordan the same day to the east bank, so that he and his men would not perish before the attack of Absalom's army.

entries.section: (3) Hushai informs the priests of the counsel

paragraphs.text: Ahimaaz and Jonathan: the sons of the priests Zadok and Abiathar (ch. 15:27). Ahimaaz and Jonathan were waiting by a well near Jerusalem called En-rogel, preferring not to stay inside the city, so that no one would suspect them when they left it to carry the news to David, and Zadok and Abiathar sent a maidservant to their sons carrying the news that had to be delivered to David.

entries.section: (3) Hushai informs the priests of the counsel

paragraphs.text: Fine flour: choice flour from which various cakes are made.

Absalom also had spies in the area, and one of them discovered the movements of Ahimaaz and Jonathan and the maidservant and informed Absalom. Ahimaaz and Jonathan sensed that someone was watching them and expected Absalom to seize them, so they entered the house of a man in the village of Bahurim near Jerusalem, and his wife hid them in a dry well that was inside the house, and covered the well with a covering and spread fine flour on it, so that it would appear that the covering was spread on the ground with the flour on it and there was no well in the place.

We note that at the village of Bahurim Shimei stood gloating over David and cursing him, and in the same village God arranged the rescue of David's helpers, through this woman who loved David. So when we accept insults, God gives us deliverance for the sake of our humility.

entries.section: (3) Hushai informs the priests of the counsel

paragraphs.text: What Ahimaaz and Jonathan had expected indeed happened, for some of Absalom's men came searching for them, as some of the inhabitants of the area had pointed them to the house they had entered. When the messengers asked the woman about them, she denied that they were in the house and claimed that they had crossed a brook near the house, so the messengers searched for them in the place and around it, and when they did not find them, they returned to Absalom. This was of course a lie, but God did not expose her, in order to save His good priests.

entries.section: (3) Hushai informs the priests of the counsel

paragraphs.text: After the place was emptied of Absalom's messengers, Ahimaaz and Jonathan came out of the well in which they had been hidden and went at once to David and conveyed to him the message that came from Hushai the Archite and his advice that he cross the Jordan immediately, because Ahithophel had advised Absalom to attack him, but Hushai had postponed the attack for a few days so that he could prepare.

entries.section: (3) Hushai informs the priests of the counsel

paragraphs.text: David acted on Hushai's advice, lest Absalom turn back and follow Ahithophel's words and attack him, so he and his men crossed to the east of the Jordan, and their crossing lasted all night, so that by the time daylight broke all had crossed. That is, all the events mentioned in this chapter took place in one day, ending with this night in which David crossed the Jordan River, which was very wearying for David and those with him.

The priests' sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan bore the risk to their lives in order to save David and those with him. So be courageous and help the needy and the wronged, even if you sacrifice some effort or money or anything you can offer, for you offer it to God in the person of these needy ones.

entries.section: (4) Preparation for war

paragraphs.text: Ahithophel saw that his counsel had not been followed, and expected that Hushai's plan would lead to David's victory, so that he would return to his kingdom and take vengeance on him for his betrayal in joining Absalom. So he saddled his donkey and returned to his town, set his house in order, and then killed himself by hanging, and they buried him in the tomb of his father. Ahithophel here is a type of Judas Iscariot: after trying to kill David, who is a type of Christ, and failing, and feeling his sin, he despaired and killed himself.

Suicide is a great sin, for it means loss of hope and failure to surrender to God in all circumstances, so we must not lose confidence in His promises, but cling to them and never despair of His mercy. Whatever our faults, we repent and ask for His help, and He will save us and forgive our sins.

entries.section: (4) Preparation for war

paragraphs.text: Mahanaim: it lies east of the Jordan and north of the Jabbok River, one of the tributaries of the Jordan, and it is fortified, so it suited David as a place to hide in.

After David crossed the Jordan, he reached Mahanaim, and Absalom acted on Hushai's counsel, gathering a huge army from all the tribes of Israel, and he also crossed the Jordan in preparation to meet the army of David his father.

entries.section: (4) Preparation for war

paragraphs.text: Amasa: he is the son of Abigail, David's sister, so he is considered the cousin of Joab, the commander of David's army; he was an Ishmaelite on his father's side and an Israelite on his mother's side, and later Joab stabbed him treacherously with his sword. Abigail the daughter of Nahash: a half-sister of David.
Ithra the Israelite: an Ishmaelite man who married Abigail, David's sister, and was called the Israelite (1 Chr 2:17) because he joined the Jews.

Nahash: probably the king of the children of Ammon, who married a woman and then divorced her, and Jesse, David's father, married her and had two daughters by her, Zeruiah and Abigail, so they are David's sisters but only on the father's side.
Absalom appointed a man named Amasa as commander of his army, because Joab remained loyal to David. This Amasa was a son of Ithra.

entries.section: (4) Preparation for war

paragraphs.text: Gilead: a large region lying east of the Jordan.
Absalom encamped with his great army in the hill country of Gilead, near the place where David had encamped, in preparation for attacking him.

entries.section: (4) Preparation for war

paragraphs.text: Shobi the son of Nahash: an Ammonite man from Rabbah, the capital of the children of Ammon, who brought food for David and the people who were with him.

Machir the son of Ammiel: a man famous for doing good, who hosted in his house Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan until David summoned him to Jerusalem (ch. 9:3, 4). Lo-debar: a place in Gilead, now "Umm ed-Diyar," south of Wadi el-Arab east of the Jordan. Barzillai the Gileadite: a Gileadite man who was a friend of David and treated him well during his flight from Absalom, so David showed kindness to his family and charged Solomon his son to show kindness to the sons of Barzillai. Rogelim: a city in the land of Gilead, whose site today is Wadi er-Rujayla near Irbid. Beds: rugs and mats to lie on.
Basins: vessels in which food is placed.

Men loyal to David came to him at Mahanaim and brought him gifts, moved by love for him, loyalty to him, and compassion for their brothers who were with him. The men who came to him were Shobi the son of Nahash, Machir the son of Ammiel, and Barzillai the Gileadite.
The gifts they brought were as follows: beds to sit on, basins for putting water in for washing or for putting food in, and earthen vessels for cooking food.
Foodstuffs: wheat and barley, flour and parched corn; pulses: beans, lentils, and parched pulse; honey and butter, sheep for slaughter, and cheese of kine.

These loyal men appreciated the difficult circumstances surrounding the flight of David and his followers from Jerusalem, for they had left in haste and had not taken with them the means of living they needed, and had left behind everything they owned, walking long distances in the wilderness. They saw that the people were weary and hungry and thirsty, and they did not hesitate to supply them with what they saw they needed.
Some commentators hold that David sang Psalms 4 and 23 at this time, because they carry the meanings of trust in God and enjoyment of His care.

Great is God in His arrangements: He did not abandon David and those with him because they were wronged, but provided for all their material needs. So do not worry if you face problems or fear things that will happen in the future, because your God is responsible for you as long as you hold fast to Him, and He will never leave you.
Absalom's defeat and death

entries.section: (1) Victory over Absalom's army

paragraphs.text: David organized his army and appointed commanders over its divisions; although his army was small in number, he organized it with military skill.

entries.section: (1) Victory over Absalom's army

paragraphs.text: David divided his forces into three divisions headed by Joab, Abishai and Ittai the Gittite, and David wanted to go out himself to the field of battle to lead them all as supreme commander.

entries.section: (1) Victory over Absalom's army

paragraphs.text: The people insisted that David not go out to the field of battle, because he would be the target sought by Absalom and his men. They told him that if half of their men fled from the field or were killed, the enemy would not care about them, but in his being wounded or killed would be the end, and victory would be achieved for Absalom, since his life meant the continuance of his kingdom.

entries.section: (1) Victory over Absalom's army

paragraphs.text: David acted according to his people's counsel, so he stood beside the gate of the city, and the men of his army went out in ranks and orderly numbers, according to the division David himself had made before, so that each company consisted of a hundred fighters headed by a commander, and every ten companies made a thousand fighters headed by a greater commander, and each third was headed by one of the three commanders he had appointed before (v. 2).

entries.section: (1) Victory over Absalom's army

paragraphs.text: Despite all that Absalom had done against his father of rebellion and disobedience, the merciful father's heart feared that harm might touch his son, so he charged his commanders that if Absalom fell into their hands they were not to insult him or kill him, and the men of his army heard him as he commanded the commanders concerning his son.

Is this not an example of what the Lord of glory did with us sinners, for while we were yet sinners He gave His only Son as a redemption for us, and forgave even those who crucified Him while He was on the Cross? So be merciful and make excuses for those who wrong you; for just as the devil made them fall into evil, he can make you fall; and ask for God's help and mercy for yourself and for them, and you will be like your Lord Christ.

entries.section: (1) Victory over Absalom's army

paragraphs.text: Wood: the wood is land thick with trees, in addition to pits, difficult roads and wild beasts.

The wood of Ephraim: Ephraim dwells west of the Jordan and this place is east of the Jordan, and it was so called because Ephraim was defeated in it before Jephthah and the Gileadites (Judg 12:6); and this place is not the wood of Ephraim that is west of the Jordan (Josh 17:18). David's men went out to meet Absalom's army, and the field of battle was the thickly wooded lands of Ephraim.

entries.section: (1) Victory over Absalom's army

paragraphs.text: Absalom's men were severely defeated there, and a slaughter took place in which twenty thousand were slain, most of them from Absalom's army. This victory was due to God's help to David and his wronged men, and the Lord used the skill of David's men in war, while Absalom's men were less trained than they.

entries.section: (1) Victory over Absalom's army

paragraphs.text: The field of battle was broad, spread over a large area of land, and the flight of the men of Absalom's army was disorderly, so they scattered in the surrounding forests, and most of them died of hunger and thirst and unfavorable weather conditions, so that they were more than those who were slain by the swords of David's men. God saved David's men from the wood because they were defending their good king, and He allowed the death of many in Israel's army because they were enemies of David the good king whom God had chosen.

entries.section: (2) Joab kills Absalom

paragraphs.text: The oak: a huge tree with tangled branches.

It happened that a fighting party from David's army met Absalom as he was riding on his mule, and as soon as he saw them he was confused and tried to flee quickly from before them, so he went under a great tree with tangled branches, and his long hair became entangled and caught in the branches while the mule went on its way, leaving him in this position. Thus Absalom was left hanging by his hair in the branches of the tree between heaven and earth.

entries.section: (2) Joab kills Absalom

paragraphs.text: One of David's men made sure of Absalom's identity, and hurried to tell Joab his supreme commander that he had seen Absalom hanging in the tree.

The hair that was a source of pride and boasting to Absalom was also the cause of the calamity that befell him. Let our adornment not be "the outward adornment but the adornment of the spirit" (1 Pet 3:3).

entries.section: (2) Joab kills Absalom

paragraphs.text: Joab asked him in disapproval why he had not struck him down at once and killed him; if he had done this, he would have given him a valuable reward (150 grams of silver, which was a large sum at that time), in addition to a belt such as is given to one who has shown courage in battle.

entries.section: (2) Joab kills Absalom

paragraphs.text: The man showed his obedience to his king David, and his answer to Joab was that even if the reward to be given him were a hundred times what was mentioned, he would not be willing to do harm to Absalom, and he reminded Joab of the king's strict charge to his commanders not to harm Absalom.

entries.section: (2) Joab kills Absalom

paragraphs.text: I should have wrought falsehood against mine own life: I should have put my life in danger.
There is no matter hid from the king: this shows David's strength and wisdom and God's support for him.

The man told Joab that if he dared to kill Absalom, he would expose himself to severe punishment by King David, because the king would surely come to know of the matter, and Joab himself would then testify against him that he was the killer.

entries.section: (2) Joab kills Absalom

paragraphs.text: Joab said to the soldier, "I will not waste time speaking with you"; then he took three darts and thrust them into the heart of Absalom, who was still alive and hanging in the tree, and Joab commanded ten of his soldiers to finish killing Absalom; then the ten of Joab's men surrounded him and struck him until he died. In this way responsibility for the killing of Absalom was diffused, since eleven persons took part in killing him, among them the commander of the army, and it would be hard for David to order all of these put to death. Joab did this to protect himself from David's anger when he heard of his son's death. Joab did not obey David's charge because he saw that Absalom's life represented a danger to David's life: if he remained alive despite his defeat, he could try to gather another army as he had done at first and attack David again.

Absalom's death was a punishment from God for violating the commandment to honor one's parents, so we must not take lightly that commandment, which is the first commandment with promise, "that thy days may be long upon the land" (Ex 20:12).

entries.section: (2) Joab kills Absalom

paragraphs.text: As soon as Absalom was killed, Joab blew the trumpet announcing the end of the war, and commanded his men not to continue pursuing Absalom's men.
David here is a type of Christ, who triumphed over Satan in the battle of the Cross and bound him, as David triumphed over his enemies and Absalom was killed, who is a type of Satan.

entries.section: (2) Joab kills Absalom

paragraphs.text: The end was very sad, for no official funeral was held for Absalom as a prince, and he was not buried even in the tombs of his forefathers or in Jerusalem, and they did not carry him to his father at Mahanaim, but his body was cast into a deep pit in the very forest that had been the scene of the fighting, and they threw stones upon him until they formed a heap of stones, and this was a punishment from heaven for the son's disobedience.

entries.section: (2) Joab kills Absalom

paragraphs.text: The King's Dale: a valley lying east of Jerusalem.

Absalom had made for himself a memorial pillar in the King's Dale because he had no son left alive; he set it up with the aim of preserving his memory after his death, and sadly the pillar became a reminder to people of his rebellion and evil, not of his righteousness and purity of heart. More important than building tombs is that a person dwell in righteousness, so that he may have a place in heaven.

Among the most important things we must strive to leave behind on earth after our departure is the good remembrance that the people who lived in our time will keep of us, so let us strive that our memory be, as is that of the righteous, for blessing and not for a curse.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: Ahimaaz wanted to run to Mahanaim to bring the king David the good news of the victory achieved by his men and the defeat of his enemies, but Joab tried to stop him, advising him not to go, because what he thought was good news for the king would grieve him greatly because of the death of Absalom his son.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: Cushi: a man from Cush, that is, Ethiopia, and perhaps he was named after his country.

Joab called a Cushite man from among his men and commanded him to go and tell the king the news, and he obeyed and bowed down before Joab and ran to tell David what had been achieved on the field of battle.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: Ahimaaz was very happy with the victory that had been achieved, and he himself had had a part in achieving this victory, since he had earlier informed David of the counsel of Ahithophel and Hushai the Archite, and he remained convinced that the victory was good news worth bringing to the king, so he urged Joab to let him go too after the Cushite, whatever the result. Joab tried once more to stop him from going because he would receive no reward.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: The way of the plain: the road of the plain.

Ahimaaz remained insistent on going to David to tell him of the victory whatever the result, whether he was rewarded or not, and in the face of his insistence Joab allowed him, and Ahimaaz ran, shortly after the Cushite had run for the same purpose, but he took a different road from the one the Cushite took, which was the road of the plain, so that he arrived at David before the Cushite arrived.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: The two gates: a double wall around the city, each with a gate.
The watchman: a person assigned to watch any movements in the area around the city.

The wall of the city was a double wall, and each wall had a gate, and David was sitting in the area between the two gates, and the watchman had gone up to the roof over the gate and taken his place on the wall of the city to watch the movements coming toward the city, and he saw a man running toward the city.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: The watchman called to the gatekeeper to tell the king about this man running toward the city, and the king was reassured, because it was customary that a messenger who came alone would usually bring joyful news, but if the news was not pleasant, more than one person would come in great sorrow.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: After a short time the watchman saw another person also running alone toward the city (he was the Cushite), so the watchman called to the gatekeeper a second time to tell the king. And David said that he also was bringing good news since he was coming alone.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: As the two men drew near one after the other, their features became clearer, and he knew that the first was Ahimaaz, and David remarked on this that Ahimaaz was a man of good tidings.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: No sooner did Ahimaaz draw near the gate of the city than he called out to reassure the king, saying:
Peace, that is, all is well. And when he reached the king he bowed down before him and blessed the Lord, David's God, who had delivered into his hand the rebels who had resisted him.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: David's concern was directed toward the safety of his son, so he hastened to ask Ahimaaz, "Is Absalom safe?" Ahimaaz was wise, for although he knew what had befallen Absalom, he did not wish to tell the king, but claimed that when Joab sent him and the Cushite to go to him, he saw a great crowd of people and did not know the reason for their gathering.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: The king commanded him to stand where he was until the other messenger arrived, so that they might hear the news he brought.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: Ahimaaz had hardly finished his report when the Cushite arrived where the king was and cried out with good news: Good tidings, my lord the king, for the Lord hath avenged thee this day of all them that rose up against thee.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: The king was anxious for his son, so he hastened to ask the Cushite about his safety. The Cushite answered, praying that God would put to death all the enemies of the king as that young man had been put to death, and that their fate would be like his.

entries.section: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

paragraphs.text: It was clear from the Cushite's words that Absalom had been killed in the battle, and the king was shaken by the news and went up to the chamber over the gate, and from the intensity of the inner turmoil that seized him he began to walk about in the chamber in deep sorrow, crying out, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!", wishing that he had died instead of his son.

David's heart was full of fatherhood and mercy even toward his son who tried to kill him, and he wept bitterly over him at his death. May you be merciful and seek the salvation of sinners, even if they are your enemies and wrong you. David's return to the kingdom

entries.section: (1) Joab rebukes David for his grief

paragraphs.text: Joab came back in great joy at having killed Absalom and triumphed over his armies, in preparation for David's return to his throne, and he expected to hear praise from David, or at least thanks to the commanders of his army and his soldiers for their great effort, but he was surprised to find David absorbed in his grief over Absalom's death, which of course affected the whole army, so that they were in gloom instead of joy.

entries.section: (1) Joab rebukes David for his grief

paragraphs.text: The people too longed to hold victory celebrations for the great victory that had been achieved, but when they saw David weeping, grieving over the loss of his son, the celebrations turned to sorrow and the songs of victory were changed into a great mourning.

entries.section: (1) Joab rebukes David for his grief

paragraphs.text: Instead of the soldiers entering the city of Mahanaim, where David was, exulting in the victory they had achieved, they entered the city in complete silence, with heads bowed, as if they were defeated soldiers.

entries.section: (1) Joab rebukes David for his grief

paragraphs.text: David remained withdrawn into himself, covering his face with his hands from those around him, as though he did not wish to see anyone, repeating one cry in a loud voice: "O my son Absalom... O Absalom, my son... my son!"

entries.section: (1) Joab rebukes David for his grief

paragraphs.text: Joab was not pleased with the king's attitude toward the victory that had been achieved, so he entered the house where the king was and rebuked him severely for his behavior toward his people and his disregard of them and of the effort they had made to achieve the victory, for they had saved his life and the lives of his sons, his wives and his concubines from being killed by Absalom had victory in the war been his.

entries.section: (1) Joab rebukes David for his grief

paragraphs.text: Joab continued to reproach David, saying: You have shamed this day the faces of all your servants by your excessive grief over Absalom, who hated you and rebelled against you, while you did not appreciate what your men did, who loved you and fought for you. You have treated your men lightly as though they were of no account; indeed, perhaps you would be content with the death of all your soldiers and rejoice in the life of Absalom your enemy.

entries.section: (1) Joab rebukes David for his grief

paragraphs.text: Joab urged David to stop his lamenting and go out to receive his soldiers who had come to congratulate him and to show them the appreciation due to them, and he warned him in a severe and harsh tone that if he did not, he would command his soldiers not to guard him, and he would spend the night alone in the tent and be exposed to being killed treacherously by anyone.

entries.section: (1) Joab rebukes David for his grief

paragraphs.text: The king realized the seriousness of the matter, so he responded to Joab's warning, took courage, went out to the gate of the city and sat down. The warriors learned of the king's coming out, so they came to congratulate him on the victory, while Absalom's supporters were overtaken by shame and fled to their homes.
Do not indulge in your grief over the loss of one of your loved ones to the point of harming those around you, but be moderate, have hope in God, and ask for His help and consolation.

entries.section: (2) All the tribes ask for David's return

paragraphs.text: After Absalom's death, the people were at odds with themselves, and each party began to blame the other for supporting Absalom, but they all agreed that David was the one who had saved them in the past from their enemies and from the Philistines, and that he had now left his throne in flight from Absalom, so he was the true king of the people.

entries.section: (2) All the tribes ask for David's return

paragraphs.text: Absalom, whom they had supported and anointed king over them, had been killed, and so the throne was empty of both David and Absalom, so the situation was not sound and matters had to be put right by their inviting David to reign over them and return to his throne.

entries.section: (2) All the tribes ask for David's return

paragraphs.text: David did not wish to return to his throne except on the basis of a new pledge of allegiance from the people. He had learned that the tribes of Israel, except the tribe of Judah, had all agreed on proclaiming him king again, so he sent Zadok and Abiathar, the two great priests, to Judah, reproaching them for their delay in inviting him to return to his throne in Jerusalem while the other tribes had preceded them in that invitation.

entries.section: (2) All the tribes ask for David's return

paragraphs.text: Among the things David said to the tribe of Judah was that they were his brethren, his bone and his flesh, because he himself was of the tribe of Judah, so it was not fitting for them to be behind the rest of the tribes in inviting him to return.

entries.section: (2) All the tribes ask for David's return

paragraphs.text: David wished to win to his side Amasa, who had been the commander of Absalom's army and was, besides, a skilled commander, so he asked the two priests to inform him that David reminded him of his kinship to him (for David was his maternal uncle), and that he had sworn to appoint him commander of his army for life in place of Joab (David was angry with Joab despite his loyalty and zeal for him, for he had done some things that angered David, such as his killing of Abner (ch. 3), his killing of Absalom (ch. 18), and the harshness of his rebuke of him when he was weeping for Absalom (vv. 5-7). By this action he won Amasa and all his soldiers who followed him, as they felt that David was the king who embraced all his people and forgave them their faults.
David here is a type of Christ, who transforms those subject to Satan "that is, Amasa, subject to Absalom"
into righteous people, servants in the Church of God, as He transformed Saul of Tarsus into the great Apostle Paul.

entries.section: (2) All the tribes ask for David's return

paragraphs.text: The men of the tribe of Judah responded to David's message, for they saw that although they had been behind the rest of the tribes in inviting him, he was not angry with them but spoke to them gently, so they came to themselves and remembered that they were indeed his kinsmen and that he belonged to their tribe, and they agreed to send to him inviting him to return to Jerusalem with all his men.

By wisdom, humility and gentle words David was able to put an end to the evil into which the tribe of Judah had fallen, for they were liable to split away from David under the leadership of Amasa, but by kindness he was able to win them, so they submitted to him and he won Amasa also. May you, by humility and kindness, face the angry and so break every evil that meets you, win those around you, and live in peace.

entries.section: (2) All the tribes ask for David's return

paragraphs.text: The king made ready on the bank east of the Jordan to cross, returning to Jerusalem, and at the same time the leading men of Judah reached Gilgal west of the Jordan on their way to cross to the east bank to receive the king there and bring him back to Jerusalem, the capital of the kingdom, which lies in the territory of their tribe.

entries.section: (3) Shimei apologizes to David

paragraphs.text: Many came to meet David and welcome him on his way back to his throne in Jerusalem, and with them Shimei son of Gera, from the town of Bahurim, who had cursed the king and thrown stones and dust at him when he was fleeing from Absalom, trying by this to apologize for his fault, hoping that King David would be pleased with him (ch. 16:5).

entries.section: (3) Shimei apologizes to David

paragraphs.text: Shimei came to receive the king with a delegation of a thousand men; so also came Ziba, who had been a servant of Saul and of his son Mephibosheth after him, accompanied by his fifteen sons and his twenty servants, and they crossed the Jordan River at the head of the returning king's procession.
Ziba came because he knew that the king would discover his deceit and his accusation against Mephibosheth, and so he wanted to appease the king.

entries.section: (3) Shimei apologizes to David

paragraphs.text: Shimei prepared a special boat for the king and his household to cross in, putting himself at his service and ready to carry out his requests, and when Shimei met the king face to face he bowed down to the ground, showing respect and reverence for his person.

entries.section: (3) Shimei apologizes to David

paragraphs.text: Shimei begged the king to forgive him what he had previously done against him of cursing and insult when he was fleeing from Absalom, and asked him not to keep any grudge against him in his heart.

entries.section: (3) Shimei apologizes to David

paragraphs.text: The house of Joseph: he means that he came as the first group of the sons of Rachel, namely the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, and the tribe of Benjamin, for Shimei wished to show how great his concern was, so he came as the first group of these three tribes.

Shimei confessed that he had indeed sinned when he had previously wronged the king, and here he was atoning for his fault by coming with his men to receive the king, so he was the first of the house of Joseph to come.

May we look at matters more deeply, so that we do not slip into actions we will regret later and whose remedy may become difficult, if not impossible, for we will not always meet a good-hearted person who forgives the one who wronged him, as David did.

entries.section: (3) Shimei apologizes to David

paragraphs.text: Abishai son of Zeruiah was always impetuous in his zeal for David and loyalty to him, so he considered that everyone who was an enemy of David must be killed; in the past he asked David to kill Saul, and when Shimei was cursing David he asked his permission to kill him, and he now repeats his request because he saw that he had insulted David, the Lord's anointed. In addition, he felt that Shimei's apology was out of fear and not out of love, and perhaps it carried hypocrisy.

entries.section: (3) Shimei apologizes to David

paragraphs.text: David rejected Abishai's proposal, because it was not fitting that anyone of God's people be killed; today was a day of joy for all, and there should be no mourning in any house of Israel, and he rebuked Abishai for not taking into account this day of joy at David's return to his throne once more. In addition, if Shimei were killed, then everyone who had been his enemy and joined Absalom ought to be killed too, and in this way a civil war could break out through the killing of many.

entries.section: (3) Shimei apologizes to David

paragraphs.text: The king reassured Shimei and swore to him that no one would harm him. This was forbearance on David's part, although he knew that Shimei was insincere and deserved punishment, but he postponed that to the days of Solomon his son (1 Kgs 2:8, 9), and perhaps by this he gave Shimei an opportunity to repent and change his conduct, for his heart was not upright even now. David's forbearance toward Shimei was a waiver of his personal right against him, but Shimei had sinned against the Lord's anointed, so he had to be punished if he did not repent. Solomon warned him not to leave Jerusalem, but he left, and Solomon killed him. This signifies the one who goes outside the Church and so becomes liable to perdition. David here is a type of Christ on earth, who is forbearing toward those who wrong Him, and Solomon is a type of Christ in His glory when He judges the whole world.

entries.section: (4) Mephibosheth receives David

paragraphs.text: Mephibosheth son of Jonathan was also among those who came to receive David, and it appeared from his look that he was very sad over the tragedies to which the king had been exposed, for he had neglected to care for his weak feet by applying some medical treatments to them, and he had not trimmed his beard or taken care of his clothes. All these signs contradict the slander in which Ziba had claimed that he was gloating over the tragic events that had befallen the king (ch. 16:3).

entries.section: (4) Mephibosheth receives David

paragraphs.text: When Mephibosheth came to Jerusalem and met the king, the king reproached him for not accompanying him among the people who went out with him from Jerusalem when the rebellion arose.

entries.section: (4) Mephibosheth receives David

paragraphs.text: Mephibosheth answered him that he had indeed intended to go out with the king, and had asked his servant Ziba to prepare a donkey for him to ride, since he was lame and could not walk long distances, but his servant Ziba deceived him, for he did not prepare the donkey for him, and went to the king by himself without taking him along.

entries.section: (4) Mephibosheth receives David

paragraphs.text: Ziba was not content with that, but slandered me with what would inflame the king against me. And I know, my lord the king, that you are as an angel of God, able to distinguish between what is true and what is a false claim, and your judgment will be sound, so do what seems good to you.

entries.section: (4) Mephibosheth receives David

paragraphs.text: I know the measure of your justice and compassion, for when you took the kingdom you could have killed all those left alive of the house of Saul, as kings do with the offspring of the kings who preceded them, but you did not do so; instead you honored me and invited me to your table as one of the members of your family, so after all this that you have done for me of kindness and honor, it is not right for me to covet a kingdom or authority, for David's accusation of Mephibosheth meant that he had stayed in Jerusalem out of covetousness for the kingdom after him.

entries.section: (4) Mephibosheth receives David

paragraphs.text: The king asked him to stop speaking about matters that concerned him, for he had learned the truth of things before and had already corrected the situation, commanding that Mephibosheth take half the land and Ziba take the other half, because David had given all the possessions to Ziba and now corrected the situation by returning them to Mephibosheth, while Ziba would take half the produce in return for cultivating and looking after Mephibosheth's possessions. David was not harsh in punishing Ziba for his lie to David about Mephibosheth, because Ziba had done a good thing, namely not following Absalom but supporting David with food.

entries.section: (4) Mephibosheth receives David

paragraphs.text: Mephibosheth showed no eagerness to recover the land, for he made clear to David that it did not matter to him much even if all of it went to Ziba, since his true joy was in the king's return to his seat in peace.

entries.section: (5) Barzillai's farewell to David

paragraphs.text: Rogelim: a city in the land of Gilead in which Barzillai lived. Its site today is "Wadi er-Rujayla" near Irbid.
Barzillai was one of the important figures who hosted David during his flight from Absalom, and he came to bid him farewell at the Jordan River on his return to his throne.

entries.section: (5) Barzillai's farewell to David

paragraphs.text: Crossing the Jordan was hard work for Barzillai, who had reached the age of eighty, but he bore it in honor of David, and he had already shown great love for the king, for when David was at Mahanaim he brought gifts and food for him and his companions and provided for them during their stay.

entries.section: (5) Barzillai's farewell to David

paragraphs.text: While they were crossing the Jordan, the king offered him to go with him to Jerusalem to live beside him, so that he might repay his kindness and honor him as Barzillai had honored him when he was at Mahanaim.

entries.section: (5) Barzillai's farewell to David

paragraphs.text: Barzillai excused himself because he was an old man of eighty and no longer could taste kinds of food or drink, nor enjoy the voices of the singing men and singing women who sing in the houses of kings. And he did not wish to be a burden to the king, for he needed special care of the kind the aged generally require, such as attention to certain kinds of food and a regular manner of life because of the weakness and sickness that are marks of old age.

entries.section: (5) Barzillai's farewell to David

paragraphs.text: He asked the king to bid him farewell by crossing the Jordan with him, even for a short distance, and then there would be no need of any other reward for him, for this honor was enough for him.

entries.section: (5) Barzillai's farewell to David

paragraphs.text: He asked permission to return afterward to his city, and when the time came to depart from this world, to be buried in the tomb of his father and mother, and if there had to be a reward, let his son Chimham cross over with the king, who would take him with him and honor him as he pleased in his place.

entries.section: (5) Barzillai's farewell to David

paragraphs.text: The king welcomed Barzillai's proposal to take Chimham with him, and promised to reward him as much as Barzillai wished for him, and to do for him and for Barzillai himself all that he asked. It is said that he became ruler of Bethlehem (Jer 41:17), and Jewish tradition says that in his house Christ was born when He became incarnate.

entries.section: (5) Barzillai's farewell to David

paragraphs.text: The king bade Barzillai farewell, kissing him with the kiss of love and asking the Lord's blessing for him, and he went back to his city in Gilead, and the people completed the crossing of the Jordan with the king.

Barzillai was an example to be followed in dignity and wisdom, and not like some of the aged who behave with a recklessness like the conduct of young boys. So let those of us who are advanced in years crown their old age with goodness and let their conduct be marked by balance and reason, so that they detach themselves from material things and prepare, by a spiritual life, for eternity.

entries.section: (5) Barzillai's farewell to David

paragraphs.text: The king crossed the Jordan River from east to west and reached the city of "Gilgal" near Jericho, and Chimham was in the king's company, as were also in his company the men of the tribe of Judah and half the tribes of Israel (the other half were late in coming at the proper time, perhaps because of the distance between the dwelling place of those tribes, which lived in the north of Palestine, and the region of "Gilgal"). In this way David took along many kinds of his people, for he is a type of Christ, who receives everyone:
1 -The tribe of Judah: which signifies the whole Church.
2 -Amasa: who signifies the wicked and rebellious whom God changes by repentance, so that they return to Him.
3 -Shimei and Ziba: who signify sinners who try to repent.
4 -Mephibosheth: who signifies broken and wronged souls.
5 -Barzillai: who signifies the pious who are occupied with eternity.
6 -Chimham: who signifies souls new to the faith.

entries.section: (5) Barzillai's farewell to David

paragraphs.text: Why have our brethren stolen thee away: the men of Judah monopolized the king in their celebration of his return.

When the rest of the tribes arrived after the king had crossed westward, they protested against the tribe of Judah, which, as they said, had monopolized the honoring of the king, and had crossed the Jordan with the king and his household without waiting for them to share in the honoring.

entries.section: (5) Barzillai's farewell to David

paragraphs.text: The tribe of Judah grew heated in answering the tribes' objection, claiming that the king was of their tribe and there was a bond of kinship between him and them, and that the tribes had no right to be angry at Judah's crossing with the king, and they said, Have we eaten at all of the king's cost? or hath he given us any gift? That is, we did not monopolize gifts we received from the king and did not obtain a special grant of which you were deprived.

entries.section: (5) Barzillai's farewell to David

paragraphs.text: The men of the tribes did not keep silent, but answered the men of Judah that they were the majority, for they represented ten tribes and Judah was one tribe, and therefore they had the greater right to bring the king back, and the men of Judah answered the men of the tribes with harsh words; that is, a quarrel of words took place between them.
The rebellion of Sheba son of Bichri

entries.section: (1) Sheba declares himself king

paragraphs.text: As a result of the quarrel between the men of Judah and Israel (ch. 19), a wicked man of the tribe of Benjamin took advantage of the situation by declaring separation from David's kingdom, and incited the tribes not to follow David but to return to their homes.

The discussion began as a show of zeal for enthroning David but ended in separation between the tribes. This teaches us not to enter into a discussion that is pointless and may even lead to the opposite of what is hoped from it. The Apostle Paul said: "But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes" (2 Tim 2:23). So do not argue with an angry person, but absorb his anger with your love and patience, and you will draw him and spare yourself many problems.

entries.section: (1) Sheba declares himself king

paragraphs.text: Sheba's call found attentive ears among all the tribes, for as soon as he called them they answered his call and left their allegiance to the king, following this wicked man, declaring thereby their revolt against David's rule, and none remained loyal to him except the tribe of Judah, which accompanied him until his entry into Jerusalem. Thus we see the quick fickleness of the mind of the crowds.
God allowed this as discipline for David, who had wavered in his relationship with God when he sinned in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.

entries.section: (1) Sheba declares himself king

paragraphs.text: The king reached his house in Jerusalem, and shut up his ten concubines whom he had left to keep his palace, and with whom Absalom had lain (ch. 16:22); he did not live with them, because it was not fitting, and he treated them with honor, and they lived out their lives in chastity.

entries.section: (2) David commissions Amasa and Abishai to deal with Sheba

paragraphs.text: David had appointed Amasa commander of his army after removing Joab, because he was troubled by his actions, and he charged him to assemble an army from the tribe of Judah within three days and then return to him in Jerusalem.

entries.section: (2) David commissions Amasa and Abishai to deal with Sheba

paragraphs.text: Amasa obeyed, but it seems that matters did not go as expected, for the three days passed without his returning at the time David had set for him.

entries.section: (2) David commissions Amasa and Abishai to deal with Sheba

paragraphs.text: David saw, with his leader's shrewdness, that it was not wise to wait any longer for Amasa's return, for his delay gave the enemy, Sheba son of Bichri, room to arrange his ranks and occupy fortified places so that it would be hard to seize him, so he charged Abishai to take the king's special guard and go to pursue Sheba, for David expected that Sheba's rebellion would be more dangerous than Absalom's rebellion.

entries.section: (2) David commissions Amasa and Abishai to deal with Sheba

paragraphs.text: Abishai carried out the king's command and took the soldiers, heroes of wars, who had been under Joab's leadership, among them David's special guard and the battalions of infantry, and they went out of Jerusalem to go after Sheba and fight him.

It is not wise to be lazy and slow in facing the enemy, Satan; rather, sin must be cut off quickly, lest it grow within a person and become hard to resist. So drive out the thought from its beginning and do not be lax about evil talk, so that you do not fall into wicked deeds.

entries.section: (3) Joab kills Amasa treacherously

paragraphs.text: Gibeon: a city north of Jerusalem about 8 km away from it.
