On their march they came to a famous rock in Gibeon, and there they met Amasa returning with the soldiers he had gathered and heading for Jerusalem to meet the king. Joab accompanied his brother Abishai, and he was wearing his war clothes, and over his garment a girdle with a sword fastened to it, and Joab had deliberately made the fastening loose so that it would fall, and Joab would take hold of it with his left hand as though he did not want the sword to fall to the ground, but in truth he was preparing to deal treacherously with Amasa, as will appear.

entries.section: (3) Joab kills Amasa treacherously

paragraphs.text: Joab received Amasa with feigned affection, asking after his welfare, and took hold of his beard with his right hand to kiss him, as was the custom of close friends at that time.

entries.section: (3) Joab kills Amasa treacherously

paragraphs.text: Joab was holding Amasa's beard with his right hand to kiss him, and in his left hand the sword that had slipped from its fastening to the girdle, and Amasa did not expect treachery from Joab, so Joab struck him with the sword in the belly with a single blow that killed him at once, and then Joab and Abishai went after Sheba to put an end to his rebellion. Here appear Joab's jealousy and his grudge against Amasa, because David had set him up as commander of the army in his place, and this was because of Joab's harshness in his words to David, in addition to his treachery in killing Abner before, and also the killing of Absalom, and now he adds another crime to his crimes by killing an innocent man, Amasa, so he deserved punishment at the hand of Solomon the son of David.

Do not run after positions and honor, lest you clash with others and hold a grudge against them and live in gloom and misery; rather seek the Kingdom of God and trust that He will give you peace and honor, so that you live happier than all those around you.

entries.section: (4) Joab and Abishai put an end to the rebellion

paragraphs.text: The soldiers were lingering in their march at the body of Amasa, so one of Joab's followers stood beside the body, and his task was to urge the soldiers not to linger but to keep marching behind Joab, and in partiality to Joab he coupled Joab's name with David's name, proclaiming that he was still the commander of the armies and not Amasa, though this was not true, but this plan succeeded and the soldiers followed Joab.

entries.section: (4) Joab and Abishai put an end to the rebellion

paragraphs.text: Amasa lay on the roadside, wallowing in his blood, and everyone who passed him was affected by the horror of the sight and hesitated to continue marching, so when the man, Joab's follower, saw that the presence of Amasa's body was delaying the soldiers from following Joab, he moved the body into a field away from the road and covered it with a garment, and the soldiers' march became orderly, without stopping, behind Joab to go after Sheba son of Bichri.

entries.section: (4) Joab and Abishai put an end to the rebellion

paragraphs.text: Abel of Beth-maachah: a fortified city in the land of the tribe of Naphtali. It is now a small village lying northwest of Lake Huleh.

During the army's march behind Joab, many were joining it from the tribes until it reached a city called "Abel of Beth-maachah," in which Sheba son of Bichri had fortified himself, and there joined him members of a large family famous in that region, the "Berites."

entries.section: (4) Joab and Abishai put an end to the rebellion

paragraphs.text: Mound: a barrier or wall of stones and earth.

The commanders of David's army learned from their own reconnaissance sources that Sheba son of Bichri and his men were in the city of "Ayil Beth-maachah," so they besieged it to seize him and set up mounds around it, and prevented people from entering and leaving the city. After a period of siege, David's men began to open breaches in the wall to be able to enter the city.

entries.section: (4) Joab and Abishai put an end to the rebellion

paragraphs.text: At this time, when it seemed that the city was exposed to invasion and destruction, a wise woman appeared who was the cause of her city being spared the destruction that threatened it. That woman called to Joab's soldiers to ask him to come near the wall so that she could speak with him.

entries.section: (4) Joab and Abishai put an end to the rebellion

paragraphs.text: Joab responded to her request, and she asked him whether he was Joab and whether he was ready to hear what she would say, and he answered yes, and she spoke to him with respect and humility, saying "thine handmaid," that is, your servant.

entries.section: (4) Joab and Abishai put an end to the rebellion

paragraphs.text: The woman began her speech by mentioning what the wise men of her city "Abel" were famous for, how everyone who sought counsel resorted to them and they solved their problems and judged the cases brought before them. Their opinion was always sound and ended the problem in the best way, so she invited Joab to reach an understanding as the Law commands (Deut 20:10) and not to rush into destroying the city so as not to do evil.

entries.section: (4) Joab and Abishai put an end to the rebellion

paragraphs.text: The woman speaks on behalf of her city, saying that it is a city that loves peace and is faithful to the people of Israel, and you, Joab, have come with your armies to destroy and wipe out a city that is a mother in Israel (so called because of the wisdom of its people). Then the woman went on to say, why do you seek to destroy one of the cities of the Lord, which He gave as an inheritance to His people?!

entries.section: (4) Joab and Abishai put an end to the rebellion

paragraphs.text: Joab answered that he did not allow himself to destroy and ruin, and that the matter was not as she had presented it, for all there was, was that a man named Sheba son of Bichri from the region of the hill country of Ephraim had declared his rebellion against the king and revolted against him, and if the people of her city delivered him to him, he would depart at once and lift the siege from it. The woman answered him that if that was so, the people of her city would seize Sheba and kill him and throw his head over the wall.

entries.section: (4) Joab and Abishai put an end to the rebellion

paragraphs.text: The woman went to the people of the city and persuaded them by her wisdom that they should spare their city destruction and ruin rather than shelter one rebellious and disobedient person, and being sensible, they seized Sheba and killed him and threw his head to Joab from over the wall. Then Joab blew the trumpet, giving his soldiers the signal to end the war, and they departed to their country, and Joab returned to King David in Jerusalem. Thus God allowed this rebellion as discipline for David for his old sin, but He ended the trouble quickly by the killing of Sheba, for God wants us to understand His discipline and repent, and it is not His pleasure that we fall into hard sufferings.

The intervention of the wise by their wisdom spares many difficult situations. So let us be positive in confronting events and act with the wisdom with which God favors us in dealing with matters, so that we may be messengers of peace in the environment in which we live; for wisdom, as the Book of Proverbs describes it, "is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her: and happy is every one that retaineth her" (Prov 3:18).

entries.section: (5) David's appointment of religious, military and administrative heads

paragraphs.text: The Cherethites and the Pelethites: the Cherethites are the police and the royal guard, and the Pelethites are the infantry of the army.

As a reward for his victory in the matter of Sheba son of Bichri, David pardoned Joab and restored him to the command of the army and confirmed him in his position, and David also set Benaiah son of Jehoiada over the royal guard and the infantry of the army.

entries.section: (5) David's appointment of religious, military and administrative heads

paragraphs.text: Adoram: a man whom David set to oversee the collection of tribute, and he remained in this office throughout the reign of Solomon and until the time of Rehoboam.
Tribute: the tax imposed on the other peoples, not the people of the Lord, who were subject to David's authority.
Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud: he held the office of recorder in the reign of David and Solomon.

David appointed Adoram to oversee the collection of tribute from the foreign peoples subject to him, and he appointed Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud to record the laws, regulations, administrative decisions and judicial rulings.

entries.section: (5) David's appointment of religious, military and administrative heads

paragraphs.text: Sheva: a scribe in the reign of King David.
David appointed Sheva secretary of the kingdom and the one responsible for overseeing the accounts of the state.

Zadok and Abiathar were great priests, and Zadok was of the descendants of Eleazar son of Aaron and Abiathar of the descendants of Ithamar son of Aaron, and he was the son of Ahimelech whom Saul killed in the massacre of the priests (1 Sam 22:20).

entries.section: (5) David's appointment of religious, military and administrative heads

paragraphs.text: A priest to David: that is, a special counselor, and not a priest performing the works of the priesthood in the house of the Lord.

David appointed Ira the Jairite as a special counselor to him, who would present to him the wishes of his people, and through whom the king would convey his directions to the officials in his government.

It is good that our life be organized and that there be someone in charge of each responsibility, subject to him, so that matters may proceed in peace. May you, if you are in charge, distribute the responsibilities to others and show compassion to them, and on the other hand submit to everyone in charge, so that your life may proceed in stability.
The right of the Gibeonites and the wars with the Philistines

entries.section: (1) The hanging of Saul's descendants by the Gibeonites

paragraphs.text: Enquired of the LORD: God's help and guidance.

The Gibeonites: the inhabitants of the city of Gibeon, which is 8 km north of Jerusalem, and they belong to the Amorites, and made a covenant with Joshua (Josh 9). A famine occurred in the land of Israel that lasted three years, so David prayed to the Lord, and He informed him that the famine was a divine punishment because of the treachery of Saul and the people toward the Gibeonites and his killing of some of them despite the covenant between them and Joshua. Although Joshua had erred in making the covenant with them, the covenant made in the name of the Lord must be respected or He will be angry, and perhaps the people rejoiced at taking over the land of the Gibeonites, as being part of the lands inhabited by pagans that ought to be taken by the people of God, forgetting God's covenant that Joshua made with them.

entries.section: (1) The hanging of Saul's descendants by the Gibeonites

paragraphs.text: David set about appeasing the Gibeonites, so he called their leaders and asked them what he should do for them.

entries.section: (1) The hanging of Saul's descendants by the Gibeonites

paragraphs.text: The Gibeonites were a peaceful people, so they answered David that Saul had not taken from them money, gold or silver for which they should demand restitution from his heirs, and that they had no authority over the children of Israel that they might take vengeance on them by killing one or some of them; moreover the children of Israel at the present time had not wronged them. David told them to ask what they wished and he would carry out their request, in order to appease God, as we mentioned. This shows that the Gibeonites were influenced by their association with the children of Israel, so they became peaceful and not attached to money or exploitative of others.

entries.section: (1) The hanging of Saul's descendants by the Gibeonites

paragraphs.text: Gibeah of Saul: it is the same as Gibeah of Benjamin and was the capital of the kingdom in the days of Saul, and it is present-day Tell el-Ful, 6 km north of Jerusalem.

The Gibeonites said that what would satisfy them was the killing of seven of the descendants of Saul, who had killed many of them and tried to exterminate them, and then hanging the bodies of the seven in the capital of Saul's kingdom, which was Gibeah of Benjamin, and David agreed. Here the Gibeonites did not ask for silver or gold, because the principle known from ancient times is that blood is redeemed by blood and not by money (Gen 9:6, Num 35:31). They did not name particular persons from Saul's descendants because they knew David's covenant with Jonathan not to destroy his offspring, so they left him to choose any seven. David erred in not asking God whether He agreed to the killing and hanging of the seven or not.

entries.section: (1) The hanging of Saul's descendants by the Gibeonites

paragraphs.text: Mephibosheth, who was handed over to the Gibeonites with the other six, was a direct son of Saul, and is different from Mephibosheth son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul, whom David did not wish to hand over, in order to keep the old promise he had made to Jonathan his father not to kill any of his children.

entries.section: (1) The hanging of Saul's descendants by the Gibeonites

paragraphs.text: Rizpah the daughter of Aiah: Saul's concubine, on account of whom a quarrel arose between Ish-bosheth and Abner that led to Abner's joining David.
Armoni and Mephibosheth: two sons of Saul by his concubine Rizpah, whom the Gibeonites killed with five others of Saul's family.
Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite: Saul gave him in marriage his eldest daughter Merab, whom he had promised to David.
The sons of Saul whom King David handed over to the Gibeonites were:

Two sons of Saul by his concubine Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, namely Armoni and Mephibosheth, and five who were the sons of Michal, whom her sister Merab bore to Adriel the son of Barzillai (1 Sam 18:19), and she adopted them after her sister's death.

entries.section: (1) The hanging of Saul's descendants by the Gibeonites

paragraphs.text: The Gibeonites killed the seven sons of Saul and hanged them on one of the mountains, and that was at the beginning of the barley harvest season, that is, in the month of May. This shows God's justice on account of Saul's many evils against God, David and the Gibeonites, and because he did not give Merab his daughter to David as he had promised him but gave her to Adriel. And if some of these sons were pious, torment will not touch them in eternity.

entries.section: (1) The hanging of Saul's descendants by the Gibeonites

paragraphs.text: Rizpah the daughter of Aiah grieved over the hanging of her two sons, so she set about honoring their bodies by spreading for herself coarse cloth to sit on upon the same rock on which they were hanged, and to guard the bodies so that birds of prey would not devour them, and she continued her guard until the Lord pardoned the people and had mercy on them and the rain fell, and she took the bodies down. Rizpah remained grieving in austerity, sitting on sackcloth, probably for many days until the rain fell as a declaration that God had lifted His anger and the famine was over, although the Jewish Law provides for taking down hanged bodies before evening (Deut 21:22); but this was a special case, for those who hanged these were the Gibeonites, who were not Jews and therefore not bound by the Law.

The falling of rain in the days of harvest, that is, in the months of April and May, is unusual, but God allowed it as a declaration of the ending of the famine and His pleasure with His repentant people, and He did not wait until October or November, in which the rains fall, for it would be hard for the bodies to remain hanging throughout those months.

entries.section: (1) The hanging of Saul's descendants by the Gibeonites

paragraphs.text: Jabesh-gilead: a city on Mount Gilead east of the Jordan, 16 km southeast of Beth-shan, now Tell Abu Kharaz north of Wadi Yabis.
Beth-shan: a city 8 km west of the Jordan River, whose site is now Tell el-Husn.
Gilboa: the northeastern part of Mount Ephraim.

David learned what Rizpah had endured of toil for the sake of honoring the bodies and preserving them, so he also shared in this honoring by taking the bodies of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead to bury them, for the men of Jabesh-gilead had crossed the Jordan and stolen their bodies after they were killed in the war with the Philistines (1 Sam 31:11, 12).

entries.section: (1) The hanging of Saul's descendants by the Gibeonites

paragraphs.text: The bones of those hanged: what is meant is their bodies, for it is not possible for all bodies to decay so quickly.

Zelah: a city in the land of the tribe of Benjamin (now Khirbet Salah northwest of Jerusalem). David also took the bodies of the seven who had been hanged and buried them all with honor in the tomb of Kish, Saul's father, in the city of "Zelah" neighboring "Gibeah," and by this David proved that the killing of the seven sons of Saul was not out of grudge on his part against them, but he had been compelled to do this act of atonement so that the Lord might be pleased with His people. The Lord had declared the end of His anger by the falling of rain to water the land, and so the famine ended.

entries.section: (2) The wars against the Philistines

paragraphs.text: A new war arose between Israel and the Philistines, and David went down to the battle to share the fighting with his soldiers, as kings used to do in ancient times, but he felt great exhaustion, for he was over sixty years of age and had endured many troubles in his life.

entries.section: (2) The wars against the Philistines

paragraphs.text: Ishbi-benob: one of the sons of Rapha, a Philistine giant who was about to kill David, but Abishai hastened and killed him before he came near David.
Three hundred shekels of brass: that is, about 5 kg.
Being girded with a new one: that is, girded with a new sword.

"Ishbi-benob," a son of Goliath the giant whom David killed in his youth, was among the Philistine warriors, and the weight of his spear was about 5 kg and his weapon was new. This soldier recognized David's person in the field and noticed that he was tired, so he thought it would be easy to attack him and kill him. But Abishai the brother of Joab noticed what was going on around the king and hastened to his aid and was able to kill that soldier. After this event David's men who were loyal to him swore that they would not let him go out to the wars with them any more, because he was considered an important symbol for his people and his life was a precious treasure for his men, and his being killed in any battle would mean the defeat of the whole people.

entries.section: (2) The wars against the Philistines

paragraphs.text: Gob: it is the same as Gezer, a city near Lachish bordering the land of Ephraim, and now called Tell el-Jazar, 30 km northwest of Jerusalem.

Sibbechai the Hushathite: one of the heroes of King David, and he is the one who killed "Saph," one of the sons of Rapha. Saph: one of the sons of Rapha, one of the Philistine giants, and he is also called "Sippai" (1 Chr 20:4). The war with the Philistines was a series of successive battles, no sooner had one ended than another began. The next battlefield was "Gob," and in this battle Sibbechai, one of David's heroes, killed "Saph," one of the Philistine giants and a son of "Rapha," one of the Philistine commanders.

entries.section: (2) The wars against the Philistines

paragraphs.text: Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite: he is the one who slew the brother of Goliath the Gittite.

The previous battle at "Gob" had hardly ended when another battle broke out in the same place, in which the name of another of David's heroes shone, "Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim," for he killed a giant from the city of Gath named Goliath, the staff of whose spear was as long as the beam used in weaving. This Goliath is another person than the one David killed in his youth; perhaps he was his brother and was named after him in memory of him, and his real name is Lahmi, as mentioned in (1 Chr 20:5).

entries.section: (2) The wars against the Philistines

paragraphs.text: Another battle took place at Gath, one of the five great Philistine cities, in which appeared a Philistine of strange stature, the fingers and toes of whose hands and feet were twenty-four in number and not twenty as with any ordinary person, and he also was a son of "Rapha," and he appeared defying the Jews as the old Goliath had done, taunting the children of Israel, which kindled the zeal of Jonathan the son of Shimeah, David's brother, who is "Shammah" as mentioned in (1 Sam 16:9), and he killed him.

entries.section: (2) The wars against the Philistines

paragraphs.text: In the battles mentioned, four of the strongest Philistine soldiers were killed by the hand of David's heroes, and these four are:
1- Ishbi-benob, whom Abishai killed
2- Saph, whom Sibbechai killed
3- Goliath, whom Elhanan killed
4- The man with twenty-four fingers and toes, whom Jonathan killed; and these four are the sons of "Rapha" who was of "Gath."
And when it says "fell by the hand of David," it means by this his men, for David is the commander of the armies and his men are the ones who killed the heroes of the Philistines.

The Lord always stands by His children as long as they hold fast to Him, and guards them and gives them victory in wars, whether they are wars between men or spiritual wars stirred up against them by the enemy of good. Let us know that victory in all circumstances is from the Lord, so let us trust in Him and not be troubled because of the threats around us, and lift our hearts in prayer, confident of His protection of us.
David's song

entries.section: (1) The Lord delivers David

paragraphs.text: David had many enemies, among them Saul, then Absalom the son of David himself, Shimei son of Gera and Sheba son of Bichri; this concerns his enemies from among his own people, while his foreign enemies were no less fierce than these, for he had battles with many of the surrounding peoples such as the Philistines, the children of Ammon, the Edomites and the Jebusites; and the Lord delivered him from them all and gave him victory over them, so he composed this song to sing to the Lord and praise Him.
This song corresponds to a large extent to the eighteenth Psalm, with slight changes in some words to suit the musical instruments used in public worship.

entries.section: (1) The Lord delivers David

paragraphs.text: David likens the Lord to a rock, for as a rock protects whoever hides behind it, the Lord protects him when he trusts in Him. He likens Him also to a fortress, for as fortresses are built to be military defenses against the enemy, so the Lord did with David, surrounding him with His care and power so that the enemies could not overcome him, and so He delivered him from everyone who tried to harm him or get at him.

entries.section: (1) The Lord delivers David

paragraphs.text: Shield: a wooden disc covered with leather having a loop on the inside through which the soldier puts his hand to move this disc in front of his face and body to protect him from the enemies' arrows.
Refuge: the place in which he hides to be protected.

He repeats his taking refuge in the Lord for protection, as the rock protects those who shelter in it, and as the shield protects the soldier from the enemy's blows; so God protected him from all the blows aimed at him. And as an animal butts its opponent with its horn, the divine power intervened on David's side and strengthened him and delivered him from the schemes and evils of the enemies, for he used to take refuge in the Lord in every distress that befell him, as is said in (Ps 90).

entries.section: (1) The Lord delivers David

paragraphs.text: Worthy: an intensive form meaning deserving of much praise.

Whenever hardship or distress surrounded David, he would take refuge in the Lord in prayer, and He would hear his prayer and deliver him from his hardship, so He deserves all praise and thanks. In this same sense David sang in (Ps 50:15): "Call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me."

May we, instead of being troubled and anxious if evil overtakes us, take refuge in prayer, lifting up our hands, asking the Lord to rescue us and deliver us from the temptation, holding fast to His promises; the Lord is near and will not delay, and if He does not lift the temptation from us, His presence with us in the depths of the temptation is enough for us, as He did with the three youths in the fiery furnace.

entries.section: (1) The Lord delivers David

paragraphs.text: Snares: traps.

David portrays the dangers to which he was exposed as huge waves that surrounded him on every side and almost destroyed him, and he also likens them to sweeping floods whose rushing terrifies and frightens him. He describes his state as though hell had stretched out its cords to seize him and take him into itself, so that it was as though death had set its snares around him and he had no escape from death.

God allowed the afflictions to surround David so that God's power might be manifest in delivering him and he might glorify Him, for God does not take us out of the evil world but keeps us from its evils and delivers us from its dangers.

entries.section: (1) The Lord delivers David

paragraphs.text: Afflictions seized him on every side and set snares around him to surround him and put him to death, so he cried out then, calling on the Lord for help, and the Lord answered from His holy house (the tabernacle of meeting) his prayers and supplication, because the house of the Lord is the place of His dwelling.

If you face afflictions, hasten to the Church your mother, and you will find in her bosom rest and strength when you are fed by the Body and Blood of the Lord, and you will feel reassured however much problems surround you.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: The Lord responded quickly to the cry of His servant David and rose up to deliver him from his afflictions. The Lord's anger was great against the wicked who opposed David, so the earth shook and trembled at the declaration of the Lord's anger, and the heavens also quaked, as though they stood upon foundations and pillars that were moved from their places in fear and distress at the Lord's declaring His anger.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: David expressed the Lord's anger against the wicked in a figurative picture, as though smoke went up from His nostrils as a sign of the intensity of the Lord's wrath against them, and fire came out of His mouth to devour them, and burning coals from His being destroying those who troubled him.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: David completed his figurative picture, imagining as though the heavens bowed and lowered themselves so that the Lord might come down upon them and come to his help, and the cloud carried Him swiftly to deliver him from his enemies.

So our Lord Jesus Christ did: He emptied Himself and took the form of a servant and came down from His height to save the human race, and He is ready every day to hasten to you to deliver you from your afflictions. So trust that He is nearest to you in the time of affliction, and you will feel it when you seek Him and press Him.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: Cherub: an angelic order that bears the throne of God.
David describes the Lord's coming, riding upon a cherub, swiftly as the speed of the wind, as though this wind were a bird with wings.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: Dark waters: many waters gathered together.

David expressed God's hidden mysteries by the darkness surrounding Him (that is, no one comprehends the reality of God's matters and His wisdom), as though they were canopies or pavilions that hide those matters from creation, for God's mysteries are hidden from men and their minds do not grasp them, as though thick clouds full of water surrounded them and hid what is behind them.

If by reason we perceive the existence of God, reason does not help us to know the essence of God, so let us complete by faith what reason does not supply, and not think of ourselves more highly than we ought to think.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: David continues his eloquent figurative pictures, portraying the coming of the Lord preceded by a ray of light, kindling in its power a fire expressing the Lord's burning anger against the wicked.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: David portrays here natural phenomena proceeding by God's command and power to express His majesty and authority over His creation. The thunder coming from heaven is as the voice of the Lord declaring His wrath against the transgressors.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: He likens the Lord to a warrior who looses arrows from His bow and scatters the enemies, and He commands the clouds of heaven to flash lightning, which alarms them and disperses them.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: As the Lord hastened yesterday to deliver His people from the pursuit of the armies of the Egyptians, here He hastens with the same eagerness now to rescue David from his enemies. And David recalls in his song what happened when the Lord rebuked nature when His anger grew fierce against the wicked, so that the waters of the sea receded at the hand of Moses, and the bed of the sea was uncovered, which he calls the foundations of the world because it is a very low place.

When temptation grows fierce upon us, it is fitting for us to remember God's many past merciful works with us, so that our souls may be reassured and calm, confessing that He who brought us out of previous temptations safely is Himself able to draw us out of the present temptation.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: In the midst of these many disturbances that troubled nature as they troubled the Lord's enemies, the Lord did not leave His servant David to drown in the midst of those disturbances, but stretched out His hand and drew him out, and he was saved from drowning.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: David's enemies were many, and in terms of the balance of material forces they were stronger than he, so if the Lord had left him to himself they would have overcome him and destroyed him, but the Lord intervened by His power and delivered him out of their hands and frustrated all their plots against him.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: David was indeed exposed to their harm and suffered much from their troublemaking and their challenges to him, and endured from them many injuries and calamities, but the Lord did not let them triumph over him but supported him and strengthened him and gave him victory over them.

entries.section: (2) The Lord does not delay in helping David

paragraphs.text: David says that while he was suffering from a stifling siege by the enemies around him, the Lord delivered him from their hands by drawing him out from the midst of this siege and brought him forth into a large place, because He loved him.

entries.section: (3) The Lord rewards each one according to his deserving

paragraphs.text: David prays that the Lord may reward him for his forbearance toward those who wronged him, for he treated everyone well and did only good even to those who were his enemies, and he acted according to the Lord's commandments and His Law and did not disobey Him in any of His judgments; the Lord's judgments were always before his eyes and the object of his concern, and he did not turn aside from the Lord's statutes which He bound His people to keep.

entries.section: (3) The Lord rewards each one according to his deserving

paragraphs.text: David affirms his care to obey the Lord in all that He commanded, in pursuit of perfection and out of care not to commit sin and to avoid falling into iniquity.

Absolute perfection belongs to the Lord alone, but we must strive toward relative perfection as far as we can and as far as our human nature allows us, taking care to discipline this nature of ours so that we are not led by the desires of the flesh, but surrender our leadership to the Spirit, who leads us in the way of righteousness and goodness.

entries.section: (3) The Lord rewards each one according to his deserving

paragraphs.text: The Lord's working with David and supporting him in fighting his enemies was a reward for the works of righteousness he had done, his distance from works of evil, and the purity of his heart from hatred and grudge toward others, and he was justified before the Lord because of the purity of his heart according to the Lord's heart: "I have found David ... a man after mine own heart" (Acts 13:22).

entries.section: (3) The Lord rewards each one according to his deserving

paragraphs.text: The Lord deals with men according to their deserving, so He is merciful to those who treat others with mercy, and the man who walks in perfection before the Lord He rewards generously and recompenses for his deed.

entries.section: (3) The Lord rewards each one according to his deserving

paragraphs.text: The man who lives in purity and cleanness the Lord rewards with every good, and the man who deviates from uprightness and whose way becomes crooked is overtaken by troubles and calamities as the recompense of his deviation from the Lord's ways.

entries.section: (3) The Lord rewards each one according to his deserving

paragraphs.text: God exalts the humble and brings down the proud. God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble (1 Pet 5:5).

Let us put away from ourselves every thought that aims at self-aggrandizement, and walk in humility first before God and then toward our brothers among men, remembering always that the fall of humanity in the person of Adam was because of his striving toward being made god, "Ye shall be as gods," as Satan suggested to him, and likewise the fall of Satan, after he had been the "shining morning star," was because of his desire to put his throne above the throne of God.

entries.section: (4) The Lord guides and supports those who love Him

paragraphs.text: It is the Lord who lights the way for those He loves and dispels the darkness around them, so that they walk in His ways and enjoy His pleasure, and fears and cares vanish from before them.

entries.section: (4) The Lord guides and supports those who love Him

paragraphs.text: David attributes his victories in wars to the power of the Lord that helps him, for his overcoming the armies of the giants and storming their strong fortifications could not have come about without the Lord's being with him.

It is the Lord who gives victory to His children and strengthens their weakness, and every time we pray the prayer of thanksgiving we ask "that He remove from us and from all His people the rising up of the enemies, hidden and visible"; the visible are the material, seen enemies, while the hidden are the enemies of good, that is, the spiritual enemies, who are the demons.

entries.section: (4) The Lord guides and supports those who love Him

paragraphs.text: The Lord is just, and all His ways are straight, His works are good, His word is living and His commandment is true. In Him all who love His holy name take refuge, for He defends them as the shield that the warrior carries protects him from the enemy's blows.

entries.section: (4) The Lord guides and supports those who love Him

paragraphs.text: The question here carries the meaning of denial, for David says that there is no other god but the Lord, in whom we take refuge and find fortification, and find support and rest.

entries.section: (4) The Lord guides and supports those who love Him

paragraphs.text: God is the one who supplies David with the strength by which he triumphs over his enemies. And He is the one who leads him in the way of righteousness and guides him, so that he lives in safety and his steps do not stumble.

entries.section: (5) The Lord is my helper in wars

paragraphs.text: In addition to strength, the Lord gives me the swiftness of gazelles, so that I hide from my enemies where they cannot overtake me, and He gives me lightness of movement so that I fortify myself on the heights, where I am able to deal with the enemy while he cannot get at me.

entries.section: (5) The Lord is my helper in wars

paragraphs.text: The hand of the Lord is over my hands in battle, for it is He who gives them strength and skill in wars, so that my arms become able to nullify the enemy's forces and destroy his defenses in which he takes shelter, and his shields are put out of action and spoiled and lose their effectiveness.

entries.section: (5) The Lord is my helper in wars

paragraphs.text: And You, O Lord, arm me with Your strength and Your protection of me; Your tender dealing with me raises my morale and abilities, and steadies my steps on the road so that I run without stumbling; when I flee from the enemy he does not overtake me, and when I pursue them I overtake them and prevail over them.
It is the Lord who helps His children and supports them in their spiritual journey without stumbling or falling into transgression, and if they fall, He raises them up.

entries.section: (5) The Lord is my helper in wars

paragraphs.text: The Lord increases my resolve to pursue my enemies, so I overtake them and attack them and destroy them and humble them, and they fall under my feet and have no standing thereafter.

entries.section: (5) The Lord is my helper in wars

paragraphs.text: You clothe me with strength from You, so my frame is strong and my head is firm, and I overcome those who resist me and they submit to me.

entries.section: (5) The Lord is my helper in wars

paragraphs.text: Thou hast also given me the necks of mine enemies: my enemies run before me, so I see their necks and pursue them, and they fear me. The enemies are defeated before me and flee from my face, so I follow them and overtake them and destroy them.

entries.section: (5) The Lord is my helper in wars

paragraphs.text: They looked to the right and to the left for someone to save them but found no one, and if they cry out to the Lord, He does not answer them, because they rejected Him and He rejected them.

entries.section: (5) The Lord is my helper in wars

paragraphs.text: The Lord gives me strength to crush them as the dust of the earth is crushed under the feet, and I trample them as mud is trampled in the streets.

entries.section: (6) God is David's keeper from his own people and from strangers

paragraphs.text: David thanks the Lord for delivering him from those of his people who rose up against him in rebellion, as He delivered him from those of the surrounding nations who declared war on him, for God kept him from the treachery of them all and gave him victory over them, so that he took possession of their lands and ruled over them. He means by this the pagan peoples with whom he had no association, who became subject to his rule.

entries.section: (6) God is David's keeper from his own people and from strangers

paragraphs.text: The peoples foreign to him became subject and show him loyalty and obedience, and when the news of his victories, achieved with the Lord's support, reaches them, they surrender to him, declaring their obedience and their courting of his person.

entries.section: (6) God is David's keeper from his own people and from strangers

paragraphs.text: The hostile peoples are overtaken by decay, like a garment that wears out, that is, their resolve is eroded and their strength vanishes so that they become as nothing, and if they expect an early military confrontation with me, they come out of their strongholds and come to me obedient and submissive.

entries.section: (6) God is David's keeper from his own people and from strangers

paragraphs.text: David repeats his likening of the Lord's support of him and protection of him to the rock that protects those who take refuge in it from the aggression of others. And the Lord is a living God, not like the lifeless gods of the nations, and He is exalted above every name and every thought and above all that is in heaven and on earth.

entries.section: (6) God is David's keeper from his own people and from strangers

paragraphs.text: God avenges David on all who oppose him, whether individuals or peoples, for He gave him victory over them all and brought them under his authority.

entries.section: (6) God is David's keeper from his own people and from strangers

paragraphs.text: The Lord delivered me from their grasp and made me head of my people and king over all and also over those who resisted, as He delivered me from Saul, who wronged me much and pursued me and sought to kill me without cause.
God is able to give you awe in the eyes of those around you, so that they honor you and fear to hurt you, and you walk in tranquility, and even, by your love and wisdom, are able to draw them to God.

entries.section: (7) David praises and glorifies the Lord

paragraphs.text: David praises the Lord for all His gifts and graces and glorifies Him for the majesty of His power, so that the nations hear of God's works with those who love Him, and His name is glorified and exalted.

If it is part of faith to take refuge in God when we are exposed to a temptation or a problem, it is also part of faith to thank Him in times of joy and peace and to praise Him for the judgments of His justice. Our seeking the Lord should not be only in times of distress, but when all things around us grow calm, God should also be in our thought and in our hearts.

entries.section: (7) David praises and glorifies the Lord

paragraphs.text: God is a strong tower to which David flees and in which he fortifies himself and so escapes the schemes of his enemies. The Lord has shown mercy to him, for He established him on his throne and delivered him from the wicked surrounding him. God's mercy extended to David's descendants also, for the Lord promised David, saying: "If thy children will keep my covenant and my testimony that I shall teach them, their children shall also sit upon thy throne for evermore" (Ps 132:12). David's last words - the names of David's heroes

entries.section: (1) David rules in the fear of God

paragraphs.text: David spoke the following words at the end of his life, stating that his words were a revelation to him from the Lord. He had been a simple shepherd of sheep, and God raised him up and entrusted him with the highest office by anointing him king to lead His people. He himself was the arranger of the sweet psalms with which he sang to the Lord.

Singing is the work of the angels, for they praise God day and night. Therefore one of the most beautiful things a person can do is to sing and praise the Lord, so that he is filled with peace and joy, his troubles vanish, and he enjoys the vision of God and fellowship with Him.

entries.section: (1) David rules in the fear of God

paragraphs.text: David did not speak from himself; rather his words were a revelation from the Holy Spirit, and the Lord spoke through his tongue.

entries.section: (1) David rules in the fear of God

paragraphs.text: David affirmed that the One who spoke is the God of Israel and their Rock on whom they rely, and he says that when the righteous king rules his people, he rules them with justice and in the fear of God.

entries.section: (1) David rules in the fear of God

paragraphs.text: After the rain: after the rainfall.

Such a king is a guide to his people and lights the way for them, as the light of the sun shines when it rises in the morning. He leads them to fulfill their good aspirations, and his rule over them is a flourishing and splendid rule, as the grass of the field flourishes after it is watered by the rain.

entries.section: (1) David rules in the fear of God

paragraphs.text: The beautiful qualities of rule that David described in the preceding verses will be the qualities that adorn the manner of his rule and the rule of his descendants after him. They rest on righteousness, because his covenant with God is an everlasting covenant that does not end with the end of his life, but his descendants are bound by it from generation to generation. It is a firm and preserved covenant, and it confirms the continuance of his delight and joy and the fulfillment of his salvation.

We must remember that God's covenants are conditioned on a person's conduct in the fear of the Lord. It is good that we hold fast to His covenants and recall them persistently in our prayers, but we must know that the fulfillment of these covenants depends on how firmly we ourselves hold to God's commandments. Only the righteous enjoy God's covenants, which fill their lives with salvation and joy.

entries.section: (1) David rules in the fear of God

paragraphs.text: Belial: a pagan god, and "sons of Belial" is a name given to the wicked who do not fear the Lord. As for the wicked from whom nothing good is to be expected, David likened them to thorns thrown on the ground, worthless. A person does not try to take hold of them with his hand, because the sharp points of the thorns will wound him; they harm everyone who deals with them. Therefore whoever wants to touch them must deal with them with severity and force, using strong tools such as iron and the staff of a spear, so that he is safe from injury and guards against the pricking of the thorns, and deals with them from a distance without hurting his hands. If he strikes them with the staff of a spear and with iron, these wicked ones perish in their place.

entries.section: (2) The heroes of the first rank

paragraphs.text: David was concerned to put capabilities to work and to establish and organize leaders. Therefore this chapter lists the names of his mighty men who supported him in his wars. The list begins with the names of three heroes of the first rank, that is, those who surpassed the others in courage, valor and military rank. They are: Josheb-basshebeth the Tachmonite, or the Hachmonite, who is the same as Jashobeam as mentioned in (1 Chr 11:11). He used his spear in the wars against David's enemies and killed 800 soldiers of the enemy.

(In Chronicles (1 Chr 11:11) it is said that the number of those he killed was 300. The explanation of this difference is that Josheb himself killed 300 warriors with his own hands, while the men of his company killed the remaining five hundred, so the whole work was attributed to him figuratively. Josheb was regarded as the chief of the first three heroes.

entries.section: (2) The heroes of the first rank

paragraphs.text: Was weary: grew tired.

The second hero is Eleazar the son of Dodo the son of an Ahohite, who joined David in fighting the Philistines at a place called "Dammim," west of Judah. When the Philistines went out to battle and the men of Israel withdrew, this hero remained alone defying the Philistines, and he kept fighting them until his hands were weary from striking them, and he killed a great number of them. Since his hand clung to the sword for a long time, it almost stuck to it, and he found it difficult to open his grip from the sword. When the men of Israel saw him achieving this great victory, they gathered again and went after him to plunder the belongings of the slain and the spoils of war.

entries.section: (2) The heroes of the first rank

paragraphs.text: The third hero is Shammah the son of Agee the Hararite. His heroism came when the Philistines attacked the children of Israel in a field planted with lentils. The children of Israel were afraid and left the field when Shammah confronted the Philistines alone, for he stood in the midst of the field and delivered it from the hand of the Philistines and struck them with a great blow, and the Lord wrought a great salvation by his hand.

entries.section: (2) The heroes of the first rank

paragraphs.text: The cave of Adullam: it lies west of Bethlehem.

After speaking of the individual feats of heroism achieved by each of the first three heroes, the inspired text mentions here a collective heroic deed done by the three together. This heroic deed took place during the first war with the Philistines, after David had taken Jerusalem (ch. 5:17-21). The war was in the hot days of summer, at harvest time, and David was then in the cave of Adullam to make his war plans, while the Philistines were gathered in "the valley of Rephaim."

entries.section: (2) The heroes of the first rank

paragraphs.text: The garrison of the Philistines: detachments from the army of the Philistines.
David was staying in the stronghold, which is the cave, while some detachments of the Philistine army had taken Bethlehem and prepared to fight David.

entries.section: (2) The heroes of the first rank

paragraphs.text: In this extremely hot weather David became very thirsty, and he expressed his thirst by longing for the well of Bethlehem, which is at the gate of the city where he was born and raised.

entries.section: (2) The heroes of the first rank

paragraphs.text: It grieved the first three heroes to see their king sighing from the intensity of his thirst, so they risked their lives and broke through the camp of the Philistines with all boldness and courage until they reached the well, and they drew water and returned with it to David to quench his thirst. But David saw that this water was very costly, for its price was the blood of his heroes, because they had exposed themselves to death in order to bring it. So he refused to drink it and poured it out on the ground before God, and he said that he refused to quench his thirst with a drink of water that had been brought by his heroic men putting their lives in danger.

May you be austere and detached, not seeking your own comfort at the expense of others, and inclined to self-giving rather than selfishness, just as David refused to give himself comfort at the expense of his enemies, and his heart pricked him because he had asked for water from a well held by the enemies. And be, on the contrary, ready to toil for the sake of others in order to give them rest.

entries.section: (3) The heroes of the second rank

paragraphs.text: The following verses recount the feats of heroism done by the three heroes of the second rank, beginning with the first of them and their chief, Abishai the brother of Joab, who killed three hundred of the enemy's soldiers by himself and so deserved to have a position of leadership among the three heroes.

entries.section: (3) The heroes of the second rank

paragraphs.text: Abishai was the most capable of the heroes of the second rank, so he was regarded as their chief, but in his feats of heroism he did not reach the standing of the first three, "Josheb, Eleazar and Shammah."

entries.section: (3) The heroes of the second rank

paragraphs.text: Kabzeel: in the south of Judah, and it is now Khirbet Hura.

The second hero in this group is "Benaiah the son of Jehoiada," who was chief over the Cherethites and the Pelethites under David (ch. 20:23). He was the son of the high priest in the days of David and became the commander of Solomon's army (1 Kgs 4:4). The inspired text says of him that he was a strong man who had done many great deeds, and that he was originally from the town of Kabzeel. The inspired text relates some of his heroic deeds: in one of them he killed two lions that were coming out of the land of Moab and devouring people, and he confronted them and killed them. The second heroic deed was his entering the den of a lion, on a day when the lion was sheltering in it from the rain and the cold, and he killed the lion. The third heroic deed was his killing a mighty Egyptian man who used to attack people and trouble and harm them. He killed him in a manner similar to the story of David and Goliath the Philistine, for he went down to him with no weapon but a staff, and struck him and took his spear from him and killed him with it.

entries.section: (3) The heroes of the second rank

paragraphs.text: His confidants: those close to the king, who know his secrets and keep them, such as military secrets.

These heroic deeds of Benaiah made his name among the three of the second rank, so that he held a higher position than the three who are of the third rank, but in standing he did not reach the first three. The inspired text did not mention the name of the third hero in this group, and perhaps he is Amasa, to whom David promised that he would become the commander of his army.

If you rely on God, He will give you mighty strength, and you will overcome your enemies the demons, however great their power, and you will even lead others in the way of the spiritual life, so that you stand firm in God and serve Him and enjoy His work in you.

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: From here the inspired text mentions thirty other heroes who form the third class of heroes. They are:
Asahel: the brother of Joab and Abishai, whom Abner killed in self-defense (ch. 2:23). Elhanan the son of Dodo: his homeland was Bethlehem.

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Shammah the Harodite: from the town of "Harod," whose site is now "Khirbet Hazidan," lying about 5 km southeast of Jerusalem. He is also called "Shammoth the Harorite" in (1 Chr 11:27), and he is the same as "Shamhuth the Izrahite" in (1 Chr 27:8). Elika the Harodite: he is also from Harod.

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Helez the Paltite: he is the same as "the Pelonite" (1 Chr 11:27), and he is from the tribe of Ephraim.
Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite: from the town of Tekoa, from which came the wise woman of Tekoa (ch. 14), and Tekoa lies about 5 km southeast of Bethlehem.

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Abiezer the Anethothite: from "Anathoth," the town of the prophet Jeremiah, which is today a small village named "Anata," 4 km from Jerusalem.
Mebunnai the Hushathite: he is the same as "Sibbechai" in (1 Chr 11:29, 2 Sam 21:18), and his homeland was "Hushah," which is now the village of "Husan," southwest of Bethlehem.

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Zalmon the Ahohite: he is the same as "Ilai" in (1 Chr 11:29), and he was called the Ahohite after one of his ancestors.
Maharai the Netophathite: from the tribe of Judah, of the descendants of Zerah (1 Chr 27:13), and he is from Netophah, whose site is now Khirbet "Yad Faluh," which is 8 km south of Bethlehem.

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Heleb the son of Baanah the Netophathite: he has another name, "Heled" (1 Chr 11:30), and he is also from Netophah.
Ittai the son of Ribai: from Gibeah, the birthplace of Saul.

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Benaiah the Pirathonite: from Pirathon, one of the cities of Ephraim. It is now "Fara'ata," about 12 km southwest of Nablus.
Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash: these are among the valleys near the heights of Mount Gaash in the land of Ephraim, and it lies northeast of Lod by about 20 km.

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Abialbon the Arbathite: named for "Beth-arabah," which is now "Ain al-Arabah" in the valley of al-Qilt.
Azmaveth the Barhumite: or "the Baharumite" (1 Chr 11:33), named for "Bahurim," which is now "Ras al-Tamim," near the Mount of Olives.

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Eliahba the Shaalbonite: from "Shaalbin" or "Shaalabbin," which is now Salbit, lying about 3 km north of Ajlun.
Jonathan of the sons of Jashen: "Jashen" is also called "Hashem" (1 Chr 11:34).

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Shammah the Hararite: he is the same as Shammah, one of the first chiefs (v. 11), and he is mentioned here because he was one of those serving under the command of Asahel, but he excelled in war and so was counted among the first three. Ahiam the son of Sharar the Ararite: Arar is the same as "Harar" (v. 11).

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite: he is also called "Abiphelet" and "Eliphal" (1 Chr 11:35). He is attributed to one of his ancestors, "the Maachathite," that is, his origin is from "Maacah," a small kingdom in the northeast of Palestine (2 Sam 10:6). Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite: the son of Ahithophel, David's counselor, who followed Absalom, and he is from "Giloh," which was described earlier.

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Hezrai the Carmelite: his name is also "Hezro" (1 Chr 11:37), and he is a native of "Carmel," whose site is now a ruin of the same name, 11 km northeast of "Hebron." Paarai the Arbite: he is also called "Naarai" (1 Chr 11:37), and he is from a town named "Arab" in Judea, in its hill country.

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah: he is from the kingdom of Aram-zobah, which lies west of the Euphrates. Bani the Gadite: from the tribe of Gad.

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Zelek the Ammonite: of the children of Ammon.
Naharai the Beerothite: the armorbearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah, and he is from Beeroth, one of the cities of the Gibeonites in the portion of Benjamin, and its name now is "al-Bireh."

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Ira the Ithrite: named for the founder of the family, "Jether." Gareb the Ithrite: also of the descendants of "Jether."

entries.section: (4) The third class of heroes

paragraphs.text: Uriah the Hittite: whom David exposed to death unjustly in order to be rid of the traces of his sin, and he married his wife after he was killed.
The total is 37, among them the three heroes of the first rank, the three heroes of the second rank, and 31 heroes of the third rank, and the commander of them all was Joab.

It should be noted that the thirty-one are in truth only thirty, as stated in (v. 24), because Shammah is repeated, as we mentioned in (v. 33). We find that Joab is not mentioned here because it was known that he was the commander of all David's armies, and perhaps the reason he is not mentioned is his wrong in killing two innocent men, Abner and Amasa, in addition to his rebuking David. We also see that other names of David's heroes are mentioned in (1 Chr 11) that are not mentioned here, and this shows that there were many heroes by whom David's army was distinguished, as a divine grace supporting him. The mention of the lists of heroes proclaims the following:
1- Honor and glorification for the striving of these heroes, and God's appreciation of them, so that their names are remembered throughout the generations.
2- Glorification and exaltation of David, who took care to train them, coordinate their work, and give them the opportunity for their heroic deeds to appear.
3- A proclamation of the faith of these heroes, which made God work by His power in them so that their heroic deeds appeared.

The Lord remembers for His beloved, the living and the departed, their striving and their works. The inspired text mentions their names in appreciation of what they offered, so as to make of them a good example for the faithful. So if we seek a portion like the portion of the saints, we must walk as they walked.
The census of the people

entries.section: (1) David's order to number the people

paragraphs.text: The text states here that it was the Lord who moved David to number the people, whereas in the First Book of Chronicles (1 Chr 21:1) this is attributed to Satan. The explanation of this is that the Lord does not drive people to evil. When people incline of themselves toward the enticement of the enemy of good, He leaves them to do what they wish, and this takes place with God's permission.

The purpose of David's desire for the numbering was to boast of their multitude, and the people supported him in that. This purpose was not in harmony with the will of God, who had prescribed the taking of a census for specific religious and ritual purposes that God had already appointed for them (Ex 30:11): paying a ransom for the males, or counting those fit for military service, or preparing the Levites who would take part in the service of the house of the Lord...

So the kindling of God's anger was because of the sin of David and the people, which was fundamentally pride. He permitted David to order the numbering, but He was angry about it, and so He punished him, as we shall see in this chapter. God's anger had been kindled many times before against the people because of their sins, from the days of Moses and before, until now. He permitted them to be humbled in Egypt and the murmurers to fall dead in the wilderness of Sinai, and He was also angry with the people because of Saul's sin in the matter of the Gibeonites (ch. 21). Therefore it says, "And again the anger of the Lord was kindled."... David's sin in the numbering was great, for the following reasons:

1- Pride, as we mentioned, especially since he had been victorious in many wars and his kingdom had grown wide, so he wanted to know his strength and boast in it. The people shared with him in the pride, and they forgot that God alone was the cause of their victories.
2- He did not consult God before the numbering.
3- Perhaps after the numbering he wanted to use his strength in new wars or in some works of his own that God had not commanded.

4- It is mentioned that he ordered the numbering of Israel and Judah, separating the tribe of Judah from the rest of the tribes, because David was of this tribe, and the number of this tribe had increased, so he wanted to boast of it.
5- Perhaps he had other personal purposes, such as using the people to carry out some of his interests or to collect taxes from them.
6- He did not collect from them the value of the ransom, which is half a shekel, offered to the Temple as the Law prescribed (Ex 30:12).
7- The Book of Chronicles (1 Chr 27:23, 24) tells us that he counted those who were under twenty years of age, and this is contrary to the Law.

8- He forgot that the people are the people of God and not his own people, for God alone is the One who blesses them and boasts of them because they are His workmanship, so it is not right to steal the glory of God.

entries.section: (1) David's order to number the people

paragraphs.text: The king commanded Joab, the commander of his army, to go through the regions of the land from the farthest north (Dan) to the farthest south (Beersheba) to number the people and bring him the result.

entries.section: (1) David's order to number the people

paragraphs.text: Joab wanted to dissuade David from his desire to number the people, praying that the Lord would multiply His people a hundredfold so that the king might look upon their multitude with joy, and he asked him what he desired by this request. This was a wise act on Joab's part, for although he was violent and bloody, he warned the king of the danger of numbering the people, since this carries pride, but he warned him with great courtesy, for Joab was careful for the good of the king and the kingdom.

entries.section: (1) David's order to number the people

paragraphs.text: David did not listen to the attempt of Joab and the captains of the army to dissuade him from his desire, but rebuked them and insisted strongly on carrying out his command. So they were compelled to yield to his wish, and they went out from him to go through the regions of the kingdom and number the people.

It is not wise to neglect the advice of others. Rather, let us accustom ourselves to benefit from the counsel of the wise around us and not insist on our own opinions in pride, even if the guidance comes from people younger than we are, or lower in position or knowledge.

entries.section: (1) David's order to number the people

paragraphs.text: These verses describe the route of the journey made by Joab and the captains of the army.

They began by crossing the Jordan River to the east bank and passed near "Aroer," one of the cities of the tribe of Gad. Their passing was to the right of the city, in the direction of the town of "Jazer," and they came to Gilead to number the tribes dwelling there, the two tribes of Reuben and Gad. Then they continued to "Tahtim-hodshi" in the land of "Tahtim," and from there they reached "Dan-jaan," then turned around to Zidon, then to the stronghold of Tyre and to all the cities that the children of Israel had taken from the Hivites and the Canaanites. On the way back toward the south they gathered the numbers of the tribes dwelling west of the Jordan until they reached the lands of Judah and then Beersheba in the far south. Their journey thus covered all the lands in which the children of Israel dwell, east and west of the Jordan. It took nine months and twenty days, and ended with their arrival at Jerusalem, the same city from which they had set out to begin their work. The route mentioned is a circuit from the south to the east of the Jordan, and from there to the farthest north of Palestine, then to the west, returning to the west of the Jordan River, and then from its farthest north to its farthest south.

entries.section: (1) David's order to number the people

paragraphs.text: On the return of Joab and his men, they presented the king with a report of the results of the census. It showed that the number of males of the tribes of Israel (apart from the tribe of Judah) from twenty years old and upward was 800 thousand. This number does not include the Levites or the tribe of Benjamin, which lay at the end of the return route, so it appears that the men who carried out the census had become exhausted, in addition to not having been convinced from the start of the usefulness of this numbering. The number of males of twenty years and upward of the tribe of Judah was 500 thousand, so the total of the tribes of Israel with the tribe of Judah added to them is 1,300,000 (one million three hundred thousand). If the number of soldiers represents about a fifth or a sixth of the people, this means that the number of the people at that time reached 6 or 7 million. This is a great number, owing to God's blessing and care for them.

The First Book of Chronicles (1 Chr 21:5) states that the number of Israel was 1,100,000, which is 300 thousand more than their number here, and it also states that the number of Judah was 470 thousand men, which is 30 thousand fewer than their number here. The explanation of this difference is as follows:

The extra three hundred thousand in Chronicles are those actually enlisted permanently to bear arms, whereas the eight hundred thousand are those fit to bear arms if necessity calls. There is another opinion about the three hundred thousand, namely the difference between the number of the enlisted of the tribes of Israel mentioned in Chronicles, that is 1,100,000, and their number here, which is 800,000. This opinion says that the Book of Samuel mentions that the eight hundred thousand are "men of valor," that is, tested men of greater ability in war, while the remaining three hundred thousand are of lesser ability.

Likewise the 30 thousand whom the Book of Chronicles did not include in the numbering are "the chosen men of Israel" (ch. 6:1), who were charged with keeping security and with the royal guard permanently.

It is noted that the tribe of Levi was not counted here because they do not take part in wars but are consecrated to the service of the Lord. As for the tribe of Benjamin, their number may be the thirty thousand, which is the difference between the number of the tribe of Judah here and what corresponds to it in the Book of Chronicles.

entries.section: (2) God's punishment

paragraphs.text: David felt his fault and regretted the command he had issued to carry out the numbering, and he confessed to the Lord that what he had done was folly without justification, and he began to beseech the Lord to forgive him this fault. This shows an important trait in David, namely repentance, by which he obtains God's favor and mercy whatever his sins may be. It also shows that the numbering was not from God, because David did not rejoice but was grieved, and his heart smote him.
We often rush after our personal desires and make decisions that we later regret. Let us be patient in our choices so that we do not fall into error and then regret and grieve.

entries.section: (2) God's punishment

paragraphs.text: David spent the night weeping, regretting his fault, praying to the Lord to pardon him and forgive him, and in the morning of the next day Gad the prophet came to him with a message from the Lord.

entries.section: (2) God's punishment

paragraphs.text: The message of the Lord that Gad the prophet carried to David was to give him a choice among three punishments, one of which the Lord must bring upon him. This shows God's justice in punishing sin, and at the same time His mercy in giving David a choice of one of the punishments.

entries.section: (2) God's punishment

paragraphs.text: Gad conveyed to David the text of the message, and the three punishments among which he gave David the choice were: the first: that there be a famine in the land lasting seven years.
The second: that his enemies pursue him for three months while he flees before them.
The third: that the Lord strike the people with a pestilence for three days.

It is stated in the Book of Chronicles (1 Chr 21:12) that the famine in the first punishment was for three years and not seven years as it appears here. The explanation of this difference is that the Book of Chronicles did not include the period that precedes the beginning of the famine and follows its end, which is usually lighter in severity than the middle period, in which the intensity of the famine is at its height.

entries.section: (2) God's punishment

paragraphs.text: David was perplexed and felt that he had put himself in a predicament from which there was no escape. After thinking, he chose one of the three things in which he would be under the Lord's vast mercy, and not fall into the choice that would put him at the mercy of his enemies. For the Lord wounds and binds up, crushes and His hands heal, disciplines and then has compassion, whereas man is hard of heart and strikes without mercy.

entries.section: (2) God's punishment

paragraphs.text: To the appointed time: most likely the time of offering the evening sacrifice, which is offered every day in the house of the Lord. David's choice was to be in the hand of God, that is, the first punishment or the third, which is "the pestilence." So the Lord carried out the third punishment and destroyed by the pestilence 70 thousand from all the tribes, from the farthest north to the farthest south. They kept falling throughout the day, from the morning until the time of the daily evening offering (1 Kgs 18:29). The punishment that came upon them treats the problem of the pride of David and the people in the greatness of their number, for behold, their number is diminished so that they might not be proud but rely on God alone.

entries.section: (2) God's punishment

paragraphs.text: Threshingfloor: that is, a threshing place, a place for gathering and storing the produce of the land.

Araunah the Jebusite: the name "Araunah" appears in Samuel and "Ornan" in Chronicles, and the two names are for one person who owned a threshingfloor on Mount Moriah, east of Jerusalem. David bought it from him to offer burnt offerings on it, and it is the same mountain on which Solomon's Temple was built (1 Chr 21). One of the angels, the one charged with carrying out the punishment, continued in it until the turn came to Jerusalem to destroy its inhabitants. But the Lord had compassion on "the city of the great King" and accepted the supplications of its people and their repentance, and He commanded the angel to stop the plague, saying it was enough for those who had died up to that time, who, as in the preceding verse, were 70 thousand.

When the command was given to the angel to stop the plague, he was at that time at a granary owned by a man of Jebusite origin who had embraced Judaism. This confirms God's mercy and compassion on David and his repentant people who cried out to Him, so He stopped the plague.

entries.section: (3) The building of the altar and the lifting of the plague

paragraphs.text: David saw the angel charged with carrying out the plague, and he grieved greatly and suffered, confessing his fault once again, and he acknowledged that his people had not sinned: if he deserved the punishment, these had not shared his fault. As a faithful shepherd who has compassion on his flock, he asked the Lord not to destroy his people but to destroy him and his father's house in place of the innocent people. This shows how much David took responsibility for his fault, although the people truly shared with him the feeling of pride in the greatness of their number and the boasting of their strength. But he wanted to redeem his people by bearing the punishment himself and his household in place of the people, after the likeness of Christ the Redeemer. Yet God punished all, because all had sinned.

entries.section: (3) The building of the altar and the lifting of the plague

paragraphs.text: The Lord answered the prayers of David and the entreaties of his people, and He had mercy on them and sent Gad to David to tell him to go up to Mount Moriah and build there an altar to the Lord on the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite, and to offer sacrifices to the Lord as an atonement for himself and for the people. The Book of Chronicles (1 Chr 21:20) states that God opened the eyes of Araunah the Jebusite and he saw the angel of the Lord, and so he sensed the seriousness of the matter and the coming of King David to him.

The Lord does not rejoice in punishing His children, but feels their afflictions and grieves for what befalls them, as Isaiah the prophet says: "In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them" (Isa 63:9). Let us always turn to God, asking for His many mercies and His countless kindnesses.

entries.section: (3) The building of the altar and the lifting of the plague

paragraphs.text: David carried out the command of the Lord that had come to him by the mouth of Gad the prophet, and came to the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite. Araunah saw the king and his men coming toward him, so he went out to meet him and bowed down before him as an expression of his respect for him.

entries.section: (3) The building of the altar and the lifting of the plague

paragraphs.text: Araunah asked David the reason for his coming to him, and David told him that it was for the purpose of buying his threshingfloor in order to build on it an altar to the Lord on which to offer sacrifices, so that the plague would be stayed from the people.

entries.section: (3) The building of the altar and the lifting of the plague

paragraphs.text: Araunah was a generous man who showed his readiness to give up ownership of the threshingfloor to the king so that he might offer on it whatever sacrifices he wished. He even wanted to donate the sacrifices and the wooden threshing instruments used in threshing, for David to use as fuel on the altar. All this Araunah placed at the king's disposal without payment. Araunah prayed for the king that the Lord would accept from him the offerings he presented to Him, and would answer his prayer and lift the plague from the people. Because of Araunah's love, which appeared in his welcoming the king to build the altar on his land and his readiness to give his animals and the threshing instruments to help in offering the sacrifice, God gave him the grace not only that the plague be stayed at his threshingfloor but also that the altar be built on his land, and perhaps he also saw the destroying angel as he stopped the plague. For God blesses everyone whose heart is full of love and giving.

entries.section: (3) The building of the altar and the lifting of the plague

paragraphs.text: The shekel: weighs about 1 gram.

David refused to accept this free offer from Araunah, because he did not wish to offer burnt offerings that were not from his own possessions and at the expense of another, but wanted the honoring of the Lord to be from his own money. In keeping with the king's determination, Araunah agreed to sell the threshingfloor and the oxen and their implements to the king for 50 shekels of silver, which he received from the king (750 grams of silver), and this was the suitable price at that time.

entries.section: (3) The building of the altar and the lifting of the plague

paragraphs.text: David built the altar and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings to the Lord, and the Lord accepted those offerings in answer to David's prayers for his people. The Book of Chronicles (1 Chr 21:26) states that fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offerings as a sign of their acceptance by the Lord. The plague was stayed from the people, and from that day David began to offer his sacrifices and the sacrifices of his people in that place.

Mount Moriah, on which David offered his sacrifice in the field of Araunah the Jebusite, is the same place where Abraham long before offered his son Isaac as a sacrifice (Gen 22), and there is a Jewish tradition that it is the same place where the Lord of glory Jesus Christ was crucified. The three events all revolve around the idea of redemption, which was accomplished on the Cross.

Thank God who loved you and redeemed you on the Cross, and whose mercies are open to you to forgive all your sins when you come to Him repentant. So hold fast to confession and Holy Communion that you may enjoy God's work in you, and do not despair however many your sins may be.

The life of David - the youngest, the eighth son of Jesse, and the meaning of his name is beloved (1 Sam 16:10, 11, 17:13-14). He lived in Bethlehem and tended his father's sheep, and he was fair in appearance and very courageous (1 Sam 17:

34-36.) - Samuel anointed him king, and that was in the year 1065 B.C. (1 Sam 16). - Saul summoned him to play the harp for him so that the unclean spirit that had come upon him would depart from him (1 Sam 16:19-23). - He killed Goliath, and the women cheered for him more than for Saul, so the latter was enraged (1 Sam 17, 18). - He killed two hundred Philistines as a dowry for Michal the daughter of Saul and then married her (1 Sam 18). - He became a friend of Jonathan the son of Saul, then Saul tried to kill him, especially after David's victory over the Philistines, and Jonathan interceded to prevent him (1 Sam 19). -
